title: Statistical Plots
text:
A statistical plot shows an estimate together with its uncertainty, or checks a model, instead of only the raw data. Each section below answers one question and names what to read in the plot.
library(tidyverse); library(broom); library(patchwork)
ncd <- read_csv("../data/ncd_survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")),
         education = factor(education, levels = c("No schooling", "Primary", "Secondary", "Graduate+")))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Categorical: proportions with confidence intervals

prev <- ncd |> filter(!is.na(education)) |> group_by(education) |>
  summarise(x = sum(htn), n = n()) |>
  mutate(p = x / n,
         lo = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) prop.test(x, n)$conf.int[1]),
         hi = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) prop.test(x, n)$conf.int[2]))
ggplot(prev, aes(x = education, y = p)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = "#2c3e50") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), y = 0.05, size = 3.5, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Adults with hypertension (95% CI)", title = "A proportion is an estimate: show its CI")








prop.test() gives a confidence interval for each proportion. The smallest group (no schooling) has the widest interval: read the interval, not only the point.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Continuous: density with quantile shading, histogram with a fitted curve
text:
Continuous: density with quantile shading, histogram with a fitted curve

q <- quantile(ncd$sbp, c(0.25, 0.75))
d <- density(ncd$sbp); dd <- tibble(x = d$x, y = d$y)
p1 <- ggplot(dd, aes(x, y)) + geom_line() +
  geom_area(data = filter(dd, x >= q[1], x <= q[2]), fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Density", title = "Middle 50% shaded")
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 5, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mean(ncd$sbp), sd = sd(ncd$sbp)), colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = NULL, title = "Normal curve (same mean, SD)")
p1 + p2








The shaded band is the interquartile range (120 to 143 mmHg). The red curve is what a normal distribution with the same mean and SD would look like: here the data follow it closely, with a slightly longer right tail.

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Category vs category: chi-square residuals

tab <- table(ncd$phys_act, ncd$tobacco)
ct <- chisq.test(tab)
as.data.frame(ct$stdres) |> setNames(c("phys_act", "tobacco", "residual")) |>
  ggplot(aes(tobacco, phys_act, fill = residual)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", residual))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3498db", high = "#e74c3c", limits = c(-3, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Tobacco use", y = "Physical activity", fill = "Std. residual",
       title = sprintf("Chi-square p = %.2f: which cells drive it?", ct$p.value))








A standardised residual compares each cell with what independence predicts: beyond about ±2 the cell contributes noticeably. Here no cell comes close, matching the large p-value.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Continuous vs continuous: regression line, correlation matrix, residuals
text:
Continuous vs continuous: regression line, correlation matrix, residuals

m <- lm(sbp ~ bmi, data = ncd)
ggplot(ncd, aes(bmi, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#e74c3c") +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 185, hjust = 0, size = 4,
           label = sprintf("SBP = %.0f + %.2f × BMI\nr = %.2f", coef(m)[1], coef(m)[2], cor(ncd$bmi, ncd$sbp, use = "complete.obs"))) +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "The band is the CI of the mean, not of individuals")









library(ggcorrplot)
r <- cor(select(ncd, age, bmi, waist, salt_g, sbp, dbp), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ggcorrplot(r, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 3.5, colors = c("#3498db", "white", "#e74c3c"),
           title = "Pairwise correlations")








BMI and waist are almost the same measurement (r close to 1): putting both in one model causes collinearity.

a <- augment(m)
p1 <- ggplot(a, aes(.fitted, .resid)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = "#e74c3c") + labs(x = "Fitted SBP", y = "Residual", title = "Residuals vs fitted")
p2 <- ggplot(a, aes(sample = .resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.3) + stat_qq_line(colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Residual quantile", title = "Normal Q-Q")
p1 + p2








A flat smooth around zero (no curve, no funnel) and points near the Q-Q line support a straight-line model with roughly normal residuals.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Visualising model output: a coefficient plot
text:
Visualising model output: a coefficient plot

m2 <- lm(sbp ~ age + sex + bmi + salt_g + tobacco + phys_act, data = ncd)
tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = fct_reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = "#2c3e50") +
  labs(x = "Difference in systolic BP (mmHg), 95% CI", y = NULL, title = "Adjusted coefficients")








Each row is one coefficient with its 95% CI; intervals crossing the dashed line at 0 are compatible with no difference. Note that coefficients for different units (per year, per kg/m², per category) are not comparable in size.

title: Statistical Plots
section: Category vs continuous: notched box and violin with median and IQR
text:
Category vs continuous: notched box and violin with median and IQR

tt <- t.test(sbp ~ sex, data = ncd)
p1 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(sex, sbp)) + geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, fill = "grey85") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = sprintf("Welch t-test p = %.3f", tt$p.value))
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) + geom_violin(fill = "grey90") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, fun.min = \(x) quantile(x, 0.25), fun.max = \(x) quantile(x, 0.75), colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = NULL, title = "Median and IQR")
p1 + p2








The notch is a rough 95% interval for the median; notches that do not overlap suggest the medians differ. Print the actual test (here in the title) rather than stars.

title: Statistical Plots
Statistical Plots
section: Map: a choropleth with statistical class breaks
text:
Map: a choropleth with statistical class breaks

library(sf)
blocks <- st_read("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
br <- quantile(blocks$dengue_per_100k, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2))
blocks$class <- cut(blocks$dengue_per_100k, breaks = br, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 3)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "OrRd", name = "Per 100,000\n(quintiles)") +
  labs(title = "Five classes with the same number of blocks") + theme_void()








Quintile breaks put the same number of areas in each colour; equal-interval breaks would leave most blocks in one class. State the method in the caption: the choice of breaks changes the story a map tells.

title: Statistical Plots
text:
Checklist








Show
With
Read




A proportion or mean
point + 95% CI
the interval, with the n


A distribution
density/histogram + quantiles or a fitted curve
shape, tails, the middle 50%


A table of counts
standardised residuals
cells beyond ±2


A relationship
scatter + regression line + CI
slope, r, the band is for the mean


A model
residual plots, coefficient plot
patterns in residuals; CIs crossing 0


Groups
notched box, violin + median/IQR
overlap; the test, not stars


Seasonal counts
decomposition
trend vs season vs remainder


Areas
choropleth with stated breaks
the break method

A cell’s standardised chi-square residual is +2.6. What does it suggest?

On a coefficient plot, a 95% CI crosses 0. What does that mean?

The effect is exactly zero in the population
The data are consistent with no effect
The model failed to converge for that term
The variable should be removed from the data

title: Interactive Plots
text:
A static figure is right for a paper. An interactive one helps when readers explore: hover for the exact value of one point, zoom into a busy period, switch groups on and off, or click a district on a map. Interactive figures work in HTML output (a Quarto web page, a dashboard, a Shiny app); in PDF or Word they are not available, so keep a static version for the paper.
This page uses three packages, each an htmlwidget that Quarto embeds in the page: plotly (charts), DT (tables) and leaflet (maps), plus crosstalk to link them. Data: the NCD survey (data/ncd_survey.csv) and the district blocks of the GIS track.
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1],
                show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")))

title: Interactive Plots
text:
1. Any ggplot, made interactive: ggplotly()
Build the plot as usual, then pass it to ggplotly(). The text aesthetic sets what the tooltip shows.

p <- ggplot(ncd, aes(age, sbp, colour = sex,
                     text = paste0("id ", id, "<br>age ", age, "<br>SBP ", sbp, " mmHg<br>BMI ", bmi))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", colour = NULL)
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Hover a point to read its values; drag to zoom; double-click to reset.
Click a legend entry to hide that group, double-click to show it alone.
tooltip = "text" limits the tooltip to the text you wrote; the default lists every aesthetic.

title: Interactive Plots
section: 2. Categories: bars and boxes with hover labels
text:
2. Categories: bars and boxes with hover labels

by_act <- ncd |> group_by(phys_act) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pct = round(100 * mean(htn), 1))
p <- ggplot(by_act, aes(phys_act, pct, text = paste0(pct, "% of ", n, " people"))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Hypertension (%)")
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






ggplotly(ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
           labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"))





The box tooltip gives the median, quartiles and fences of each group: useful in a meeting, where nobody can read values off a static axis.

title: Interactive Plots
section: 3. Native plotly: a histogram with a group switch
text:
3. Native plotly: a histogram with a group switch
plot_ly() builds charts directly. Here two overlaid histograms; click a legend entry to compare one sex at a time.

plot_ly(ncd, x = ~bmi, color = ~sex, type = "histogram", alpha = 0.6, nbinsx = 30) |>
  layout(barmode = "overlay", xaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"), yaxis = list(title = "People"))

title: Interactive Plots
section: 4. Time: a line with a range slider
text:
4. Time: a line with a range slider

dengue <- read_csv(c("../data/dengue_wards.csv", "data/dengue_wards.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/dengue_wards.csv", "data/dengue_wards.csv"))][1],
                   show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  group_by(date) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain_mm = mean(rain_mm))
plot_ly(dengue, x = ~date, y = ~cases, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Dengue cases") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = NULL, rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)), yaxis = list(title = "Cases per month"))





Drag the ends of the slider to zoom into one season; the y-axis keeps its scale, so seasons stay comparable.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
5. A searchable table: DT

library(DT)
ncd |> select(id, village, age, sex, bmi, sbp, dbp, htn) |>
  datatable(rownames = FALSE, filter = "top", options = list(pageLength = 5))






filter = "top" adds a filter box above each column; sort by clicking a header.
Use it for lists readers look things up in (facilities, villages); not as a substitute for a summary table.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
6. Linked views: crosstalk
crosstalk::SharedData lets two widgets use the same rows: select points in the scatter plot and the table shows only those people.

library(crosstalk)
shared <- SharedData$new(ncd |> select(id, age, sex, sbp, dbp, bmi))
bscols(widths = c(6, 6),
       plot_ly(shared, x = ~dbp, y = ~sbp, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", alpha = 0.5) |>
         layout(xaxis = list(title = "Diastolic BP"), yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP")) |>
         highlight(on = "plotly_selected", off = "plotly_deselect"),
       datatable(shared, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 6, dom = "tp")))















Choose the box select tool (top right of the plot), drag over the points with high systolic BP, and the table lists who they are. This works in a static HTML page: no server is needed.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
7. Maps: leaflet

library(leaflet); library(sf)
blocks <- st_read(c("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", "data/gis/district_blocks.geojson")[file.exists(c("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", "data/gis/district_blocks.geojson"))][1],
                  quiet = TRUE)
pal <- colorNumeric("YlOrRd", blocks$dengue_per_100k)
leaflet(blocks) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) |>
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(dengue_per_100k), fillOpacity = 0.8, color = "white", weight = 1,
              label = ~block_name,
              popup = ~paste0("<b>", block_name, "</b><br>Population: ", format(population, big.mark = ","),
                              "<br>Dengue: ", dengue_per_100k, " per 100,000")) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~dengue_per_100k, title = "Dengue per 100k")






Hover a block for its name; click it for the popup.
The base map tiles load from the internet; the shaded blocks do not need a connection.
Mapping rules (class breaks, rates rather than counts) are in the GIS track.

title: Interactive Plots
text:
When to use interactivity







Use it when
Avoid it when




Readers explore many points or groups
The figure has one message: a static plot says it faster


Exact values matter on hover
The output is PDF, Word or print


Dashboards, teaching, data checking
Hiding information behind a hover that every reader needs









TipChecklist




Keep a static version for the paper; the interactive one goes in the supplement or a web appendix.
Write the tooltip yourself: units, rounding, the n.
Large data (more than about 50,000 points) makes the page slow: summarise first, or use toWebGL().
Save a widget as its own file with htmlwidgets::saveWidget(widget, "fig.html").
Other packages: ggiraph (interactive ggplot2 layers), highcharter, echarts4r; Shiny when a reader should change the analysis, not just the view.

title: Iteration: Doing the Same Thing Many Times
text:
Medical analyses repeat: the same summary for 12 variables, the same test for 5 outcomes, the same plot for each district. Copy-pasting code 12 times is how mistakes get in (one copy keeps an old variable name). This page shows four safer ways, from simplest to most general. Data: the NCD survey (data/ncd_survey.csv).

library(tidyverse)
ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE)




ncd |> summarise(across(c(sbp, dbp, bmi), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
    sbp   dbp   bmi
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  132.  59.7  23.0



across(columns, function) applies the function to each column inside summarise() or mutate().
\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) is a small unnamed function; x stands for “the column”.
Pick columns by name, c(a, b), or by type, where(is.numeric).
Several functions at once, with names:


ncd |> summarise(across(c(sbp, bmi), list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd = \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))))

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  sbp_mean sbp_sd bmi_mean bmi_sd
     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1     132.   16.8     23.0   3.58



ncd |> mutate(across(c(sbp, dbp), \(x) x / 10)) |> select(sbp, dbp) |> head(3)    # the same change to two columns

# A tibble: 3 × 2
    sbp   dbp
  <dbl> <dbl>
1  13.1   5.7
2  13.5   6.1
3  12.7   5.7






for (v in c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")) {
  cat(v, ": mean", round(mean(ncd[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), 1), "\n")
}

sbp : mean 132.3 
dbp : mean 59.7 
bmi : mean 23 



for (v in <items>) { <what to do> } runs the block once for each item, and v holds the current item.
ncd[[v]] picks the column whose name is stored in v (ncd$v would look for a column called “v”).
A loop prints or stores results; it only shows output if you ask (print(), cat()).
A loop that adds up:


total <- 0
for (i in 1:4) total <- total + i
total

[1] 10






sapply(ncd[c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")], mean, na.rm = TRUE)       # a named vector of means

      sbp       dbp       bmi 
132.28500  59.68833  22.95258 



# one t-test per outcome, results kept in a tidy table
outcomes <- c("sbp", "dbp", "bmi")
map_dfr(outcomes, \(y) {
  t <- t.test(reformulate("sex", y), data = ncd)
  tibble(outcome = y, difference = unname(diff(rev(t$estimate))), p = t$p.value)
})

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  outcome difference       p
  <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>
1 sbp         -3.78  0.00595
2 dbp         -1.61  0.0385 
3 bmi          0.387 0.193  



map() / sapply() return one result per item, collected for you: no empty vector to grow by hand.
reformulate("sex", y) builds the formula y ~ sex from text, so the loop can change the outcome.
map_dfr() stacks tibbles into one table; map_dbl() returns numbers.





pct_above <- function(x, cut) {
  mean(x >= cut, na.rm = TRUE) * 100      # the last value is returned
}
pct_above(ncd$sbp, 140)

[1] 32

pct_above(ncd$bmi, 30)

[1] 2.405498



A function has arguments (x, cut), a body in { }, and returns its last expression.
Write one when you copy the same 3 or more lines twice. Name it for what it does.
Test it on a case where you know the answer: pct_above(c(1, 5, 10, 20), 10) should be 50.










Warning




Growing a vector inside a loop (res <- c(res, new)) is slow and error-prone; use sapply() / map().
Forgetting na.rm = TRUE inside the function you repeat: one NA turns every result into NA.
ncd$v vs ncd[[v]]: with the variable name in v, use [[ ]].
Overwriting the original data in a loop; save results to a new object.
Many tests at once means many p-values: see multiple testing on the Statistical Tests page.

Overwriting the original data in a loop; save results to a new object.
Many tests at once means many p-values: see multiple testing on the Statistical Tests page.

title: Iteration: Doing the Same Thing Many Times
text:
Self-check quiz

What does mutate(across(c(sbp, dbp), \(x) x / 10)) do?

Creates one new column called x
Divides both columns by 10
Divides only the first column by 10
Returns the mean of the two columns



v <- "sbp". Which code returns the sbp column of ncd?

ncd$v
ncd["v"]
ncd$"v"
ncd[[v]]



Why use map_dfr() or sapply() rather than growing a vector with res <- c(res, new) in a loop?

They save every result to a file on the disk
They return one result per item, collected
They give each test a smaller p-value
They remove missing values for you



pct_above <- function(x, cut) mean(x >= cut, na.rm = TRUE) * 100. What does pct_above(c(1, 5, 10, 20), 10) return?

text:
Creating Hypertension Categories

Question: Classify baseline BP using clinical guidelines




Show the code
bp_with_category <- bp_clean |> 
  mutate(
    bp_category = case_when(
      sys_bp_0m < 120 & dia_bp_0m < 80 ~ "Normal",
      sys_bp_0m >= 120 & sys_bp_0m < 130 & dia_bp_0m < 80 ~ "Elevated",
      (sys_bp_0m >= 130 & sys_bp_0m < 140) | 
        (dia_bp_0m >= 80 & dia_bp_0m < 90) ~ "Stage 1",
      sys_bp_0m >= 140 | dia_bp_0m >= 90 ~ "Stage 2"
    )
  )

Dates are complex (leap years, time zones, daylight savings)

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Age Calculation from Dates

Question: Calculate age from birthdate




Show the code
# Example with made-up birthdates
example_data <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:3,
  birthdate = ymd(c("1980-05-15", "1965-12-20", "1990-03-08")),
  visit_date = ymd(c("2024-01-15", "2024-01-15", "2024-01-15"))
)

  mutate(
    age_years = interval(birthdate, visit_date) / years(1),
    age_months = interval(birthdate, visit_date) / months(1)
  )

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text: The galleries show what each chart type is. This page shows the last step: turning a correct chart into a figure that tells one message, the kind of work you see collected on sites such as Dataviz Inspiration and the R Graph Gallery. Every figure uses a dataset from this course and follows the caveat flash cards: a title that states the finding, direct labels instead of legends, grey for context and one accent colour for the message. Open Show the code under each figure to see how.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
section: 1. A dumbbell instead of grouped bars
text:
1. A dumbbell instead of grouped bars


Show the code
bp <- readxl::read_excel(dat("PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx"))
db <- bp |>
  group_by(Region, TreatmentGroup) |>
  summarise(n = n(), base = mean(SysBP_0m), m6 = mean(SysBP_6m), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(row = fct_rev(paste0(Region, " · ", TreatmentGroup, " (n = ", n, ")")),
         change = m6 - base)
ggplot(db, aes(y = row)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = base, xend = m6, yend = row), colour = grey, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = base), colour = "grey55", size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = m6, colour = TreatmentGroup), size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = pmin(base, m6) - 0.6, label = if_else(abs(change) < 0.5, "0", sprintf("%+.0f", change)), colour = TreatmentGroup),
            hjust = 1, size = 3.8, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey45", Intervention = accent), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(118, 147), breaks = seq(120, 145, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP fell by about 10 mmHg with the intervention, in every region",
       subtitle = "Mean systolic BP at baseline (grey) and at 6 months (coloured); number = change in mmHg",
       x = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)", y = NULL,
       caption = "Data: simulated blood-pressure trial, 200 patients (data/README.md)") +
  theme_showcase() + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Why it works: two values per group become one line each, so the change is read directly; the arms differ by colour and the number prints the effect. Cards: Two values per group? Try a dumbbell · Show the sample size · Make the title say something.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text:
2. A ranking with uncertainty


Show the code
ncd <- read_csv(dat("ncd_survey.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
overall <- mean(ncd$htn)
vil <- ncd |> group_by(village) |>
  summarise(n = n(), x = sum(htn), p = x / n, .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) binom.test(x, n)$conf.int[1]),
         hi = map2_dbl(x, n, \(x, n) binom.test(x, n)$conf.int[2]),
         above = lo > overall,
         village = fct_reorder(paste0(village, " (", n, ")"), p))
ggplot(vil, aes(p, village, colour = above)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = overall + 0.005, y = levels(vil$village)[1], label = sprintf("survey average %.0f%%", 100 * overall),
           hjust = 0, vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0, orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey55", `TRUE` = accent), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.8)) +
  labs(title = if (sum(vil$above) == 1) "Only one of 20 villages is clearly above the survey average" else
                 sprintf("Only %d of 20 villages are clearly above the survey average", sum(vil$above)),
       subtitle = "Adults with hypertension, % with 95% confidence interval (n per village in brackets)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Data: NCD survey, 600 adults in 20 villages (simulated)") +
  theme_showcase() + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Why it works: sorted, so the ranking is free; the intervals stop readers over-reading a 53% from 30 people; the highlight only goes to villages that are clearly above average. Cards: Sort your bar chart · Show the sample size · Use colour on purpose.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text:
3. Small multiples instead of spaghetti


Show the code
dengue <- read_csv(dat("dengue_wards.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(date = seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 36)[month_index],
         rate = cases / population * 1e5)
ord <- dengue |> group_by(ward) |> summarise(tot = sum(cases) / first(population) * 1e5, slum = first(slum)) |>
  mutate(lab = paste0(ward, if_else(slum == 1, " · slum", ""))) |> arrange(desc(tot))
dd <- dengue |> left_join(ord, by = "ward") |> mutate(lab = factor(lab, ord$lab))
ggplot(dd, aes(date, rate)) +
  geom_line(data = rename(dd, other = lab), aes(group = other), colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 6) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(c("2023-07-01", "2024-07-01", "2025-07-01")), date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "Every ward peaks each monsoon; the highest burdens are mostly in slum wards",
       subtitle = "Monthly dengue cases per 100,000, 2023–2025; each panel highlights one ward over the other 29 (grey), ordered by total incidence",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Data: 30 city wards (simulated, counts workshop)") +
  theme_showcase(11) + theme(strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"), panel.spacing = unit(0.8, "lines"))









Why it works: thirty lines on one panel are unreadable; here each ward is legible and the grey background keeps the comparison. Panels are sorted by burden, and the shared y-axis keeps them comparable. Cards: The spaghetti plot · Share the y-axis · Reorder.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text:
4. An ordered heat map


Show the code
ggplot(dd, aes(date, fct_rev(factor(ward, ord$ward)), fill = rate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1, name = "Cases per 100,000",
                       guide = guide_colourbar(barwidth = 12, barheight = 0.6, title.position = "top")) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = seq(as.Date("2023-06-01"), as.Date("2025-06-01"), by = "6 months"),
               date_labels = "%b %Y", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Three monsoon seasons; W17 and W27 are in the top four wards every year",
       subtitle = "Monthly dengue cases per 100,000; wards ordered by total incidence",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, caption = "Data: 30 city wards (simulated)") +
  theme_showcase(11) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank())









Why it works: the rows are ordered by burden, so structure appears (seasons as columns, high wards on top); a sequential palette shows “more” as darker. Cards: Reorder your heat map · Numbers need a sequential palette.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
section: 5. Linked panels on a shared time axis
text:
5. Linked panels on a shared time axis


Show the code
monthly <- dengue |> group_by(date) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain = mean(rain_mm))
r0 <- cor(monthly$cases, monthly$rain)
r1 <- cor(monthly$cases[-1], monthly$rain[-36])          # cases vs last month's rain
p_rain <- ggplot(monthly, aes(date, rain)) + geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 25) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rain (mm)") + theme_showcase(11) + theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())
p_dengue <- ggplot(monthly, aes(date, cases)) + geom_line(colour = accent, linewidth = 1) + geom_point(colour = accent, size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Dengue cases") + theme_showcase(11)
p_rain / p_dengue + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.6)) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Dengue rises and falls with the monsoon rain",
                  subtitle = sprintf("Monthly rainfall (mean of wards) and dengue cases (all wards)\nCorrelation of cases with the same month's rain r = %.2f; with last month's rain r = %.2f", r0, r1),
                  caption = "Data: 30 city wards (simulated)", theme = theme_showcase())









Why it works: two series in different units are not forced onto a dual axis; the panels share the x-axis and are stacked, so the timing of the two can be compared month by month. Cards: Be wary of two y-axes · Link charts that share an axis.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text:
6. Distributions, many groups at once


Show the code
ridge <- ncd |> mutate(age_band = cut(age, c(29, 39, 49, 59, 69), labels = c("30–39", "40–49", "50–59", "60–69")))
share <- ridge |> group_by(age_band) |> summarise(n = n(), hi = mean(sbp >= 140))
ggplot(ridge, aes(sbp, age_band)) +
  geom_density_ridges(fill = base_col, alpha = 0.75, colour = "white", scale = 1.15, quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 140, linetype = 2, colour = accent) +
  geom_text(data = share, aes(x = 205, y = age_band, label = sprintf("%.0f%% ≥ 140 (n = %d)", 100 * hi, n)),
            hjust = 1, vjust = -1.2, size = 3.5, colour = "grey25") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 210)) +
  labs(title = "Systolic BP shifts upward with every decade of age",
       subtitle = "Distribution of systolic BP by age band; white line = median, dashed red line = 140 mmHg",
       x = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)", y = NULL, caption = "Data: NCD survey, 600 adults (simulated)") +
  theme_showcase()









Why it works: four overlapping densities would tangle; ridgelines keep each visible with the medians marked and the share above the threshold printed beside it. Cards: Too many distributions at once · Annotation is crucial.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
section: 7. A map that shows rates, with its legend as a histogram
text:
7. A map that shows rates, with its legend as a histogram


Show the code
blocks <- st_read(dat("gis/district_blocks.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |> st_transform(32644)
fac <- read_csv(dat("gis/facilities.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(type %in% c("PHC", "CHC")) |> st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644)
brks <- unname(quantile(blocks$dengue_per_100k, seq(0, 1, 0.2)))
blocks <- blocks |> mutate(cls = cut(dengue_per_100k, brks, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 4))
pal <- setNames(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(5, "YlOrRd"), levels(blocks$cls))
m <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = blocks, aes(fill = cls), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = fac, shape = 17, size = 2, colour = "grey10") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") + theme_void()
h <- ggplot(st_drop_geometry(blocks), aes(dengue_per_100k)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = after_stat(cut(x, brks, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 4))),
                 bins = 20, colour = "white") +        # each bar coloured by the class of its centre
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Dengue per 100,000", y = "Blocks") + theme_showcase(10)
m + h + plot_layout(widths = c(2.2, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(title = "High dengue incidence clusters in one part of the district",
                  subtitle = "Dengue cases per 100,000 by block (quintiles); triangles = PHC/CHC. The histogram is the legend.",
                  caption = "Data: synthetic district of 79 blocks (gis/make_gis_data.R)", theme = theme_showcase())









Why it works: rates, not counts; quintile classes stated; the histogram-legend shows how many blocks fall in each colour. Whether the cluster is real is a test, not a picture: see Global Moran’s I. Cards: Normalise your maps · Use colour on purpose.

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text:
Your final output
Make one finished figure from your own data (or a course dataset) as the capstone of the Data Visualization track.

Ask one question and write the answer as the title, in one sentence.
Choose the chart with Matching Data to Plots; sketch it on paper first.
Build it in ggplot2; then go through the caveat flash cards and fix every card that applies.
Finish it: one accent colour, direct labels, units on the axes, n and source in the caption, alt text.
Export it at the journal’s size and resolution (ggsave(..., width = 18, units = "cm", dpi = 600)), and a static version if you also make an interactive one.

For ideas, browse the hundreds of examples on Dataviz Inspiration and the R Graph Gallery: pick one whose idea fits your question, and rebuild the idea with your data, not the design with theirs.






TipChecklist before you call it finished




Could someone who reads only the title state the finding?
Is every colour doing a job? Is there a legend you could replace with labels?
Are the axes honest (bars from zero, shared scales where panels are compared)?
Are the n, the units, the source and the uncertainty on the figure?
Does it work in greyscale and for colour-blind readers?

title: Showcase: From Chart to Figure
text:
Self-check quiz

In figure 2, several villages have percentages well above the average. Why is only one of them red?

Red marks the village with the most adults surveyed in it
Its whole confidence interval lies above the average
Red marks villages above 50%, a fixed cut-off
Red is assigned at random to show the palette



Figure 5 shows rainfall and dengue in two stacked panels. Why not one chart with two y-axes?

ggplot2 cannot draw a second y-axis on one plot
The two series are measured in the same units
Two axes can be scaled to suggest any relationship
Stacked panels need less ink than a single combined panel



What makes a figure title like ‘Dengue rises and falls with the monsoon rain’ better than ‘Dengue and rainfall’?

It is shorter, so it fits above the plot on a slide
It states the message the reader should take away
It avoids naming the variables that are plotted
Journals require a full sentence as the title


Your score:  (first attempt counts)

Choropleth Map - Code

Purpose: Show values across geographic regions using color
Goal: 🟣 Geographic + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Get US state map data
us_states <- map_data("state")

# Create region to state mapping (simplified for demonstration)
region_states <- data.frame(
  region_name = c("North", "South", "East", "West"),
  states = c("new york,pennsylvania,ohio,michigan",
            "texas,florida,georgia,alabama",
            "massachusetts,connecticut,rhode island,maine",
            "california,oregon,washington,nevada")
)

# Expand and join
state_regions <- region_states %>%
  separate_rows(states, sep = ",") %>%
  rename(region_lower = states)

# Join with map data
map_data_full <- us_states %>%
  left_join(state_regions, by = c("region" = "region_lower")) %>%
  left_join(region_summary, by = c("region_name" = "Region"))

# Create choropleth map
ggplot(map_data_full, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = mean_bp)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", size = 0.3) +
  coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 45) +  # Albers projection
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "plasma",
    name = "Mean Systolic BP\n(mmHg)",
    na.value = "gray90",
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      barwidth = 1.5,
      barheight = 15,
      title.position = "top"
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Average Blood Pressure by Region",
       subtitle = "Darker colors indicate higher blood pressure",
       caption = "Data: PublicHealth BP Dataset") +
  theme_map()

Point/Bubble Map - Code

Purpose: Show individual locations with value-sized markers
Goal: 🟣 Geographic + 🟡 Distribution


Code
# Create sample patient locations (simulated for demonstration)
set.seed(123)
patient_locations <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(SysBP_0m)) %>%
  mutate(
    # Simulate coordinates within regions
    lat = case_when(
      Region == "North" ~ runif(n(), 40, 45),
      Region == "South" ~ runif(n(), 30, 35),
      Region == "East" ~ runif(n(), 39, 43),
      Region == "West" ~ runif(n(), 35, 42)
    ),
    lon = case_when(
      Region == "North" ~ runif(n(), -85, -75),
      Region == "South" ~ runif(n(), -100, -80),
      Region == "East" ~ runif(n(), -75, -70),
      Region == "West" ~ runif(n(), -125, -115)
    ),
    hypertensive = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140, "Yes", "No")
  ) %>%
  sample_n(200)  # Sample for clarity

# Create point map
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = us_states, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "white", color = "gray70") +
  geom_point(data = patient_locations,
            aes(x = lon, y = lat, color = hypertensive, size = SysBP_0m),
            alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_map("albers", lat0 = 39, lat1 = 45) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("No" = "#00A087", "Yes" = "#DC0000"),
                    name = "Hypertensive") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 6), name = "Systolic BP\n(mmHg)") +
  labs(title = "Patient Locations by Blood Pressure Status",
       subtitle = "Point size = BP value | Color = Hypertension status (≥140 mmHg)",
       caption = "Sample of 200 patients") +
  theme_map()

# Load required packages

  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m),
               names_to = "TimePoint",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Month = case_when(
    TimePoint == "SysBP_0m" ~ 0,
    TimePoint == "SysBP_3m" ~ 3,
    TimePoint == "SysBP_6m" ~ 6
  ))

# Create theme
theme_custom <- function() {
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),

}

Smoothed Trend with LOESS - Code

Purpose: Show underlying trend while reducing noise
Goal: 🔵 Evolution


Code
# Calculate mean BP by treatment group over time
trend_data <- time_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP)) %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bp = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_bp = sd(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Create smoothed trend plot
ggplot(trend_data, aes(x = Month, y = mean_bp, 
                      color = TreatmentGroup, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  # Raw data points
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  # Smoothed trend line
  geom_smooth(method = "loess",     # Locally weighted smoothing
              span = 0.75,          # Smoothness (larger = smoother)
              alpha = 0.2) +        # Confidence band transparency
  labs(title = "Blood Pressure Trends by Treatment Group",
       subtitle = "Smoothed LOESS curves with 95% confidence bands",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       color = "Treatment",
       fill = "Treatment") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  theme_custom()

Area Chart with Confidence Bands - Code

Purpose: Emphasize magnitude and uncertainty over time
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + 🟡 Distribution


Code
# Calculate confidence intervals manually
trend_ci <- trend_data %>%
  mutate(
    lower = mean_bp - 1.96 * se_bp,  # 95% CI
    upper = mean_bp + 1.96 * se_bp
  )

# Create area chart with confidence band
ggplot(trend_ci, aes(x = Month, y = mean_bp, 
                    color = TreatmentGroup, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  # Confidence band as ribbon
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), 
              alpha = 0.3, color = NA) +
  # Mean line
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Points at measurement times
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Blood Pressure Changes with 95% Confidence Intervals",
       subtitle = "Shaded areas show uncertainty in estimates",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       color = "Treatment",
       fill = "Treatment") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  theme_custom()

Annotated Time Series - Code

Purpose: Highlight important events and changes
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + context


Code
# Prepare data for one treatment group
treatment_a_data <- trend_ci %>% filter(TreatmentGroup == "Treatment A")

# Create annotated plot
ggplot(treatment_a_data, aes(x = Month, y = mean_bp)) +
  # Area under curve
  geom_area(fill = "#4DBBD5", alpha = 0.3) +
  # Line and points
  geom_line(color = "#4DBBD5", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "#4DBBD5") +
  # Annotate starting point
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 142, 
           label = "Baseline\n140 mmHg", 
           hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.5, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  # Annotate 6-month check
  annotate("segment", x = 6, y = 125, xend = 6, yend = 130,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), 
           color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 6, y = 123, 
           label = "First improvement\n-15 mmHg", 
           hjust = 0.5, size = 3.5, color = "red") +
  # Annotate final result
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 118, 
           label = "Final: 120 mmHg\n✓ Target achieved", 
           hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1.2, size = 4, fontface = "bold", color = "darkgreen") +
  # Add horizontal reference line for target BP
  geom_hline(yintercept = 120, linetype = "dashed", 
             color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Treatment A: Blood Pressure Reduction Over 12 Months",
       subtitle = "Green line shows target BP of 120 mmHg",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +
  ylim(110, 145) +
  theme_custom()

Percent Change Plot - Code

Purpose: Show relative changes from baseline
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + comparison


Code
# Calculate percent change from baseline
pct_change_data <- time_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP)) %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Month) %>%
  summarise(mean_bp = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline = first(mean_bp),           # Get baseline value
    pct_change = 100 * (mean_bp - baseline) / baseline  # % change
  )

# Create percent change plot
ggplot(pct_change_data, aes(x = Month, y = pct_change, 
                           color = TreatmentGroup, group = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Percent Change in Blood Pressure from Baseline",
       subtitle = "Negative values indicate improvement",
       x = "Time (months)",
       y = "Change from Baseline (%)",
       color = "Treatment") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12)) +

title: Time Series - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Interpreting Percent Change

Why Use Percent Change?

Normalizes different baselines

Groups with different starting points comparable

Shows relative effect size

Treatment A: ~15% reduction
Treatment B: ~12% reduction
Control: ~0% change

Makes communication easier

“15% reduction” more intuitive than “20 mmHg decrease”

Useful for different scales

Can compare BP, cholesterol, weight, etc. on same plot


Limitation: Can mislead if baseline values are very small

title: Time Series - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Slope Graph - Code

Purpose: Highlight individual changes between two time points
Goal: 🔵 Evolution + individual patterns


Code
# Prepare data: baseline vs 12-month by treatment
slope_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP_0m), !is.na(SysBP_6m)) %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 15) %>%  # Sample 15 patients per group
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, SysBP_6m),
               names_to = "Time",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Time = ifelse(Time == "SysBP_0m", "Baseline", "6 Months"))

# Create slope graph
ggplot(slope_data, aes(x = Time, y = SysBP, group = PatientID,
                      color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Individual Patient Blood Pressure Changes",
       subtitle = "Each line represents one patient (n=15 per group)",
       x = "",
       y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

Treatment groups show mostly downward slopes

Most patients improved

Control group shows mixed results

Some up, some down (natural variation)

Individual variability is visible

Not all patients respond equally
Some non-responders in treatment groups

Response heterogeneity matters

Need to identify why some don’t respond


Advantage: Shows both group trend AND individual variation

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
How to Read Violin Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Median BMI: East 26.9, West 25.5, North 25.0, South 24.4 - West has the widest spread (SD 5.1), North the narrowest (SD 4.4) - Every region has a thin lower tail: a few BMI values near 11–12 - The bulk of each violin sits between about 22 and 30
INTERPRETATION: - BMI is similar across regions; East is about 2 units higher than South - The lower tails are implausible BMI values, visible in every region - A violin shows the tail that a box plot reduces to a few dots
IMPLICATIONS: - Check the very low BMI values before comparing regions - A difference of 2 units may matter clinically; test it, with region sizes of 40 to 65
ACTIONS: - Use violins when the shape matters (tails, two peaks); keep the inner box for the median and quartiles

Scatter with Regression Line - Code
⚫ Goal: Show correlation with statistical trend


Code
# Scatter plot with linear regression line and confidence interval
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue", size = 2.5) +  # Add points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#E74C3C", 
              fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.2, size = 1.2) +  # Add regression line + CI
  # Calculate and display correlation
  annotate("text", x = 25, y = 160, 
           label = paste("r =", round(cor(data_clean$Age, data_clean$SysBP_0m), 3)),
           family = "serif", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Age vs. Baseline Systolic BP with Regression Line",
       subtitle = "Linear trend with 95% confidence interval",
       x = "Age (years)", 
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12))

text: Scatter with Regression - Plot

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Reading Advanced Continuous Plots
Using the regression plot:

OBSERVATION: - Correlation between age and baseline systolic BP: r = −0.09 (p = 0.22) - The regression line is almost flat (about −0.07 mmHg per year) - The confidence band is wide compared with the slope - Ages 18–79; systolic BP 110–159 mmHg
INTERPRETATION: - No evidence of a linear association between age and baseline BP in this sample - This is unusual: in most populations BP rises with age. With simulated data, or a small or selected sample, the expected pattern can be absent
IMPLICATIONS: - Do not draw a trend from a line that the data do not support: read the CI band and r together - Check how the sample was selected before generalising - A flat line here is a result, not an error in the plot

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Violin vs. Box Plot


Box Plot Shows: - 5-number summary - Median (50th percentile) - Quartiles (25th, 75th) - Outliers - Missing: Distribution shape
Use When: - Quick comparison needed - Focus on median/quartiles - Outliers are important

Violin Plot Shows: - Full distribution shape - Density at each value - Can see bimodal patterns - Shows skewness clearly - Missing: Exact quantiles
Use When: - Shape matters - Want to see multiple peaks - Comparing distributions - Publication quality needed

title: Continuous Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Violin plots show what box plots hide (distribution shape)
Ridgeline plots scale well to 5-10 groups
2D density reveals clustering patterns
Hexbin solves overplotting automatically
Always show confidence intervals on regression lines

Common Mistakes: - Using violin plots with < 20 observations per group - Too many groups in ridgeline (>10 gets cluttered) - Forgetting to show confidence intervals - Interpreting weak correlations as strong relationships - Not checking for non-linear patterns
Pro Tips: - Add boxplot inside violin for best of both worlds - scale parameter in ridgeline controls overlap - Use alpha transparency to show density overlaps - Always report correlation coefficient with regression

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
section: What is Category vs. Continuous Data?
text:
What is Category vs. Continuous Data?


Definition:
Combining categorical variables (groups) with continuous variables (numeric measurements)

Compare numeric values across categories
Show distributions within groups
Analyze differences between segments


Examples in Our Dataset:

BMI by Gender
Blood Pressure by Treatment Group
Cholesterol by Region
Age by Smoking Status
Blood Sugar by Exercise Frequency

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals

What questions can we answer?

🟡 Distribution - How do values spread within each category?
🟢 Ranking - Which group has highest/lowest values?
🔴 Part of Whole - How do groups contribute to total?
⚫ Correlation - Do patterns differ across groups?

Charts we’ll learn:

Box Plot
Grouped Bar Chart
Stacked Bar Chart

Box Plot - Code

Code
# Create box plot comparing BMI by Treatment Group

  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.color = "red", outlier.size = 3) +  # Add box plots
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C",

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text: Box Plot - Plot

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
How to Read Box Plots
Using the previous plot:

Reading the 5-Number Summary (Control / Intervention): - Bottom whisker: lowest value within 1.5 × IQR of the box - Bottom of box (Q1): 25th percentile (22.4 / 23.0) - Line in box (Median): 50th percentile (24.6 / 25.8) - Top of box (Q3): 75th percentile (27.7 / 29.3) - Top whisker: highest value within 1.5 × IQR - Red dots: outliers beyond 1.5 × IQR (1 in Control, 2 in Intervention; the lowest BMI is 11.4)
OBSERVATION: - Median BMI 24.6 (Control) and 25.8 (Intervention) - Intervention box slightly taller (IQR 6.3 vs 5.4): a little more spread - Boxes largely overlap - A few very low BMI values appear as outliers
INTERPRETATION: - A difference of about 1 BMI unit between the groups at baseline; small next to the spread within each group - The groups look broadly comparable on BMI - The very low values (below 15) are implausible and should be checked
IMPLICATIONS: - A baseline difference this small is unlikely to confound a treatment comparison, but it can be adjusted for - Report the medians and IQRs in Table 1 - Decide what to do with implausible values before the analysis, and say so in the methods

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Understanding Box Plots


The Box: - Bottom edge: Q1 (25th percentile) - Middle line: Median (50th percentile) - Top edge: Q3 (75th percentile) - Box height: IQR (Q3 - Q1)
The Whiskers: - Extend to 1.5 × IQR - Show data range (excluding outliers)

Outliers: - Points beyond whiskers - May indicate: - Data entry errors - Natural extreme values - Different population
Comparing Boxes: - Non-overlapping: likely different - Overlapping: may not be different - Check median positions - Compare IQR widths

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Box plots show distribution - not just means
Order categories - by median or logically
Grouped vs. Stacked bars - different purposes
Always show units - in axis labels
Handle outliers thoughtfully - investigate but don’t automatically remove

Common Mistakes:

Too many categories in one plot (>8)
Not ordering categories logically
Confusing grouped and stacked bars
Ignoring outliers without investigation
Comparing means without showing variation

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
What is Categorical Data?


Definition:
Data that represents categories, groups, or labels

Finite set of discrete values
No inherent numerical order (usually)
Qualitative rather than quantitative


Examples in Our Dataset:

Treatment Group (Control, Intervention)
Gender (Male, Female, Other)
Region (North, South, East, West)
Smoking Status
Alcohol Use
Exercise Frequency
Chronic Disease

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Categorical Data

What questions can we answer?

🟢 Ranking - Which category is most/least common?
🟡 Distribution - How are observations spread across categories?
🔴 Part of Whole - What proportion does each category represent?

Charts we’ll learn:

Bar Chart (Vertical & Horizontal)
Pie Chart
Donut Chart
Stacked Bar Chart

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Setup: Load Libraries and Data


Code
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)    # For creating plots
library(dplyr)      # For data manipulation

# Load the dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Handle missing data: filter to complete cases for ExerciseFreq
data_clean <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq))  # Remove rows with missing exercise frequency

# Preview the data
head(data_clean %>% 
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, Gender, Region, SmokingStatus))

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Bar Chart (Vertical) - Code
🟢 Goal: Ranking / Distribution


Code
# Create vertical bar chart showing patient count by region
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Region)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +  # Add bars with color
  labs(title = "Patient Distribution by Region",
       x = "Region", y = "Count of Patients") +  # Add labels
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +  # Apply serif font theme
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))




Line 1-2: Set up plot with Region on x-axis, counts automatically calculated
Line 3: Add bar geometry with steel blue fill and transparency
Line 4-5: Add descriptive title and axis labels
Line 6: Apply minimal theme with serif font for professional look
Line 7-9: Customize title and axis text sizes

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Horizontal Bar Chart - Code
🟢 Goal: Ranking (ordered by value)


Code
# Create horizontal bar chart with categories ordered by count
smoking_counts <- data_clean %>%
  count(SmokingStatus) %>%  # Count observations per smoking status
  arrange(n)  # Arrange from smallest to largest

ggplot(smoking_counts, aes(x = n, y = reorder(SmokingStatus, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.7) +  # Use geom_col for pre-counted data
  labs(title = "Patient Count by Smoking Status (Ranked)",
       x = "Number of Patients", y = "Smoking Status") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))




Lines 1-3: Count patients per smoking status category
Line 4: Sort ascending so chart displays with largest at top
Line 5: reorder() arranges y-axis by count value
Line 6: geom_col() used when you have pre-calculated counts

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text: Horizontal Bar Chart - Plot

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Bar Charts
Using the previous plot as example:

OBSERVATION: - Non-smokers: 118 patients (largest group) - Former smokers: 43 patients - Current smokers: 37 patients (smallest group) - Clear ranking, with no group very small
INTERPRETATION: - 60% of participants are non-smokers - Current and former smokers together are 40% - Every smoking group has enough patients to describe
IMPLICATIONS: - Subgroups of smokers are still small (37 and 43): estimates within them will be imprecise - Non-smokers carry most of the weight of overall results - Consider stratified analysis by smoking status
ACTIONS: - Use smoking status as a stratification variable - Check statistical power before testing smoker subgroups - Watch for interaction effects with treatment

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Pie Chart - Code
🔴 Goal: Part of a Whole


Code
# Calculate percentages for treatment groups
treatment_summary <- data_clean %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100)  # Calculate percentages

# Create pie chart using coord_polar transformation
ggplot(treatment_summary, aes(x = "", y = n, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +  # Create stacked bar
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +  # Transform to polar coordinates (pie)
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%")), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            family = "serif", size = 5) +  # Add percentage labels
  labs(title = "Treatment Group Distribution",
       fill = "Group") +
  theme_void(base_family = "serif") +  # Remove axes for clean pie
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))



⚠️ Warning: Use pie charts only for 2-5 categories!

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text: Pie Chart - Plot

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Donut Chart - Code
🔴 Goal: Part of a Whole (modern alternative to pie)


Code
# Calculate percentages for gender distribution
gender_summary <- data_clean %>%
  count(Gender) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100)

# Create donut chart (pie with hole in center)
ggplot(gender_summary, aes(x = 2, y = n, fill = Gender)) +  # x=2 creates the hole
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5) +  # Creates the "donut hole" effect
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +  # Use professional color palette
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(Gender, "\n", round(percentage, 1), "%")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            family = "serif", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Patient Gender Distribution") +
  theme_void(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "right")

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Stacked Bar Chart - Code
🔴 Goal: Part of a Whole + Comparison across groups


Code
# Create stacked bar showing smoking status by region
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Region, fill = SmokingStatus)) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack", alpha = 0.8) +  # Stack bars on top of each other
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Current smoker" = "#E74C3C",
                                "Former smoker" = "#F39C12",
                                "Non-smoker" = "#27AE60"),
                    name = "Smoking Status") +  # Custom colors
  labs(title = "Smoking Status Distribution by Region",
       x = "Region",
       y = "Number of Patients") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.position = "right")



Stacked bars show both total count AND composition within each category

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Categorical Plots - Summary









Chart Type
Goal
When to Use
Code Complexity




Vertical Bar
🟢 Ranking / 🟡 Distribution
Few categories (3-7)
Simple (3-5 lines)


Horizontal Bar
🟢 Ranking (ordered)
Long category names, many categories
Simple (5-7 lines)


Pie Chart
🔴 Part of Whole
Only 2-5 categories!
Medium (8-10 lines)


Donut Chart
🔴 Part of Whole
Modern alternative to pie
Medium (8-10 lines)


Stacked Bar
🔴 Part + 🟢 Comparison
Composition across groups
Medium (8-12 lines)

title: Categorical Plots - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Bar charts are versatile - use for most categorical data
Order matters - arrange by value for rankings
Avoid pie charts beyond 5 categories
Color strategically - use consistent, meaningful colors
Handle missing data - filter or document approach

Common Mistakes:

Using 3D effects (distorts perception)
Too many categories (>10)
Poor color choices (similar shades)
Missing labels or titles
Inconsistent formatting

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Topics Covered

Spatial interpolation (IDW; kriging in the GIS track)
Cartograms (area distortion)
Spatial autocorrelation
Hexagon tile maps
Access: distance bands

Goal: Advanced spatial analysis

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Setup
Data: a synthetic district of 79 blocks with dengue rates, and 30 health facilities (data/gis/, built by gis/make_gis_data.R; the same data as the GIS track).


Code
library(tidyverse); library(sf)
blocks <- st_read("../../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(32644)                                   # UTM zone 44N: metres, for distances and areas
fac <- read_csv("../../data/gis/facilities.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644)

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Spatial Interpolation


Code
library(gstat)
centres <- st_centroid(blocks)
grid <- st_make_grid(blocks, cellsize = 500, what = "centers") |> st_as_sf() |>
  st_filter(st_union(blocks))                            # 500 m grid inside the district
idw_fit <- idw(dengue_per_100k ~ 1, centres, newdata = grid, idp = 2, debug.level = 0)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = idw_fit, aes(colour = var1.pred), size = 0.6, shape = 15) +
  geom_sf(data = blocks, fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "Dengue\nper 100k") +
  labs(title = "Inverse distance weighting from block centres") +
  theme_void()



Estimates values between observations. Kriging does the same with a fitted variogram and gives a standard error for each estimate (GIS track).

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Cartogram


Code
library(cartogram)
carto <- cartogram_cont(blocks, "population", itermax = 8)
ggplot(carto) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "Dengue\nper 100k") +
  labs(title = "Cartogram: block area proportional to population") +
  theme_void()



Large empty blocks shrink and crowded ones grow, so the map shows where the people are, not where the land is.

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Spatial Autocorrelation


Code
library(spdep)
nb <- poly2nb(blocks)                                   # blocks that share a border
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")
moran_result <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw)
moran.plot(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, labels = FALSE, pch = 19,
           xlab = "Dengue per 100k", ylab = "Neighbours' average",
           main = sprintf("Moran's I = %.2f, p = %.3g", moran_result$estimate[1], moran_result$p.value))



A positive slope (Moran’s I > 0) means high-incidence blocks sit next to high-incidence blocks.

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Hexagon Tile Map


Code
library(geogrid)
blocks_wgs <- st_transform(blocks, 4326)
hex_grid <- calculate_grid(shape = blocks_wgs, grid_type = "hexagonal", seed = 3)
hex_data <- assign_polygons(blocks_wgs, hex_grid)
ggplot(hex_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "Dengue\nper 100k") +
  labs(title = "Every block the same size") +
  theme_void()



Small blocks are as visible as large ones; the price is distorted positions and shapes.

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Access: Distance Bands


Code
phc <- fac |> filter(type %in% c("PHC", "CHC"))
bands <- map_dfr(c(10, 5, 2), \(km) st_sf(km = km, geometry = st_union(st_buffer(phc, km * 1000)))) |>
  st_intersection(st_union(blocks))
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = bands, aes(fill = factor(km, levels = c(2, 5, 10))), colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = blocks, fill = NA, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = phc, aes(shape = type), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = -1, name = "Within (km)") +
  labs(title = "Straight-line distance to a PHC or CHC", shape = NULL) +
  theme_void()



Straight-line bands are a first look. Isochrones (travel time by road, e.g. osrm::osrmIsochrone()) are better, but need a routing server and road data.

title: Geographic - ADVANCED
text:
Summary
Advanced geographic techniques:

Spatial interpolation - estimate unmeasured locations
Cartograms - size by variable
Spatial autocorrelation - test clustering
Hexagon tile maps - equal area representation
Distance bands - accessibility (isochrones need a routing server)

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Topics Covered

STL decomposition (trend/seasonal)
Forecasting with ARIMA
Prophet models
Change point detection
Spectral analysis (FFT)

Goal: Advanced temporal patterns

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Setup
Data: monthly dengue cases from 30 city wards, 2023–2025 (data/dengue_wards.csv, simulated; see data/README.md). A trial with three visits is not a time series: these methods need many equally spaced time points.


Code
library(tidyverse); library(forecast)
dengue <- read_csv("../../data/dengue_wards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
monthly <- dengue |>
  group_by(month_index) |>                                   # 36 consecutive months
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain_mm = mean(rain_mm), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(date = seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = n()))
cases_ts <- ts(monthly$cases, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
STL Decomposition


Code
stl_result <- stl(log1p(cases_ts), s.window = "periodic")
autoplot(stl_result) +
  labs(title = "STL decomposition of monthly dengue cases (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal()



Separates the trend, the seasonal pattern (a peak every monsoon) and the remainder. The log scale makes the seasonal swing additive.

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Forecasting with ARIMA


Code
arima_model <- auto.arima(cases_ts, lambda = 0)       # lambda = 0: model the log, forecast on the case scale
forecast_result <- forecast(arima_model, h = 12)
autoplot(forecast_result) +
  labs(title = "12-month dengue forecast (seasonal ARIMA)", x = NULL, y = "Cases per month") +
  theme_minimal()



Dark band = 80%, light band = 95% prediction interval. Three seasons are a short history: the bands are wide, and that is the honest message.

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Prophet Forecasting


Code
library(prophet)
m <- prophet(data.frame(ds = monthly$date, y = log1p(monthly$cases)),
             yearly.seasonality = TRUE, weekly.seasonality = FALSE, daily.seasonality = FALSE)
future <- make_future_dataframe(m, periods = 12, freq = "month")
fc <- predict(m, future)
plot(m, fc) + labs(title = "Prophet forecast (log cases)", x = NULL, y = "log(1 + cases)")



Prophet fits a trend plus yearly seasonality; it is easy to use but, like any model, only as good as the history.

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Change Point Detection


Code
library(changepoint)
y <- as.numeric(log1p(cases_ts))
noise_sd <- mad(diff(y)) / sqrt(2)                   # cpt.mean() assumes a noise SD of 1: rescale first
cpt_result <- cpt.mean(y / noise_sd, method = "PELT")
plot(cpt_result, cpt.col = "red", cpt.width = 3, ylab = "log(1 + cases) / noise SD", xlab = "Month (1 = Jan 2023)",
     main = "Change points in the mean level")



Code
cpts(cpt_result)


[1]  4 10 17 22 28 34


Here the “changes” are the start and end of each season: a change-point method finds level shifts, so remove the seasonal pattern first if you are looking for a shift in the underlying trend.

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Rolling Statistics Plot


Code
library(zoo)
rolling <- monthly |>
  mutate(roll_mean = rollmean(cases, k = 3, fill = NA),
         roll_sd = rollapply(cases, width = 3, FUN = sd, fill = NA))
ggplot(rolling, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cases), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = roll_mean - roll_sd, ymax = roll_mean + roll_sd), alpha = 0.2, fill = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = roll_mean), colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "3-month rolling mean ± SD", x = NULL, y = "Cases per month") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Time Series - ADVANCED
text:
Summary
Advanced time series:

STL decomposition - separate components
ARIMA forecasting - statistical predictions
Prophet - flexible, interpretable forecasts
Change points - detect regime shifts
Rolling statistics - smoothed trends

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Topics Covered

Contour plots (2D density)
3D surface plots
Parallel coordinates
Correlation matrix
Hexbin plots (large data)

Goal: Handle complex continuous relationships

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text: Setup

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Contour Plot


Code
ggplot(health_data, aes(x = BMI, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +
  labs(title = "2D Density: BMI vs Blood Pressure",
       x = "BMI", y = "Systolic BP") +
  theme_minimal()



Shows where patients concentrate: brighter bands = more patients. With 200 points the contours are rough; they pay off with thousands.

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Parallel Coordinates


Code
library(GGally)
health_subset <- health_data %>%
  select(Age, BMI, SysBP_0m, Cholesterol, BloodSugar) %>%
  na.omit()

ggparcoord(health_subset, columns = 1:5,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "Parallel Coordinates: Health Metrics") +
  theme_minimal()



Each line = one patient across multiple variables

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
3D Surface


Code
library(plotly)
d <- health_data %>% filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(SysBP_0m))
dens <- MASS::kde2d(d$BMI, d$SysBP_0m, n = 50)      # 2D kernel density on a 50 x 50 grid
plot_ly(x = dens$x, y = dens$y, z = t(dens$z)) %>%
  add_surface() %>%
  layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "BMI"), yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP"),
                      zaxis = list(title = "Density")))






Drag to rotate. The same density as the contour plot: 3D looks striking, but contours are easier to read exactly.

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Hexbin Plot


Code
ggplot(health_data, aes(x = BMI, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", trans = "log10") +
  labs(title = "Hexbin Plot: Large Dataset Visualization",
       fill = "Count (log10)") +
  theme_minimal()



Better than a scatter plot for 1000+ points; with 200 patients most bins hold 1 or 2.

title: Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Correlation Matrix


Code
library(ggcorrplot)
cor_matrix <- health_data %>%
  select(Age, BMI, SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m, 
         Cholesterol, BloodSugar) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

ggcorrplot(cor_matrix, type = "lower",
           lab = TRUE, lab_size = 3,
           colors = c("#DC0000", "white", "#00A087"))



Quick overview of all pairwise correlations. Here every |r| is below 0.12: in this simulated dataset the variables were generated almost independently, which the scatter plots on the earlier slides also show.

text:
Summary
Advanced continuous techniques:

Contour plots - 2D density

3D surfaces - interactive exploration
Hexbin - big data visualization
Correlation matrix - all pairs at once

title: Exporting plots
text: Exporting plots from R can be done in several ways, depending on the desired output format and quality. Here are some common methods to export plots:

title: Exporting plots
text:
Using R’s Built-in Functions
R provides several built-in functions for exporting plots to different formats:

Raster Formats

png(), jpeg(), tiff(), bmp(): These functions save plots in raster formats. You can specify filename, dimensions, and resolution.

# PNG format (good for web)
png("plot.png", width = 800, height = 600, res = 100)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# High-resolution TIFF for publications
tiff("plot.tiff", width = 8, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Vector Formats

pdf(): Saves plots in PDF format, vector-based and scalable.
svg(): Saves plots in SVG format, ideal for web and scalable graphics.

# PDF for high-quality prints
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# SVG for web use
svg("plot.svg", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

title: Exporting plots
text:
Exporting ggplot2 Plots
For ggplot2 plots, the ggsave() function is the most convenient way to export:
library(ggplot2)

# Create a plot
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Save in different formats
ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 6)
ggsave("plot.svg", p, width = 8, height = 6)

Controlling Output Quality

Resolution (DPI): Higher DPI for print quality (300+), lower for web (72-150)
Dimensions: Specify in inches or pixels
Aspect Ratio: Maintain proportions for consistency

# High-resolution for publications
ggsave("publication_plot.tiff", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       dpi = 300, 
       device = "tiff")

# Web-optimized PNG
ggsave("web_plot.png", p, 
       width = 800, height = 600, 
       dpi = 100, 
       units = "px")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Advanced Exporting Techniques

Exporting Multiple Plots
# Save multiple plots to PDF
pdf("multiple_plots.pdf")
plot1 <- ggplot(data1, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
print(plot1)
plot2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()
print(plot2)
dev.off()


Using Cairo for Better Quality
The Cairo graphics library can provide better quality for some formats:
install.packages("Cairo")
library(Cairo)

CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Exporting to Clipboard
For quick sharing:
# Windows
savePlot("clipboard", type = "wmf")

# Or for ggplot2
ggsave("clipboard", p, device = "png")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Best Practices

Choose the right format: PDF/SVG for vector graphics, PNG/TIFF for raster
Set appropriate resolution: 300 DPI for print, 72-150 for screen
Consider file size: Vector formats scale better but may be larger
Test outputs: Always check exported files in target applications
Use consistent dimensions: Maintain aspect ratios across exports

title: Exporting plots
text:
Common Issues and Solutions

Plot not saving: Ensure dev.off() is called after plotting
Low quality: Increase DPI or use vector formats
Wrong dimensions: Specify units explicitly (inches, cm, pixels)
Colors not matching: Check color profiles and device settings
