title: Advanced Exporting Techniques
text:
This chapter covers advanced techniques for exporting plots, including programmatic generation, batch processing, custom devices, and integration with other tools.




library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# Create plots for each cylinder group
plots <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) %>%
  map(~ ggplot(.x, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
        geom_point() + 
        ggtitle(paste("Cylinders:", .x$cyl[1])))

# Save each plot
walk2(plots, names(plots), 
      ~ ggsave(filename = paste0("plot_cyl_", .x, ".png"), 
               plot = .y, 
               width = 6, height = 4))



# Generate timestamped filenames
timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

ggsave(paste0("analysis_plot_", timestamp, ".pdf"), 
       plot = p, 
       width = 8, height = 6)






save_plot_multiple_formats <- function(plot, filename_base, 
                                     formats = c("png", "pdf", "svg")) {
  for (fmt in formats) {
    filename <- paste0(filename_base, ".", fmt)
    ggsave(filename, plot, width = 8, height = 6)
  }
}

# Usage
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
save_plot_multiple_formats(p, "mtcars_scatter")



datasets <- list(
  mtcars = mtcars,
  iris = iris,
  airquality = airquality
)

for (name in names(datasets)) {
  data <- datasets[[name]]
  # Create appropriate plot based on data
  if (name == "mtcars") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
  } else if (name == "iris") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) + 
      geom_point()
  }
  
  ggsave(paste0(name, "_plot.png"), p, width = 6, height = 4)
}






library(Cairo)

# High-quality PNG
CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600, 
         bg = "white", pointsize = 12)
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()

# PDF with embedded fonts
CairoPDF("embedded_fonts.pdf", width = 8, height = 6, 
         family = "Arial")
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()



# Create a custom device wrapper
save_high_res <- function(filename, plot_func, ...) {
  png(filename, width = 1200, height = 800, res = 150, ...)
  plot_func()
  dev.off()
}

# Usage
my_plot <- function() {
  plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, 
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       main = "High Resolution Plot")
}

save_high_res("high_res_plot.png", my_plot)






library(tikzDevice)

# Export as TikZ for LaTeX
tikz("plot.tex", width = 4, height = 3)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
dev.off()



# Export as HTML with plotly
library(plotly)
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(ggplotly(p), "interactive_plot.html")






# Create publication-ready theme
publication_theme <- theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 12, family = "Times"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  publication_theme +
  labs(title = "Publication Quality Plot")

ggsave("publication_plot.pdf", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       device = cairo_pdf)



library(cowplot)

# Create individual plots
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) + geom_boxplot()
p3 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp)) + geom_histogram()

# Combine into single figure
combined <- plot_grid(p1, p2, p3, 
                      labels = c("A", "B", "C"),
                      ncol = 2)

# Save combined figure
ggsave("combined_figure.pdf", combined, 
       width = 10, height = 8)






# For large datasets, use sampling or aggregation
large_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100000), y = rnorm(100000))

# Option 1: Sample data
sample_data <- large_data[sample(nrow(large_data), 10000), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.1)
ggsave("sampled_plot.png")

# Option 2: Use density plots
ggplot(large_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_density2d() +
  geom_point(data = sample_data, alpha = 0.1)
ggsave("density_plot.png")



# Clear graphics devices
graphics.off()

# Force garbage collection
gc()

# Monitor memory usage
library(pryr)
mem_used()






check_plot_quality <- function(filename) {
  # Check file exists
  if (!file.exists(filename)) {
    stop("File was not created")
  }
  
  # Check file size (basic quality indicator)
  size <- file.info(filename)$size
  if (size < 1000) {
    warning("File seems too small, may indicate error")
  }
  
  # For images, could check dimensions
  if (grepl("\\.png$", filename)) {
    img <- png::readPNG(filename)
    message("Image dimensions: ", dim(img)[1], "x", dim(img)[2])
  }
}

# Usage
ggsave("test_plot.png", ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point())
check_plot_quality("test_plot.png")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Module 4 Overview
Previously: - Module 1: Foundations & Geoms - Module 2: Aesthetics, Faceting & Themes - Module 3: Colors, Scales & Custom Themes
This Module (FINAL): - Complex visualizations with progressive builds - Advanced composition techniques - Exporting and reproducibility - Limitations of ggplot2 - Best practices and common pitfalls - Workshop summary

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Setup


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)
library(paletteer)
library(patchwork)
library(productplots)  # mosaic plots (ggmosaic does not work with ggplot2 4.x yet)

# Load data with all transformations
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    DiaBP_Change = DiaBP_6m - DiaBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

# Summary data
bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ci_data <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(SysBP), SE = sd(SysBP) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")

# Custom theme from Module 3
theme_clinical_report <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif") {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = base_family),
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.3, face = "bold", 
                              hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, hjust = 0.5,
                                 color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, hjust = 1,
                                face = "italic", color = "gray50"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, color = "gray20"),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray40", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )
}

              alpha = 0.3, width = 0.2,
              size = 1.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  # Box plot overlay
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  # Add mean as point
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               size = 3, color = "black", shape = 18)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Publication-Ready Plot: All Elements


Code
publication_plot <- ggplot(bp_data, 
                           aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol,
                               color = Hypertension_Baseline)) +
  # Data layer
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  
  # Scales
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Normal" = "forestgreen", "Hypertensive" = "darkred"),
    name = "Baseline BP Status") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(15, 40, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 300, 50)) +
  
  # Labels
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between BMI and Cholesterol",
    subtitle = "Stratified by baseline hypertension status",
    x = "Body Mass Index (kg/m²)",
    y = "Total Cholesterol (mg/dL)",
    caption = "Data: Public Health BP Dataset | n=200 patients | Linear regression with 95% CI"
  ) +
  
  # Theme
  theme_clinical_report(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.85, 0.15),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5)
  )

Layer Ordering Matters




Code

       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4

Coordinate Systems: coord_flip()




Code
region_summary <- bp_data %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(region_summary, 
       aes(x = reorder(Region, Mean_SysBP),

  geom_col() +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
ggsave(): Saving Plots


Code
# Create a plot
my_plot <- ggplot(bp_data, aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m, color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point() + theme_minimal()

# Save the plot
ggsave(
  filename = "blood_pressure_analysis.png",
  plot = my_plot,
  width = 10, height = 6, units = "in",
  dpi = 300)



filename: File path and name with extension
plot: ggplot object (defaults to last plot displayed)
width, height: Dimensions
units: “in” (inches), “cm”, “mm”, “px”
dpi: Resolution (72 = screen, 300 = print quality, 600 = high-res print)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4

What ggplot2 Cannot Do Well
While ggplot2 is powerful, it has limitations:

Mosaic plots / Marimekko charts - Use productplots, ggmosaic or base R mosaicplot()
3D plots - Not natively supported, use plotly or rgl
Network graphs - Use ggraph or igraph
Interactive plots - Limited, need plotly::ggplotly() or ggiraph
Sankey diagrams - Use ggalluvial or networkD3
Circular plots (beyond polar) - Use circlize
Very complex statistical diagrams - May need specialized packages

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Common Pitfalls to Avoid

Mapping constants inside aes() - Use fixed values outside aes
Too many aesthetics - Limit to 3-4 visual encodings max
Poor color choices - Always test for colorblind accessibility
Overplotting - Use alpha, jitter, or facets
Misleading axes - Always start at zero for bar charts
Too much clutter - Remove unnecessary grid lines, legends, or decorations
Inconsistent themes - Use theme_set() for consistency
Ignoring aspect ratios - Consider final output dimensions
Not saving properly - Use appropriate format and resolution
Forgetting reproducibility - Set seed, document packages

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Best Practices Checklist
Before finalizing visualizations:

Color: Use colorblind-friendly palettes (viridis, ColorBrewer)
Contrast: Ensure sufficient contrast between elements
Text size: Minimum 10pt for body text, 12pt+ for titles
Redundancy: Don’t rely on color alone (use shape, pattern, labels)
Simplicity: Remove unnecessary elements
Labels: Clear, descriptive axis labels and titles
Alt text: Provide text description for screen readers
Print: Test in grayscale/black & white
Simulation: Test with colorblind simulator
Font: Use readable fonts (avoid decorative fonts)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
The ggplot2 Building Process


Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +           # 1. Data + Aesthetics
  geom_point(aes(color = var3, size = var4)) +     # 2. Geometry + Local aes
  scale_color_viridis_d() +                        # 3. Scales
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 6)) +         # 4. More scales
  facet_wrap(~ var5) +                             # 5. Facets
  labs(title = "My Plot",                          # 6. Labels
       x = "X Label", y = "Y Label") +
  theme_minimal() +                                # 7. Theme
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",                # 8. Theme customization
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 4
text:
Key Takeaways

Grammar of Graphics provides a systematic framework for building visualizations
Layering is fundamental - data → aesthetics → geometries → scales → themes
Aesthetics map data to visual properties (inside aes())
Geoms are the building blocks - choose appropriately for your data type
Themes control appearance - use built-in or create custom ones
Colors matter - always consider colorblind accessibility
Scales control how data maps to aesthetics - customize breaks, limits, labels
Facets enable small multiples for comparing groups
Consistency is key - use global themes and organizational standards
Know ggplot2’s limitations and when to use alternatives

Code
library(patchwork)

# Create individual plots
p1 <- ggplot(bp_data, aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) + geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(bp_data, aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) + geom_point()
p3 <- ggplot(bp_data, aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m)) + geom_boxplot()
p4 <- ggplot(bp_data, aes(x = SysBP_Change)) + geom_histogram()

# Combine in various layouts

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Module 2 Overview
Previously (Module 1): - Grammar of Graphics foundations - Seven layers - Basic geoms
This Module: - Aesthetic mappings deep dive - Faceting strategies - Built-in themes - ggthemes package

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Setup: Load Data


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)  # For additional themes

# Load and prepare data
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

# Time series data
bp_time <- bp_data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "Time", values_to = "SysBP") %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(gsub("SysBP_|m", "", Time)))

bp_summary <- bp_time %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup, Months) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global vs Local Aesthetics

Global aesthetics: Defined in ggplot(), apply to all layers
Local aesthetics: Defined in geom_*(), apply to specific layer
Local aesthetics override global aesthetics
Use global for shared mappings, local for layer-specific mappings



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2)) +          # Global
  geom_point(aes(color = var3)) +                 # Local (adds color)
  geom_smooth()                                   # Uses global only

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Global Aesthetics Example




Code
# Global color applies to both layers
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m, 
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)



Both geom_point() and geom_smooth() use the color mapping

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Local Aesthetics Override




Code
# Local aesthetic overrides global
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = TreatmentGroup), 
             size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              color = "black", linewidth = 1.5)



Points are colored by treatment, but smooth line is black

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Color & Fill




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m,
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7)



color: Outlines of geoms (points, lines)
fill: Interior of geoms (bars, areas, polygons)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Size




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           size = BMI, color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6)



size: Point size or line width, mapped to continuous variable

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Shape




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = Cholesterol,
           shape = Gender, 
           color = Gender)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7)



shape: Point shape (circles, squares, triangles, etc.)
Best for categorical variables with few levels (≤6)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Aesthetics: Alpha (Transparency)




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = BMI, y = SysBP_0m,
           alpha = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "darkred")



alpha: Transparency (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque)
Useful for showing density in overplotted data

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Multiple Aesthetics Combined




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup,
           shape = Gender,
           size = BMI)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6)



Can combine multiple aesthetics, but be careful not to overwhelm!

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
section: Aesthetic Mapping: Inside vs Outside aes()
text:
Aesthetic Mapping: Inside vs Outside aes()




Code
# MAPPED to data (inside aes)
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)

# FIXED value (outside aes)
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3)



Key rule: Inside aes() = mapped to data, Outside = fixed value

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Common Pitfall: Mapping Constants




Code
# WRONG - Don't map constants
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = "blue")) +        # ❌
  geom_point()

# CORRECT - Set fixed values outside aes
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")         # ✓

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_wrap(): Single Variable Faceting




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Use for: Creating subplots for each level of one categorical variable

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_wrap(): Multiple Columns




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkred") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region, ncol = 2) +
  theme_minimal()



ncol parameter controls layout columns

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
facet_grid(): Two Variable Grid




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  facet_grid(Gender ~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Use for: Creating a grid with rows and columns from two variables
Formula: rows ~ columns

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Free Scales in Facets




Code
# Create data with different ranges
smoking_bp <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m),
               names_to = "BP_Type",
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(smoking_bp, aes(x = SmokingStatus, y = Value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ BP_Type, scales = "free_y")



scales: “fixed” (default), “free”, “free_x”, “free_y”

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Facets with Multiple Geoms




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              color = "darkred", se = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  theme_minimal()



Each facet gets all layers - points and smooth line

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Complex Faceting Example




Code
# Handle missing data
bp_complete <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq))

ggplot(bp_complete, 
       aes(x = AgeGroup, y = SysBP_Change,
           fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ ExerciseFreq, ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = 
          element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
Theme System Overview

Themes control non-data elements of plots
Affect: fonts, colors, backgrounds, grid lines, axes
ggplot2 includes 8 built-in complete themes
Each theme suited for different contexts
Can be customized further with theme() function


Basic usage: + theme_minimal()

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_gray() - Default Theme




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_gray(base_size = 14)



Characteristics: Gray background, white grid lines
Best for: General exploratory analysis, default choice

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_bw() - Black and White




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)



Characteristics: White background, gray grid lines, black border
Best for: Professional reports, publications, clean appearance

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 2
text:
theme_minimal() - Minimalist




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m, 
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

title: Best Practices
text:
Introduction to Data Visualization

“The simple graph has brought more information to the data analyst’s mind than any other device.” - John Tukey


Data visualization transforms complex data into visual insights
Good visualizations tell a story
Poor visualizations mislead or confuse
Every choice matters - especially in healthcare

title: Best Practices
text:
The Big Idea
Can you summarize your message in one sentence?

Your “Big Idea” should be:

Articulate your point of view: What do you want your audience to know?
Convey what’s at stake: Why does this matter?
Be a complete sentence: Not just a topic, but a statement

Example: “We should implement early discharge planning because it reduces readmissions by 35%”

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
text:
Principle 1: Choose the Right Chart Type
Match your visualization to your data and message
Different types of data require different visualizations:

Simple text: 1-2 key numbers
Tables: Multiple precise values
Categorical: Bar charts (horizontal preferred)
Continuous over time: Line charts, area charts
Distributions: Histograms, boxplots, violin plots, density plots
Relationships: Scatter plots, correlations
Comparisons: Slopegraphs, small multiples
Part-to-whole: Stacked bars (avoid pie charts)

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Simple Text


Effective: When you have just 1-2 key numbers, text is more impactful than a chart. Makes the metric impossible to miss and allows for immediate comprehension.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Table


Effective: Tables excel when precise values matter and units differ. Better than charts when readers need exact numbers for comparison or reference.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Heatmap


Effective: Heatmaps encode values with color, making patterns instantly visible in large tables. Ideal for spotting trends across two categorical dimensions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars are preferred for categorical comparisons. Long labels read naturally, and length comparisons are easier than height comparisons.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Grouped Bar Chart


Effective: Grouped bars allow direct comparison across two categorical variables. The gap between groups creates visual separation that aids comprehension.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels
text:
Avoid: Vertical Bars with Long Labels


Ineffective: Vertical bars with long labels force text rotation, making reading difficult. Horizontal bars solve this problem naturally.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Line Chart


Effective: Line charts emphasize continuity and trend direction over time. The connecting line helps viewers see patterns and predict future values.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Area Chart


Effective: Stacked area charts show both individual trends and cumulative total. The filled areas emphasize volume and make the overall trend prominent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Multiple Line Series


Effective: Multiple series work when normalized to comparable scales. Different colors distinguish series while the shared timeline enables pattern comparison across variables.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter Plot


Effective: Scatter plots reveal relationships between continuous variables. The trend line and confidence interval quantify the strength and uncertainty of the relationship.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Scatter with Categories


Effective: Adding categories to scatter plots reveals whether relationships hold across subgroups. Parallel slopes suggest consistent effects; diverging slopes indicate interactions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Boxplot


Effective: Boxplots show distribution shape through quartiles. The box contains 50% of data, whiskers show range, and outliers appear as points - all in one compact visual.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Violin Plot


Effective: Violin plots reveal distribution details that boxplots hide. The width at each point shows density, making bimodal distributions and skewness immediately apparent.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Density Plot


Effective: Density plots show smooth distribution curves, ideal for comparing shapes between groups. Overlapping areas make differences in location, spread, and skewness clear.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Ridgeline Plot


Effective: Ridgeline plots stack density curves for easy comparison across many categories. The slight overlap creates visual flow while maintaining distinct distributions.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Slopegraph


Effective: Slopegraphs excel at showing change between two time points. The slope angle immediately conveys magnitude and direction of change for each entity.

title: Best Practices
text:
Chart Type: Stacked Bar Chart


Effective: Stacked bars show part-to-whole relationships over time. Total height shows cumulative volume while segment heights reveal individual contributions.

title: Best Practices
section: Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero
text:
Avoid: Y-Axis Not Starting at Zero


Ineffective: Truncating the Y-axis on bar charts distorts proportional relationships. What is actually a 3% difference appears as a 3-fold difference due to the missing baseline.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Y-Axis Starting at Zero


Effective: Starting bar charts at zero shows true proportions. Now it’s clear that all hospitals perform similarly at high levels with minimal variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Avoid: Pie Charts


Ineffective: Humans struggle with angle and area estimation. Quick: is Respiratory or Other larger? Pie charts make simple comparisons unnecessarily difficult.

title: Best Practices
text:
Better: Horizontal Bar Chart


Effective: Horizontal bars make comparisons effortless. Rankings are immediately clear, and length differences are precisely perceivable unlike angles in pie charts.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 2: Eliminate Clutter
Remove anything that doesn’t add value

Remove chart borders and backgrounds
Lighten or remove gridlines

Remove redundant data labels
Direct labeling > legends (Gestalt principle of connection)
Clean up axis labels
Maximize data-to-ink ratio (Tufte’s principle)

title: Best Practices
text:
Data-to-Ink Ratio: Maximizing Information
Every drop of ink should represent data

Data ink: Ink that represents actual data points
Non-data ink: Gridlines, borders, backgrounds, decorations
Goal: Maximize the ratio of data ink to total ink
Remove chart junk: 3D effects, unnecessary colors, decorative elements
Keep only what serves comprehension

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Default Plot (Cluttered)


Ineffective: Gray background, heavy gridlines, legend requiring eye travel, and borders all compete for attention. The data-to-ink ratio is low - most ink conveys no data.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Decluttered with Direct Labels


Effective: High data-to-ink ratio achieved by removing backgrounds, excess gridlines, and legend. Direct labels connect to data via proximity (Gestalt principle).

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 3: Use Preattentive Attributes
Attention with attributes processed in <250ms

Color: Most powerful
Size: Indicates importance
Position: Spatial relationships
Intensity: Bold vs light
Use strategically - don’t dilute attention

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: All Equal (No Focus)


Ineffective: All bars are equal - where should the viewer look? No visual hierarchy means no clear message.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Strategic Highlighting


Effective: Red instantly draws the eye to the problem. Gray provides context without competing for attention.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Using Size for Emphasis


Effective: Size combined with color creates a clear hierarchy. The large red point in August demands attention while smaller gray points provide context.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 4: Gray and Bold Technique
Use color to highlight, gray to push back

Bold color for what matters most
Gray for supporting context
Maximum one bold color per chart
Creates instant visual hierarchy
Reduces cognitive load

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Too Many Colors


Ineffective: Multiple bold colors fragment attention. When everything demands attention, nothing gets it.

title: Best Practices
text:
Example: Gray and Bold Applied


Effective: One bold color directs attention immediately to the problem area. Gray bars provide necessary context without distraction.

title: Best Practices
text:
Principle 5: Think Like a Designer
Visual design principles enhance communication

Accessibility: Colorblind-safe palettes
Alignment: Create invisible structure
White space: Let your data breathe
Contrast: Guide the eye
Typography: Readable, professional fonts

title: Best Practices
text:
Accessibility: Colorblind-Safe Palettes


Always use colorblind-safe palettes. Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women have color vision deficiency. Blue-orange combinations work for nearly everyone.

title: Best Practices
text:
Design Principles: Alignment & Spacing


Effective design: Generous margins, aligned text, strategic white space, and clear visual hierarchy make the message instantly clear and professional.

title: Best Practices
text:
Using Annotations Strategically


Annotations tell the story. The chart clearly shows what happened, when it happened, and why it matters - the viewer doesn’t need to guess.

title: Best Practices
text:
Before/After: Design Transformation


Design transformation: horizontal orientation, strategic color, descriptive title, reference line, and clean styling create a professional, focused message.

title: Best Practices
section: Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
text:
Principle 6: Tell a Story with Data
Transform insights into narrative

Beginning: Set context (current state)
Middle: Show the problem/opportunity
End: Recommend action
Use descriptive titles that state your point
Guide your audience through the data

title: Best Practices
text:
Narrative vs Descriptive Titles


Narrative titles tell the story. The right chart doesn’t just show data - it communicates the achievement and its magnitude immediately.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Powerful Comparisons


Small multiples enable comparison. Same scales across panels make differences immediately visible. Trend lines show improvement rates at a glance.

title: Best Practices
text:
Small Multiples: Distribution Comparisons


Distribution comparison made easy. Procedure C clearly clusters below the target with minimal variation, while Procedure D shows high variability and longer recovery.

title: Best Practices
text:
Complete Story Example


Complete narrative: Beginning (context with peers), middle (intervention and dramatic improvement), end (current state showing success). Every element supports the story.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Handling Uncertainty


Show uncertainty honestly. Confidence intervals demonstrate that even accounting for variability, the new treatment shows meaningful improvement over the standard.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Distribution of Uncertainty


Full distribution view. The minimal overlap between distributions shows that the new treatment improvement is robust, not just a result of a few outliers.

title: Best Practices
text:
Advanced Topic: Correlation Matrices


Multivariate relationships at a glance. Correlation matrices reveal complex patterns - here showing BMI and stress as strongest blood pressure predictors.

title: Best Practices
text:
Common Pitfall: Cherry-Picking Time Ranges


Always show full context. The “growth” story disappears when viewing the complete timeline. Cherry-picking ranges is a common way to mislead.

title: Best Practices
section: Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense
text:
Edge Case: When Breaking Rules Makes Sense


Breaking the “zero baseline” rule is appropriate when zero is meaningless (temperature, stock prices, pH). The focus should be on clinically meaningful variation.

title: Best Practices
text:
Summary: Six Core Principles

Choose the Right Chart Type - Match visualization to data and message
Eliminate Clutter - Maximize data-to-ink ratio
Use Preattentive Attributes - Guide attention strategically
Apply Gray and Bold - Create visual hierarchy
Think Like a Designer - Professional, accessible presentation
Tell a Story - Transform insights into narrative

title: Best Practices
text:
Key Takeaways

Every choice matters - color, position, size, titles
Less is more - remove everything that doesn’t serve the message
Context is crucial - never cherry-pick data ranges
Accessibility counts - use colorblind-safe palettes
Focus attention - one bold color, clear hierarchy
Tell the story - guide your audience to action

title: Best Practices
text:
When to Break the Rules
Rules are guidelines, not laws

Zero baseline: not for temperature, stock prices, or indices
Pie charts: acceptable for simple two-part comparisons
Multiple colors: when showing categorical data without hierarchy
The test: Does breaking the rule serve your audience better?
Always ask: Am I making the data clearer or just different?

title: Best Practices
text:
Resources & Further Learning


Books

Storytelling with Data - Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic
The Visual Display of Quantitative Information - Edward Tufte
Good Charts - Scott Berinato


Online

ggplot2 documentation
R Graph Gallery
Data Visualization Society
Storytelling with Data blog

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Where we are

Session 3: the map is clustered (global Moran’s I)
Today: where? Which blocks form hot spots, cold spots or are odd ones out?
By the end you can:

compute local Moran’s I and classify HH, LL, HL, LH blocks
handle multiple testing
find hot and cold spots with Getis-Ord Gi*
run and read a spatial scan statistic

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
One statistic per area

loc <- localmoran(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
head(round(loc, 3), 4)

      Ii   E.Ii Var.Ii   Z.Ii Pr(z != E(Ii))
1 -0.228 -0.001  0.016 -1.773          0.076
2  0.094 -0.007  0.132  0.277          0.781
3 -0.043 -0.052  1.923  0.006          0.995
4  0.403 -0.007  0.140  1.099          0.272









Column
Meaning




Ii
this area’s local I: > 0 similar to neighbours, < 0 unlike them


Z.Ii
z-score


Pr(z != E(Ii))
two-sided p-value




The average of the local values equals the global I: the global statistic is the average of the local ones (0.499).

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Cluster types from the quadrant

z <- as.numeric(scale(blocks$dengue_per_100k)); lag_z <- lag.listw(lw, z, zero.policy = TRUE); p <- loc[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"]
blocks$lisa <- factor(case_when(p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant", z > 0 & lag_z > 0 ~ "High-High", z < 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
                                z > 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "High-Low", TRUE ~ "Low-High"),
                      levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High", "Not significant"))
table(blocks$lisa)


      High-High         Low-Low        High-Low        Low-High Not significant 
             11              10               1               0              57 



cols <- c("High-High" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low" = "#2c7bb6", "High-Low" = "#fdae61", "Low-High" = "#abd9e9", "Not significant" = "grey90")
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lisa), colour = "white") + scale_fill_manual(values = cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "LISA cluster map (p < 0.05, unadjusted)")



High-High: hot spot. Low-Low: cold spot
High-Low / Low-High: spatial outliers, unlike their neighbours: check the data first
Here: a hot spot in the south-east, a cold spot in the north-west, one outlier

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text: Cluster types from the quadrant

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Multiple testing
You ran 79 tests: at 5%, about 4 blocks look significant by chance, and the tests are correlated (neighbours share neighbours).

c(unadjusted = sum(p < 0.05), fdr = sum(p.adjust(p, "fdr") < 0.05), bonferroni = sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") < 0.05))

unadjusted        fdr bonferroni 
        22         13          3 



FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) is a sensible default; Bonferroni is the strictest
Treat LISA as exploratory: it tells you where to look
The analytic p-values assume near-normal data; localmoran_perm() gives permutation p-values for skewed rates

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Hot and cold spots directly
Gi* sums the values of an area and its neighbours (the * includes the area itself) and turns the sum into a z-score.

lw_self <- nb2listw(include.self(nb), style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
blocks$gi <- as.numeric(localG(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_self, zero.policy = TRUE))
blocks$gi_class <- cut(blocks$gi, c(-Inf, -2.58, -1.96, -1.65, 1.65, 1.96, 2.58, Inf),
                       labels = c("Cold 99%", "Cold 95%", "Cold 90%", "Not significant", "Hot 90%", "Hot 95%", "Hot 99%"))
table(blocks$gi_class)


       Cold 99%        Cold 95%        Cold 90% Not significant         Hot 90% 
              7               6               3              46               5 
        Hot 95%         Hot 99% 
              1              11 



ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = gi_class), colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cold 99%" = "#2166ac", "Cold 95%" = "#67a9cf", "Cold 90%" = "#d1e5f0", "Not significant" = "grey92",
                               "Hot 90%" = "#fddbc7", "Hot 95%" = "#ef8a62", "Hot 99%" = "#b2182b"), drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Getis-Ord Gi* hot and cold spots")

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text: Hot and cold spots directly

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Gi* or LISA?

LISA finds areas similar to their neighbours (hot or cold) and outliers.


Gi* finds where high (or low) sums concentrate: it separates hot from cold directly, but does not flag outliers.


Both run one test per area: apply the same multiple-testing caution.

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Kulldorff’s circles
Slide circles of many sizes over the map; for each ask whether it holds more cases than expected from the population. Reports the most likely cluster, its relative risk and a Monte Carlo p-value. Uses counts and population (Poisson), so no rates are needed.

cen_km <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_transform(blocks, 32644))) / 1000
set.seed(5)
sc <- scan.test(coords = cen_km, cases = blocks$dengue_cases, pop = blocks$population, nsim = 499, alpha = 0.05)
summary(sc)

  nregions max_dist cases    ex  rr stat     p
1       34     81.2   627 477.7 1.8 42.7 0.002



Read: blocks in the cluster, observed vs expected cases, relative risk, p-value
The maximum window (default 50% of the population) changes what you find; choose it deliberately
Report the model (Poisson), the window, the number of simulations

Which local tool?







Question
Tool




Which areas are clusters or outliers?
local Moran (LISA)


Where are hot and cold spots?
Getis-Ord Gi*


Is there one most likely cluster, from counts and population?
scan statistic


Are the results robust?

text:

What does the Kulldorff scan statistic report as its main result?

The most likely cluster, with its relative risk and p-value
A Moran’s I value for each one of the circles that was scanned
The spatial lag of each of the blocks in the whole study area

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Where we are

Session 1: spatial data, CRS, joins, honest maps
Every spatial test asks: are neighbouring areas more alike than chance?
First we must define “neighbour”. That definition is the spatial weights matrix, the most influential choice in the analysis
By the end you can:

build queen, rook, k-nearest and distance neighbours
turn them into row-standardised weights
compute and read a spatial lag
check how sensitive a result is to the choice

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Contiguity: share a boundary



Rook: share an edge
Queen: share an edge or a corner (the usual default)
Needs polygons; areas of similar size behave best
Watch for islands: areas with no neighbour



nb_q <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = TRUE,  snap = 1e-4)
nb_r <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = FALSE, snap = 1e-4)
c(queen_links = sum(card(nb_q)), rook_links = sum(card(nb_r)))

queen_links  rook_links 
        414         414 




summary(nb_q)

Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 79 
Number of nonzero links: 414 
Percentage nonzero weights: 6.633552 
Average number of links: 5.240506 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8 
 1  7 13 20 28  9  1 
1 least connected region:
3 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
24 with 8 links

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Seeing the links

cen <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(blocks))
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey70", main = "Queen contiguity")
plot(nb_q, cen, add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 0.4)



Check three things in summary(): the average number of neighbours (about 5 here), the least and most connected blocks, and any isolates (they break most tests unless zero.policy = TRUE).

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Distance and k-nearest neighbours

knn5 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 5))
d <- unlist(nbdists(knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 1)), cen))
nb_d <- dnearneigh(cen, 0, max(d))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "5 nearest neighbours"); plot(knn5, cen, add = TRUE, col = "blue", pch = 19, cex = 0.3)
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "Distance band"); plot(nb_d, cen, add = TRUE, col = "darkgreen", pch = 19, cex = 0.3)











Definition
Neighbours per area
Good for
Watch out for




Queen / rook
varies
polygons of similar size
islands; large areas have many neighbours


k nearest
exactly k
unequal areas, points
links across a gap that are not real


Distance band
varies
points, a travel-distance idea
too short: isolates; too long: everyone linked

text: Distance and k-nearest neighbours

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
section: A neighbour list says who; weights say how much
text:
A neighbour list says who; weights say how much







Style
Meaning




"B" binary
1 for every neighbour


"W" row-standardised
each area’s weights sum to 1; the usual choice


"S"
variance-stabilising




lw <- nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw$weights[[1]]

[1] 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25

sum(lw$weights[[1]])

[1] 1



With "W", area i gives each of its k neighbours weight 1/k. An area with 2 neighbours weights each by 0.5; one with 8 by 0.125.

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
The spatial lag

lag(x)i = Σj wij xj = the average of i’s neighbours


blocks$lag_rate <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$dengue_per_100k, zero.policy = TRUE)
c(lag_from_function = blocks$lag_rate[1], mean_of_neighbours = mean(blocks$dengue_per_100k[nb_q[[1]]]))

 lag_from_function mean_of_neighbours 
            27.825             27.825 



p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = NULL) + labs(title = "Rate")
p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lag_rate)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = NULL) + labs(title = "Spatial lag (neighbours' average)")
p1 + p2


The lag is smoother than the original. Moran’s I (Session 3) is essentially the slope of the lag on the value.

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Sensitivity

w_list <- list(queen = nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE), rook = nb2listw(nb_r, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
               knn5 = nb2listw(knn5, style = "W"), distance = nb2listw(nb_d, style = "W"))
map_dfr(w_list, \(w) { m <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, w, zero.policy = TRUE); tibble(I = round(unname(m$estimate[1]), 3), p = signif(m$p.value, 2)) }, .id = "weights")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  weights      I        p
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 queen    0.499 5   e-14
2 rook     0.499 5   e-14
3 knn5     0.511 1.80e-15
4 distance 0.543 1   e- 9



Here the pattern is strong, so the conclusion barely moves
With a weak pattern the answer can change with the weights
Justify the choice with the biology: how far does a mosquito, a patient or an exposure travel?
Report the weights and check sensitivity

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Common mistakes


Using the default without saying which one
Ignoring isolates (silently dropping areas) or areas with 15 neighbours
Using contiguity for points (they have no boundaries)
Computing distances in degrees instead of a projected CRS

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

Why are queen contiguity neighbours a poor choice for point data such as patient homes?

Points tend to have more than ten neighbours each
Queen contiguity needs the data in degrees, not in metres
Points have no boundaries to share, so contiguity does not exist
Contiguity can only be calculated for blocks with no missing data

Ignore it, since one single area will not change the results

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text: Ordinary regression assumes the residuals are independent. With areas, they usually are not: unexplained risk is shared between neighbours. This breaks standard errors, and the usual diagnostic is Moran’s I on the residuals. This page runs the whole workflow.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
1. Fit the ordinary model

ols <- lm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks)
summary(ols)$coefficients |> round(3)

              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   -101.067     61.802  -1.635    0.106
poverty_index    1.445      0.335   4.306    0.000
literacy_pct     0.981      0.603   1.629    0.107

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
section: 2. Test the residuals for spatial autocorrelation
text:
2. Test the residuals for spatial autocorrelation

lm.morantest(ols, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Global Moran I for regression residuals

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
weights: lw

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.4335, p-value = 4.635e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
     0.273945405     -0.023128244      0.004489825 


A significant, positive Moran’s I of the residuals means the model leaves spatial structure unexplained: the independence assumption fails, and standard errors are probably too small.

blocks$res_ols <- residuals(ols)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = res_ols)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", name = "Residual") + labs(title = "OLS residuals: neighbouring blocks share the same sign")

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
section: 3. Which spatial model? Lagrange multiplier tests
text:
3. Which spatial model? Lagrange multiplier tests
Two common spatial structures:








Model
Idea
Equation (sketch)




Spatial lag (SAR)
my outcome depends on my neighbours’ outcomes (spillover, contagion)
\(y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon\)


Spatial error (SEM)
unmeasured shared factors make neighbouring errors alike
\(y = X\beta + u,\; u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon\)



The LM tests and their robust versions help choose:

lm.RStests(ols, lw, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"), zero.policy = TRUE)


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

RSerr = 14.895, df = 1, p-value = 0.0001137


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

RSlag = 19.289, df = 1, p-value = 1.124e-05


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

adjRSerr = 0.15191, df = 1, p-value = 0.6967


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

adjRSlag = 4.5459, df = 1, p-value = 0.033


Rule of thumb: if both RSerr and RSlag are significant, prefer the model whose robust test (adjRSerr or adjRSlag) is larger and significant. If only one is, use that. Use theory as well: contagion points to lag, omitted shared exposures to error.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
4. Fit the spatial models

library(spatialreg)
sem <- errorsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
sar <- lagsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
summary(sem)$Coef |> round(3)

              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)    -39.286     53.414  -0.736    0.462
poverty_index    0.956      0.344   2.779    0.005
literacy_pct     0.513      0.512   1.002    0.316

c(lambda = sem$lambda, rho = sar$rho) |> round(3)

lambda.lambda       rho.rho 
        0.535         0.515 


lambda (error model) and rho (lag model) measure the spatial dependence; their likelihood-ratio tests (in the model summary()) say whether it is needed.

tibble(model = c("OLS", "Spatial error", "Spatial lag"), AIC = c(AIC(ols), AIC(sem), AIC(sar))) |> mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  model           AIC
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 OLS            698.
2 Spatial error  687.
3 Spatial lag    685.


The lower the AIC the better; compare them on the same data.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
5. Check the residuals again

moran.test(residuals(sem), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1] |> round(3)

Moran I statistic 
           -0.042 

moran.test(residuals(ols), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1] |> round(3)

Moran I statistic 
            0.274 


If the residual Moran’s I has dropped close to its expectation (about 0), the model has absorbed the spatial structure.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
6. Interpreting coefficients: a warning

In the error model the coefficients keep the OLS meaning (change in rate per unit of the covariate), but with corrected standard errors.
In the lag model a change in a block’s covariate also changes neighbours’ outcomes, which feed back. The coefficient is not the total effect; use impacts (direct, indirect and total):


set.seed(6)
imp <- impacts(sar, listw = lw, R = 199)
summary(imp, zstats = TRUE, short = TRUE)

Impact measures (lag, exact):
                       Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.9339023 0.8647157 1.798618
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.8134276 0.7531661 1.566594
========================================================
Simulation results ( variance matrix):
========================================================
Simulated standard errors
                       Direct  Indirect     Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.3400153 0.5790857 0.7998079
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.6010227 0.8975023 1.4072140

Simulated z-values:
                      Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 2.715598 1.5611009 2.284744
literacy_pct dy/dx  1.332292 0.9089538 1.148742

Simulated p-values:
                    Direct    Indirect Total   
poverty_index dy/dx 0.0066156 0.11850  0.022328
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.1827641 0.36337  0.250662

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
Other routes

Add covariates that explain the clustering (poverty here may not be the only driver); if the residual autocorrelation vanishes you may not need a spatial model.
Mixed models with a spatial random effect (CAR/BYM in INLA or brms) are the standard for small-area disease mapping with count data and different populations.
Geographically weighted regression lets coefficients vary over space.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
Take-home

Always test the residuals of a regression on areas, with lm.morantest().
LM tests (and their robust versions) suggest lag or error; theory should agree.
Report the spatial parameter (rho or lambda), compare AIC with OLS, re-check the residuals, and use impacts for the lag model.
For counts and unequal populations, look at Poisson models with spatial random effects.

Practise it: this page is the reading for GIS workshop, Session 5: Spatial regression, which has the lab.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
Self-check quiz

After fitting lm() on block rates, what should you always test?

The outcome’s normality with a Q-Q plot

The CRS of the block boundaries
Whether the map uses quantile breaks



In a spatial lag model, why is the coefficient not the total effect?

The model drops blocks with no neighbours
Changes spill over to neighbours and feed back
The coefficient is on the log scale
Lag coefficients are standardised by the block area



Robust LM tests favour the error model. How do its coefficients read?

As in OLS, but with corrected standard errors
As changes in the neighbours’ outcome only
As elasticities, in percent per percent change

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text: Moran’s I is the workhorse, but it is one of several tools. This page covers the others you will meet in papers, when each is the right one, and how to run them on the same synthetic district.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Geary’s C
Moran’s I compares each area with the mean; Geary’s C compares neighbouring values directly (squared differences), so it is more sensitive to local differences.

C ≈ 1: no spatial autocorrelation.
C < 1: positive autocorrelation (neighbours are similar).
C > 1: negative autocorrelation.

Note the direction is opposite to Moran’s I. The two usually agree; when they disagree, look at local patterns.

geary.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Geary C test under randomisation

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k 
weights: lw   

Geary C statistic standard deviate = 7.6519, p-value = 9.903e-15
alternative hypothesis: Expectation greater than statistic
sample estimates:
Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.466797918       1.000000000       0.004855649

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
section: Getis-Ord General G: do high values or low values cluster?
text:
Getis-Ord General G: do high values or low values cluster?
Moran’s I cannot tell hot-spot clustering from cold-spot clustering: both give positive I. The General G can, because it sums the products of values in neighbouring pairs. Its values must be positive.

lw_b <- nb2listw(nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)       # G uses binary weights
globalG.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Getis-Ord global G statistic

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k 
weights: lw_b   

standard deviate = 3.0397, p-value = 0.001184
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Global G statistic        Expectation           Variance 
      7.320125e-02       6.718598e-02       3.916081e-06 


If G is above its expectation with a small p-value, high values cluster together (hot spots dominate). Below its expectation: low values cluster (cold spots).

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Join counts: binary data
For a yes/no variable (“high-burden block”), count the joins (shared borders) by type: High-High, Not-Not, and High-Not. If High areas touch each other more than expected, the pattern is clustered.

joincount.test(blocks$high_burden, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Join count test under nonfree sampling

data:  blocks$high_burden 
weights: lw_b 

Std. deviate for Not high = 5.4811, p-value = 2.113e-08
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Same colour statistic           Expectation              Variance 
            125.00000              99.77118              21.18619 


    Join count test under nonfree sampling

data:  blocks$high_burden 
weights: lw_b 

Std. deviate for High = 6.1757, p-value = 3.294e-10
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Same colour statistic           Expectation              Variance 
             39.00000              18.54333              10.97242 


The output has one test per category. “High” joins observed above expected (positive z) means high-burden blocks are neighbours more often than chance. Use it when the variable is truly categorical, or after you have dichotomised a rate, but remember that cutting a continuous variable loses information.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
section: Getis-Ord Gi*: hot and cold spots
text:
Getis-Ord Gi*: hot and cold spots
The local version of G gives each area a z-score from the sum of its own value and its neighbours’ (the * means the area itself is included).

nb_self <- include.self(nb)                               # the * : include the area itself
lw_self <- nb2listw(nb_self, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
blocks$gi <- as.numeric(localG(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_self, zero.policy = TRUE))
blocks$gi_class <- cut(blocks$gi, c(-Inf, -2.58, -1.96, -1.65, 1.65, 1.96, 2.58, Inf),
                       labels = c("Cold 99%", "Cold 95%", "Cold 90%", "Not significant", "Hot 90%", "Hot 95%", "Hot 99%"))
table(blocks$gi_class)


       Cold 99%        Cold 95%        Cold 90% Not significant         Hot 90% 
              7               6               3              46               5 
        Hot 95%         Hot 99% 
              1              11 



ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = gi_class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cold 99%" = "#2166ac", "Cold 95%" = "#67a9cf", "Cold 90%" = "#d1e5f0", "Not significant" = "grey92",
                               "Hot 90%" = "#fddbc7", "Hot 95%" = "#ef8a62", "Hot 99%" = "#b2182b"), drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Getis-Ord Gi* hot and cold spots", subtitle = "z-score bands (|z| > 1.65, 1.96, 2.58)") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")














Note



Gi* and LISA ask different questions. LISA (local Moran) finds areas similar to their neighbours, hot or cold, plus outliers. Gi* finds where high (or low) sums concentrate, so it separates hot from cold directly but does not flag outliers. Compare the two maps; as with LISA, you ran many tests, so treat bands with the same caution (consider an FDR adjustment).

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
The spatial scan statistic
Kulldorff’s scan statistic (the method behind SaTScan) moves circles of many sizes over the map and asks, for each, whether it contains more cases than expected from the population. It reports the most likely cluster and its p-value (by Monte Carlo), and any secondary clusters. It is the standard tool for disease cluster detection because it uses counts and population directly (Poisson model), so it handles different populations without first computing rates.

library(smerc)
cen_km <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_transform(blocks, 32644))) / 1000     # kilometres
set.seed(5)
sc <- scan.test(coords = cen_km, cases = blocks$dengue_cases, pop = blocks$population, nsim = 499, alpha = 0.05)
summary(sc)

  nregions max_dist cases    ex  rr stat     p
1       34     81.2   627 477.7 1.8 42.7 0.002



cl <- sc$clusters[[1]]
blocks$scan <- ifelse(seq_len(nrow(blocks)) %in% cl$locids, "Most likely cluster", "Other")
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = scan), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Most likely cluster" = "#d7191c", "Other" = "grey90"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Most likely cluster (Kulldorff scan, Poisson model)")








Read the output as: the blocks in the cluster, the observed and expected cases, the relative risk inside versus outside, and the p-value. Choose the maximum circle size (default 50% of the population) deliberately; a bigger window finds larger, more diffuse clusters.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Which test should I use?






flowchart TD
  A[Spatial pattern question] --> B{Variable type}
  B -->|Continuous rate or measurement| C{Question}
  B -->|Yes/no or categories| J[Join counts]
  B -->|Case counts and population| S[Scan statistic]
  C -->|Is there clustering at all?| D[Moran's I, with Geary's C as check]
  C -->|Do high or low values cluster?| G[General G]
  C -->|Where are the clusters?| E{Interest}
  E -->|Clusters and outliers| L[Local Moran, LISA]
  E -->|Hot and cold spots| H[Getis-Ord Gi*]

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Take-home

Geary’s C (1 = none, below 1 = clustering) is a global check that reacts to local differences.
General G separates hot-spot from cold-spot clustering; Moran’s I cannot.
Join counts serve binary variables; Gi* gives hot and cold spots; the scan statistic finds the most likely cluster from counts and population.
Whatever the test, state the weights, the variable and any multiple-testing handling.
Next: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests.

Practise it: this page is the reading for GIS workshop, Session 4: Local clusters, which has the lab.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text: A choropleth colours each area by a value. It is the most common map in public health and also the easiest to get wrong. This page covers rates versus counts, classification, colour choice and an interactive version.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Counts mislead, rates do not

p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_cases)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Cases") + labs(title = "Dengue cases (counts)")
p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "per 100,000", option = "magma", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Dengue per 100,000 (rate)")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)








Counts follow population size; a populous block looks bad even when its risk is average. Map rates (or standardised ratios) for risk, counts for workload.

blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(r_cases_pop = cor(dengue_cases, population), r_rate_pop = cor(dengue_per_100k, population)) |> round(2)

  r_cases_pop r_rate_pop
1        0.67       0.16

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Classification changes the story
Continuous colour hides nothing but is hard to read; classes are easier but are a choice. Three common schemes (package classInt):

library(classInt)
cls <- function(x, style) cut(x, classIntervals(x, 5, style = style)$brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
long <- bind_rows(
  mutate(blocks, scheme = "Equal interval", cls = cls(dengue_per_100k, "equal")),
  mutate(blocks, scheme = "Quantile (equal counts)", cls = cls(dengue_per_100k, "quantile")),
  mutate(blocks, scheme = "Natural breaks (Jenks)", cls = cls(dengue_per_100k, "jenks")))
ggplot(long) + geom_sf(aes(fill = cls), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ scheme) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = "per 100,000") + theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank())









Equal interval: honest about the scale, but a skewed variable puts most areas in one class.
Quantile: every class has the same number of areas, so there is always a “worst 20%” even if all are similar.
Natural breaks: groups similar values; breaks depend on the data, so maps are hard to compare.

State the scheme and the breaks in the caption. For comparing maps, use the same fixed breaks.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Colour

Use a sequential palette (light to dark) for rates; a diverging palette only when there is a meaningful midpoint (e.g. ratio to the district average = 1).
Avoid rainbow palettes; check that the map reads in grey-scale and for colour-blind viewers (viridis is safe).


blocks$rr <- blocks$dengue_per_100k / (sum(blocks$dengue_cases) / sum(blocks$population) * 1e5)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = rr)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 1, name = "Rate ratio\nvs district") +
  labs(title = "Diverging scale centred on the district rate")

title: Maps and Choropleths
section: Layers, labels and the finishing touches
text:
Layers, labels and the finishing touches

fac <- read_csv("../data/gis/facilities.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644) |> st_transform(4326)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = fac, aes(shape = type), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Oranges", direction = 1, name = "Dengue per\n100,000") +
  labs(title = "Dengue incidence and health facilities", subtitle = "Synthetic district, 79 blocks", shape = "Facility") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())








Good maps carry a title, a legend with units, the data source, and a north arrow / scale bar when the area matters (ggspatial::annotation_scale() and annotation_north_arrow()).

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Interactive map

library(leaflet)
pal <- colorNumeric("YlOrRd", blocks$dengue_per_100k)
leaflet(blocks) |> addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") |>
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(dengue_per_100k), fillOpacity = 0.8, weight = 1, color = "white",
              label = ~paste0(block_name, ": ", dengue_per_100k, " per 100,000"),
              highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 3, color = "black", bringToFront = TRUE)) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~dengue_per_100k, title = "Dengue per 100,000")











Note



The synthetic district has made-up positions, so the base map shows empty countryside. With real boundaries the tiles give context.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Take-home

Map rates, not counts, unless you mean workload.
Classification is a choice: report it, and keep breaks fixed when comparing maps.
Use sequential colour for rates and diverging colour only around a meaningful midpoint.
A map can look clustered by eye; to test it, go to Neighbours and Spatial Weights and Global Moran’s I.

Practise it: this page is the reading for GIS workshop, Session 1: Spatial data, which has the lab.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:

Block A has 40 dengue cases and 40,000 people; block B has 20 cases and 5,000 people. What should the map show?

Counts: A has twice the burden of B
Rates: B has the higher burden per person
Counts, because rates hide the real cases
Population, since cases follow population

Quantile breaks are required by journals
Different breaks can change the map’s story
ggplot2 cannot draw a map without breaks
Readers need it to compute the p-value of the map

A diverging scheme centred on the mean

title: Welcome

🟤 Workshop Key Unlocked
GIS and Spatial Statistics Track
An elective track. A five-session workshop on spatial data and spatial statistics in R: maps with sf, neighbours and weights, Moran’s I, local clusters and hot spots, and spatial regression. All examples use a synthetic district of 80 blocks with a planted hot spot, so no real boundaries or personal data are involved. The full visualization library is in the navbar as well.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text: The global Moran’s I says the map is clustered. Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), here local Moran’s I, say where: they give each area its own statistic, test and cluster type.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
One statistic per area

loc <- localmoran(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
head(round(loc, 3))

      Ii   E.Ii Var.Ii   Z.Ii Pr(z != E(Ii))
1 -0.228 -0.001  0.016 -1.773          0.076
2  0.094 -0.007  0.132  0.277          0.781
3 -0.043 -0.052  1.923  0.006          0.995
4  0.403 -0.007  0.140  1.099          0.272
5  0.018 -0.002  0.045  0.095          0.924
6  0.327 -0.004  0.060  1.346          0.178









Column
Meaning




Ii
local Moran’s I of this area (positive: similar to its neighbours; negative: unlike them)


E.Ii, Var.Ii
its expectation and variance with no pattern


Z.Ii
z-score


Pr(z != E(Ii))
two-sided p-value



The sum of the local values divided by the sum of the weights equals the global I: the global statistic is the average of the local ones.

c(global = unname(moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1]),
  mean_local = mean(loc[, "Ii"])) |> round(3)

    global mean_local 
     0.499      0.499

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Cluster types from the quadrants
Combine the quadrant from the Moran scatterplot with significance:

z <- as.numeric(scale(blocks$dengue_per_100k)); lag_z <- lag.listw(lw, z, zero.policy = TRUE)
p <- loc[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"]
blocks$lisa <- case_when(
  p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant",
  z > 0 & lag_z > 0 ~ "High-High (hot spot)",
  z < 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "Low-Low (cold spot)",
  z > 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "High-Low (outlier)",
  TRUE ~ "Low-High (outlier)")
blocks$lisa <- factor(blocks$lisa, levels = c("High-High (hot spot)", "Low-Low (cold spot)", "High-Low (outlier)", "Low-High (outlier)", "Not significant"))
table(blocks$lisa)


High-High (hot spot)  Low-Low (cold spot)   High-Low (outlier) 
                  11                   10                    1 
  Low-High (outlier)      Not significant 
                   0                   57 



cols <- c("High-High (hot spot)" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low (cold spot)" = "#2c7bb6", "High-Low (outlier)" = "#fdae61", "Low-High (outlier)" = "#abd9e9", "Not significant" = "grey90")
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lisa), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) + scale_fill_manual(values = cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "LISA cluster map of dengue incidence", subtitle = "p < 0.05, unadjusted, queen weights") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))








In this synthetic district the generator planted a hot spot in the south-east, a cold spot in the north-west and one high block inside the cold area. The map should show all three: the red group, the blue group, and an orange High-Low outlier.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Multiple testing
You just ran 79 tests. At 5% about 4 areas appear “significant” by chance alone, and the tests are correlated because neighbouring areas share neighbours. Adjust the p-values with p.adjust() or be cautious:

p_fdr <- p.adjust(p, method = "fdr")                 # adjust the 79 p-values (Benjamini-Hochberg)
c(unadjusted_p_lt_05 = sum(p < 0.05), fdr_adjusted_p_lt_05 = sum(p_fdr < 0.05), bonferroni_p_lt_05 = sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") < 0.05))

  unadjusted_p_lt_05 fdr_adjusted_p_lt_05   bonferroni_p_lt_05 
                  22                   13                    3 



"bonferroni" is the most conservative, "fdr" (Benjamini-Hochberg) controls the false discovery rate and is a sensible default.
Treat LISA as exploratory: it shows where to look, not proof of a cluster in each area.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
A permutation version
The analytical p-values assume the data are close to normal. Conditional permutation shuffles the neighbours’ values around each area, and works better for skewed rates:

set.seed(3)
loc_perm <- localmoran_perm(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, nsim = 499, zero.policy = TRUE)
head(round(loc_perm, 3), 3)

      Ii   E.Ii Var.Ii   Z.Ii Pr(z != E(Ii)) Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim Pr(folded) Sim
1 -0.228 -0.007  0.017 -1.681          0.093              0.084          0.042
2  0.094 -0.028  0.130  0.338          0.735              0.752          0.376
3 -0.043  0.001  2.039 -0.031          0.976              0.980          0.492
  Skewness Kurtosis
1    0.151   -0.003
2   -0.188   -0.010
3    0.186   -0.158

c(analytic_sig = sum(p < 0.05), permutation_sig = sum(loc_perm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"] < 0.05))

   analytic_sig permutation_sig 
             22              22

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Reading cluster maps

A High-High area has a high value and high-value neighbours: a hot spot, where to look for a shared cause or to target an intervention.
A High-Low area is a spatial outlier: unusually high among low neighbours (a local outbreak, a data problem, a special site). Check the record before interpreting.
The result depends on the weights, the variable (rates, not counts) and the significance rule. Say which you used.
Each area’s cluster status uses its neighbours, so a hot spot typically covers several areas, not one.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Take-home

Local Moran’s I gives a statistic and p-value per area; the quadrant tells the cluster type (HH, LL, HL, LH).
You ran many tests: adjust ("fdr") or treat the result as exploratory, and consider permutation p-values.
Pair the global test with the local map, and always report variable, weights and adjustment.
Next: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, join counts and the scan statistic.

Practise it: this page is the reading for GIS workshop, Session 4: Local clusters, which has the lab.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Self-check quiz

You ran local Moran’s I on 79 blocks. About how many look ‘significant’ at 5% by chance alone?

None
About 4
About 40
All 79



A block is in the High-Low quadrant. What is it?

A low value surrounded by high values
A high value among other high values
A high value surrounded by low values
A block with no neighbours at all



How should a LISA cluster map be treated?

As proof that each marked block is a cluster
As exploratory: where to look, not proof
As a replacement for the global Moran’s I
As a map of the raw dengue counts
