title: Global Moran’s I
text: Moran’s I is the standard test for spatial autocorrelation: are areas with high values next to other high areas, and low next to low, more often than chance would give? (“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.”) It answers one global question for the whole map. Where the clusters are is the job of local Moran’s I.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
The idea in four areas
Four areas in a row, neighbours = the adjacent ones. Values: 1, 2, 9, 10.

v <- c(1, 2, 9, 10)
nb4 <- list(2L, c(1L, 3L), c(2L, 4L), 3L); class(nb4) <- "nb"; attr(nb4, "region.id") <- as.character(1:4)
lw4 <- nb2listw(nb4, style = "W")
z <- v - mean(v)
I_hand <- (length(v) / sum(unlist(lw4$weights))) * sum(z * lag.listw(lw4, z)) / sum(z^2)
c(by_hand = I_hand, moran_test = unname(moran.test(v, lw4)$estimate[1]))

   by_hand moran_test 
 0.5384615  0.5384615 


\[ I \;=\; \frac{n}{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}}\;\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}\,(x_i-\bar x)(x_j-\bar x)}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2} \]
In words: multiply each area’s deviation from the mean by the average deviation of its neighbours (the lag), add up, and scale by the variance. If high areas have high neighbours the products are positive, so \(I>0\). The two big values sit together, so \(I\) is large and positive.







\(I\)
Meaning




near \(E[I] = -1/(n-1)\) (≈ 0)
no spatial pattern (random)


clearly > 0
positive autocorrelation: similar values cluster


clearly < 0
negative: neighbours differ, like a checkerboard (rare in health data)



\(I\) is not a correlation coefficient, but with row-standardised weights it is usually between about −1 and +1. It is the slope of the spatial lag on the value (see the scatterplot below).

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Run it on the district

mi <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
mi


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k  
weights: lw    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 7.4403, p-value = 5.025e-14
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.499247498      -0.012820513       0.004736744 


Read the output from the bottom: Moran I statistic (observed I), Expectation (what I would be with no pattern), Variance, and the z-score and p-value from the normal approximation. Here I is about 0.5 against an expectation near 0, with a tiny p-value: strong positive spatial autocorrelation.

A permutation (Monte Carlo) p-value
The normal approximation assumes things about the data. The permutation test shuffles the values over the areas many times and asks how often a shuffled map has an I as large as the real one. It is assumption-light and usually the better report.

set.seed(1)
mc <- moran.mc(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE)
mc


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k 
weights: lw  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.49925, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater



ggplot(tibble(I = mc$res[-length(mc$res)]), aes(I)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mc$statistic, colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Moran's I of shuffled maps", y = "Count", title = "The observed I (red) against 999 random maps")








The smallest possible one-sided p-value with 999 shuffles is 1/1000 = 0.001.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
The Moran scatterplot
Plot each area’s value (standardised) against its spatial lag (the average of its neighbours, standardised). The slope of the line is Moran’s I.

blocks$z <- as.numeric(scale(blocks$dengue_per_100k))
blocks$lag_z <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$z, zero.policy = TRUE)
ggplot(blocks, aes(z, lag_z)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = high_burden), size = 2.2) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = c(2.2, -2.2, 2.2, -2.2), y = c(2.2, -2.2, -2.2, 2.2), label = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High"), colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Dengue rate (standardised)", y = "Average of neighbours (standardised)", colour = "Block burden",
       title = "Moran scatterplot") 







coef(lm(lag_z ~ z, data = blocks))[["z"]] |> round(3)

[1] 0.499



High-High (top right) and Low-Low (bottom left) points create positive autocorrelation.
High-Low and Low-High points are spatial outliers: they differ from their surroundings. They are what LISA will flag.

title: Global Moran’s I
section: Does it depend on how you count?
text:
Does it depend on how you count?

set.seed(2)
tibble(variable = c("Dengue per 100,000", "Dengue cases (counts)", "Poverty index", "Literacy (%)", "Population"),
       x = list(blocks$dengue_per_100k, blocks$dengue_cases, blocks$poverty_index, blocks$literacy_pct, blocks$population)) |>
  mutate(res = map(x, \(v) moran.mc(v, lw, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE)),
         I = map_dbl(res, "statistic"), p = map_dbl(res, "p.value")) |>
  select(variable, I, p) |> mutate(I = round(I, 2))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  variable                  I     p
  <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl>
1 Dengue per 100,000     0.5  0.001
2 Dengue cases (counts)  0.3  0.001
3 Poverty index          0.75 0.001
4 Literacy (%)           0.53 0.001
5 Population            -0.01 0.48 


Poverty is spatially smooth; population is a random draw per block and shows nothing. Always say which variable and which weights you tested.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Pitfalls

Weights choice: repeat with another neighbour definition (page).
Rates with small populations are noisy. Unstable rates in small areas weaken or mimic clustering. For small-area rates, smooth them first (empirical Bayes: EBImoran.mc()).
Edge effects: areas on the border have fewer neighbours, because the study region is cut off.
The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP): the same people grouped into different areas can give different values of I.
One number for the whole map. A significant I does not say where the clusters are, and a non-significant I can hide a strong local cluster.
Association, not cause. Clustering suggests shared exposures (or contagion), it does not identify them.
Trend is not clustering. A smooth north-south gradient also gives positive I; if you suspect a trend, model it and test the residuals (regression page).

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
How to report it

Dengue incidence was strongly clustered across the 79 blocks (global Moran’s I = 0.50, queen-contiguity weights, row-standardised; permutation p = 0.001 with 999 simulations).

Give the statistic, the weights, the number of simulations and the p-value; follow with local analysis to say where.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Take-home

Moran’s I tests whether similar values are neighbours; compare it with its expectation of about 0.
Prefer the permutation p-value and always state the weights.
The Moran scatterplot shows the slope and the High-High, Low-Low, High-Low and Low-High groups.
A global test cannot locate clusters: next, Local Moran’s I (LISA).

Practise it: this page is the reading for GIS workshop, Session 3: Global autocorrelation, which has the lab.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Self-check quiz

Moran’s I is 0.45 with a permutation p of 0.001. What does it mean?

Blocks with high values are placed at random
Similar values tend to be neighbours
45% of blocks belong to one single cluster
The rate rises by 0.45 per neighbour



What can a global Moran’s I not tell you?

Whether there is clustering
Where the clusters are
Whether the pattern is random
The direction of autocorrelation



What must you always state when reporting Moran’s I?

The colour scheme of the map
The weights used, and the p-value method
The CRS of the original data file
The name of the R package that drew the map


Your score:  (first attempt counts)

title: Spatial Data with sf
text: This page introduces vector spatial data in R with the sf package, using a synthetic district of 79 blocks (data/gis/district_blocks.geojson) and 30 health facilities (data/gis/facilities.csv). The boundaries and numbers are invented; the district was built so that dengue incidence clusters in space, which the later pages exploit. gis/make_gis_data.R regenerates it.

title: Spatial Data with sf
text:
What is spatial data?



Type
Example
In R




Points
health facility, a case’s home
sf (POINT)


Lines
road, river
sf (LINESTRING)


Polygons
block, district, catchment area
sf (POLYGON)


Raster
population grid, satellite image
terra / stars



An sf object is a data frame with one extra column, geometry. All the dplyr verbs you already know work on it.

title: Spatial Data with sf
text:
Read and look

blocks <- st_read("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
class(blocks)

blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |> head()

18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE

st_bbox(blocks)

    xmin     ymin     xmax     ymax 
80.19153 26.66903 81.20188 27.57382

[1] 79



ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(fill = "grey95", colour = "grey40") + labs(title = "79 blocks of a synthetic district")

title: Spatial Data with sf
text:
Coordinate reference systems (CRS)
A CRS says how numbers become places. Two families matter:

Geographic (longitude/latitude, e.g. EPSG:4326, WGS 84): units are degrees. Good for storing and web maps, wrong for distances and areas.
Projected (metres, e.g. a UTM zone, EPSG:32644 for 78°E to 84°E in the northern hemisphere): good for area, length, distance and buffers.


st_crs(blocks)$input            # stored in longitude / latitude

[1] "WGS 84"

blocks_utm <- st_transform(blocks, 32644)
st_crs(blocks_utm)$input

[1] "EPSG:32644"








Warning



Always check the CRS before measuring. st_area() on degrees gives meaningless numbers. Transform to a projected CRS first. Two layers can only be combined when they share a CRS.



tibble(block = blocks_utm$block_id[1:3],
       area_km2_recorded = blocks_utm$area_km2[1:3],
       area_km2_computed = round(as.numeric(st_area(blocks_utm))[1:3] / 1e6, 1))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  block area_km2_recorded area_km2_computed
  <chr>             <dbl>             <dbl>

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text: Every spatial test in this track asks “are neighbouring areas more alike than chance?”. The word neighbour needs a definition first. That definition is the spatial weights matrix, and it is the most influential choice you make.

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Contiguity neighbours
Two polygons are neighbours if they share a boundary:

Rook: share an edge.
Queen: share an edge or a corner (usual default).


nb_q <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = TRUE,  snap = 1e-4)
nb_r <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = FALSE, snap = 1e-4)
summary(nb_q)

Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 79 
Number of nonzero links: 414 
Percentage nonzero weights: 6.633552 
Average number of links: 5.240506 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8 
 1  7 13 20 28  9  1 
1 least connected region:
3 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
24 with 8 links

c(queen_links = sum(card(nb_q)), rook_links = sum(card(nb_r)))

queen_links  rook_links 
        414         414 



cen <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(blocks))
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey70", main = "Queen contiguity: links between neighbouring blocks")
plot(nb_q, cen, add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 0.4)








Check three things in the summary: the average number of neighbours (here about 5), the least and most connected areas, and any isolates (areas with no neighbours, which break many tests unless you use zero.policy = TRUE).

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Distance-based and k-nearest neighbours
When areas are unequal in size, or are points, use distances between centroids:

knn5 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 5))                  # always exactly 5 neighbours
d <- unlist(nbdists(knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 1)), cen))
nb_d <- dnearneigh(cen, 0, max(d))                      # everyone within the smallest distance that links all areas
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "5 nearest neighbours"); plot(knn5, cen, add = TRUE, col = "blue", pch = 19, cex = 0.3)
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "Distance band"); plot(nb_d, cen, add = TRUE, col = "darkgreen", pch = 19, cex = 0.3)

















Definition
Neighbours per area
Good for
Watch out for




Queen / rook
varies
polygons of similar size
islands (isolates); big areas have many neighbours


k nearest
exactly k
unequal areas, points
links across a gap or border that are not real


Distance band
varies
points, catchment ideas
too short leaves isolates; too long links everything

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
From neighbours to weights
A neighbour list says who; weights say how much. Styles in nb2listw():

"B" binary: 1 for every neighbour.
"W" row-standardised: each area’s weights sum to 1, so a neighbour’s influence is shared out. The usual choice.
"S" variance-stabilising.


lw <- nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw$weights[[1]]           # the first block's weights: 1/(number of neighbours) each

[1] 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25

sum(lw$weights[[1]])

[1] 1

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
The spatial lag
The spatial lag of a variable is the weighted average of the neighbours’ values. With row-standardised weights it is simply “the average of my neighbours”:

blocks$lag_rate <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$dengue_per_100k, zero.policy = TRUE)
blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(block_id, dengue_per_100k, lag_rate) |> head(5) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))

  block_id dengue_per_100k lag_rate
1      B01            53.7     27.8
2      B02            31.0     44.9
3      B03            93.6     47.3
4      B04            30.5     35.7
5      B05            57.6     48.7

# check block 1 by hand:
mean(blocks$dengue_per_100k[nb_q[[1]]])

[1] 27.825



patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Rate") + labs(title = "Rate"),
  ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lag_rate)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Lag") + labs(title = "Spatial lag (neighbours' average)"))








The lag is smoother than the original. The Moran’s I statistic on the next page is essentially the slope of the lag against the value.

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
The choice matters

w_list <- list(queen = nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
               rook  = nb2listw(nb_r, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
               knn5  = nb2listw(knn5, style = "W"),
               distance = nb2listw(nb_d, style = "W"))
map_dfr(w_list, \(w) { m <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, w, zero.policy = TRUE); tibble(I = unname(m$estimate[1]), p = m$p.value) }, .id = "weights") |>
  mutate(I = round(I, 3), p = signif(p, 2))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  weights      I        p
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 queen    0.499 5   e-14
2 rook     0.499 5   e-14
3 knn5     0.511 1.80e-15
4 distance 0.543 1   e- 9


The conclusion is similar here because the clustering is strong, but with a weak pattern the answer can change with the weights. State your weights, justify them with the biology (how far does a mosquito or a person travel?) and check sensitivity.

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Take-home

A weights matrix turns “near” into numbers; choose it deliberately (queen for polygons, k-nearest or distance for points).
Row-standardised weights make the spatial lag the average of neighbours.
Look for isolates and areas with very many neighbours; report your choice and test the sensitivity.
Next: Global Moran’s I.

Practise it: this page is the reading for GIS workshop, Session 2: Neighbours and weights, which has the lab.

k-nearest neighbours or a distance band
Neighbours by alphabetical block name



An island block has no neighbours. Why does that matter?

It doubles the weight of every other block
Its lag is undefined; tests may fail or mislead
Moran’s I then drops to zero
It must be deleted from the data before any test

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Classification changes the story

library(classInt)
cls <- function(x, style) cut(x, classIntervals(x, 5, style = style)$brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
bind_rows(mutate(blocks, scheme = "Equal interval", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "equal")),
          mutate(blocks, scheme = "Quantile", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "quantile")),
          mutate(blocks, scheme = "Jenks", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "jenks"))) |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ scheme) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = NULL) + theme_void(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")



Equal interval: honest about scale, but a skewed variable crowds one class
Quantile: always shows a “worst 20%” even if all areas are similar
Jenks: groups similar values, but breaks change with the data
State the scheme and breaks; keep them fixed to compare maps

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Where we are

Sessions 1–2: spatial data, maps, neighbours and weights
Today: is the pattern clustered? One test for the whole map
By the end you can:

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Are similar values neighbours?

I = ( n / Σ wij ) × ΣiΣj wij (xi − x̄)(xj − x̄) / Σi (xi − x̄)²


Multiply each area’s deviation from the mean by its neighbours’ average deviation (the lag), then scale by the variance
High areas with high neighbours, low with low → products positive → I > 0
Expectation with no pattern: E[I] = −1/(n−1), about 0




I
Meaning




≈ 0
no spatial pattern


clearly > 0
clustering: similar values are neighbours


clearly < 0
dispersion: neighbours differ (a checkerboard; rare)

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Four areas by hand

v <- c(1, 2, 9, 10)
nb4 <- list(2L, c(1L, 3L), c(2L, 4L), 3L); class(nb4) <- "nb"; attr(nb4, "region.id") <- as.character(1:4)
lw4 <- nb2listw(nb4, style = "W"); z <- v - mean(v)
c(by_hand = (4 / sum(unlist(lw4$weights))) * sum(z * lag.listw(lw4, z)) / sum(z^2), moran_test = unname(moran.test(v, lw4)$estimate[1]))

   by_hand moran_test 
 0.5384615  0.5384615 


The two large values sit next to each other, so I is strongly positive. The function and the formula agree.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
On the district

mi <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
mi


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k  
weights: lw    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 7.4403, p-value = 5.025e-14
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.499247498      -0.012820513       0.004736744 



Read it from the bottom: observed I (about 0.5), its expectation (about 0), and the z-score and p-value. Strong positive spatial autocorrelation.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
The permutation (Monte Carlo) test
Shuffle the values over the areas 999 times; how often does a shuffled map beat the real I?

set.seed(1)
mc <- moran.mc(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE)
ggplot(tibble(I = mc$res[-length(mc$res)]), aes(I)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mc$statistic, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Moran's I of shuffled maps", title = paste0("Observed I (red) vs 999 shuffles: p = ", mc$p.value))



Assumption-light; usually the better p-value to report
With 999 shuffles the smallest p is 0.001

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Which global test?









Test
Question
Variable
Reading




Moran’s I
Are similar values neighbours?
continuous
I > E[I]: clustering


Geary’s C
Are neighbours’ differences small?
continuous
C < 1 clustering (opposite of I)


General G
Do high or low values cluster?
continuous, positive
G > E[G]: highs cluster


Join counts
Do same-category areas touch?
binary / categorical
more same-category joins than expected

Global G statistic        Expectation           Variance 
      7.320125e-02       6.718598e-02       3.916081e-06 

joincount.test(blocks$high_burden, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)[[2]]$estimate

Same colour statistic           Expectation              Variance 
             39.00000              18.54333              10.97242 



Moran’s I is positive for both hot-spot and cold-spot clustering. Only General G says whether the high values are the ones that cluster. Join counts suit a yes/no variable.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Pitfalls


Not saying which weights; not saying which variable (counts and rates differ)
Small areas give noisy rates, which hides or mimics clustering (smooth with empirical Bayes)
Edge effects and the modifiable areal unit problem: a different grouping can change I
A trend (north-south gradient) also gives positive I
A global test cannot say where; a non-significant I can hide a local cluster

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
How to report

Dengue incidence was strongly clustered across the 79 blocks (global Moran’s I = 0.50, queen contiguity, row-standardised weights; permutation p = 0.001, 999 simulations).

Give the statistic, the weights, the number of simulations and the p-value; then say where, with local methods.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
🔧 Switch to R — Lab 3

File: gis-workshop/labs/lab3_global.R

moran.test() · moran.mc() · the Moran scatterplot data
geary.test() · globalG.test() · joincount.test()
a variable with no spatial pattern for comparison


Time: 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

Global Moran’s I is 0.49 (permutation p = 0.001). What is the best interpretation?

49% of the variation in the rate is explained by the location
Each area’s rate is 0.49 higher than its neighbours’ average rate
Neighbouring areas are more alike than expected by chance
About half of all the areas lie in a significant local cluster

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

What is the expected value of Moran’s I when there is no spatial pattern?

Exactly 1, because every area is its own neighbour
About 0 (exactly −1/(n−1))
Exactly 0.5, halfway between the two extremes
It depends on the data, so there is no expected value

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

With 999 permutations, what is the smallest possible p-value from moran.mc()?

0, if the observed I is larger than every one of the shuffled values
0.05, which is the usual cut-off used for a significant result
0.001, as the observed value is one of 1000 arrangements
It varies from one data set to another and has no fixed minimum

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

Geary’s C is 0.47. How should this be read?

Neighbours differ strongly, so negative spatial autocorrelation
There is no spatial pattern, because C is not equal to zero
The result is invalid, because C must lie between 0 and 1
Neighbours are similar, so positive spatial autocorrelation

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

Moran’s I is positive and significant. What does the General G test add?

Whether high values (hot spots) or low values cluster
The exact location of each separate cluster on the map
A correction of the p-value for the multiple testing
Nothing, because it always gives the same answer as Moran’s I

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Moran’s I: are similar values neighbours? Compare with about 0
Prefer the permutation p-value; always give the weights
The Moran scatterplot shows slope = I and the four quadrants
Geary’s C (1 = none), General G (hot vs cold), join counts (binary)

Next: Session 4: local clusters and hot spots

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Where we are

Sessions 3–4: the outcome is spatially clustered, and we know where
Today: regression on areas. The usual assumption of independent residuals often fails
By the end you can:

test regression residuals for spatial autocorrelation
use Lagrange multiplier tests to choose lag or error
fit and compare spatial lag and spatial error models
report a spatial analysis

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Fit OLS first

ols <- lm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks)
round(summary(ols)$coefficients, 3)

              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   -101.067     61.802  -1.635    0.106
poverty_index    1.445      0.335   4.306    0.000
literacy_pct     0.981      0.603   1.629    0.107

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Moran’s I on the residuals

lm.morantest(ols, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Global Moran I for regression residuals

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
weights: lw

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.4335, p-value = 4.635e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
     0.273945405     -0.023128244      0.004489825 



A significant positive residual Moran’s I means the model leaves spatial structure unexplained: independence fails and standard errors are probably too small.


blocks$res_ols <- residuals(ols)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = res_ols)) + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", name = "Residual") +
  labs(title = "OLS residuals: neighbours share the same sign")

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text: Moran’s I on the residuals

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Two structures








Model
Idea
Think of




Spatial lag (SAR)
my outcome depends on my neighbours’ outcomes
contagion, spillover


Spatial error (SEM)
omitted shared factors make neighbouring errors alike
unmeasured exposures




Lag: y = ρWy + Xβ + ε   |   Error: y = Xβ + u, u = λWu + ε

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Lagrange multiplier tests

lm.RStests(ols, lw, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"), zero.policy = TRUE)

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Lagrange multiplier tests


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

RSerr = 14.895, df = 1, p-value = 0.0001137


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

RSlag = 19.289, df = 1, p-value = 1.124e-05


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

adjRSerr = 0.15191, df = 1, p-value = 0.6967


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

adjRSlag = 4.5459, df = 1, p-value = 0.033

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Choosing from the LM tests

If only one plain test is significant, use that model
If both are, prefer the model whose robust test (adjRSerr or adjRSlag) is larger and significant
Use theory too: contagion points to lag, omitted exposures to error

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Fit and compare

sem <- errorsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
sar <- lagsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
c(lambda = sem$lambda, rho = sar$rho) |> round(3)

lambda.lambda       rho.rho 
        0.535         0.515 

AIC(ols, sem, sar)

    df      AIC
ols  4 698.4286
sem  5 687.2759
sar  5 684.6838



c(OLS = unname(moran.test(residuals(ols), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1]), SEM = unname(moran.test(residuals(sem), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1])) |> round(3)

   OLS    SEM 
 0.274 -0.042 


Lower AIC is better (same data). The residual Moran’s I should fall towards 0.

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Coefficients in the lag model

In a lag model a change in one block’s poverty also changes its neighbours’ rates, which feed back. The coefficient is not the whole effect. Report impacts: direct, indirect and total.


set.seed(6)
summary(impacts(sar, listw = lw, R = 199), zstats = TRUE, short = TRUE)

Impact measures (lag, exact):
                       Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.9339023 0.8647157 1.798618
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.8134276 0.7531661 1.566594
========================================================
Simulation results ( variance matrix):
========================================================
Simulated standard errors
                       Direct  Indirect     Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.3400153 0.5790857 0.7998079
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.6010227 0.8975023 1.4072140

Simulated z-values:
                      Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 2.715598 1.5611009 2.284744
literacy_pct dy/dx  1.332292 0.9089538 1.148742

Simulated p-values:
                    Direct    Indirect Total   
poverty_index dy/dx 0.0066156 0.11850  0.022328
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.1827641 0.36337  0.250662


In the error model the coefficients keep the OLS meaning, with corrected standard errors.

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Other routes

Add covariates that explain the clustering; the residual autocorrelation may vanish
Count data with unequal populations: Poisson models with a spatial random effect (CAR / BYM in INLA, brms)
Geographically weighted regression lets coefficients vary over space
Always map the residuals

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Reporting checklist


The outcome (rate, not count) and the areas, with the CRS if distances were used
The weights: definition, standardisation, isolates
Global result: Moran’s I, p-value type, simulations
Local results: method, adjustment, map; say they are exploratory
Regression: residual Moran’s I, LM tests, model chosen and why, parameter (rho or lambda), AIC vs OLS, impacts for a lag model
Limitations: area size (MAUP), small numbers, edge effects, association not cause

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

Residuals of an area-level regression have a significant positive Moran’s I. What is the main consequence?

The regression coefficients become zero in each of the fitted models
The model must be refitted using fewer of the areas in the data
Standard errors are probably too small, so p-values are optimistic
The outcome variable is spatially random and so should be dropped

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

Which situation points to a spatial LAG model?

An unmeasured exposure affects blocks that lie next to each other
The outcome in an area influences its neighbours’ outcomes (contagion)
The residuals are normally distributed with a constant variance throughout
The covariates are strongly correlated with each other and with the outcome

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

Both plain LM tests are significant, but only the robust lag test is. What do you conclude?

A spatial error model is the better candidate
Neither model is needed, so ordinary regression is fine
A spatial lag model is the better candidate
The tests are contradictory, so they should be ignored

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

In a spatial lag model, why is the coefficient of a covariate not its full effect?

The coefficient is divided by the number of areas in the study
Lag models estimate the effects for the neighbours, not for the area
The coefficient is measured on a different scale from the outcome
A change in one area also changes its neighbours’ outcomes

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

After fitting a spatial error model, what should you check?

The residual Moran’s I, which should now be close to 0
Whether the number of blocks has doubled during fitting
That each covariate has become significant at the 5% level
Whether the lambda value has become equal to 1

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Always test residuals of an area-level regression (lm.morantest)
LM tests (and robust versions) suggest lag or error; theory should agree
Report rho / lambda, AIC vs OLS, the residual check; use impacts for lag
For counts with unequal populations, consider Poisson models with spatial random effects

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
A checklist of the mistakes that most often make a chart mislead or confuse, as 70 flash cards in 8 groups. Read the title, decide what the problem is and how you would fix it, then open the card. Use Practise to be dealt the cards one at a time; the ones you mark Review again come back first.
Most of these points are taught in Best Practices, Matching Data to Plots and the ggplot2 modules; each card links to where. The list of topics follows the caveats collection of data-to-viz.com by Yan Holtz and Conor Healy, where many cards have a longer illustrated page (the “data-to-viz” link on the card). The original illustrated flash cards are at dataviz-inspiration.com/caveats (source, CC BY-NC 4.0, so they are linked here, not copied). The wording and the R code here are our own.

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Misleading charts




Do not cut the y-axis of a bar chart

Problem. Bars encode values by their length. Starting the axis at 120 mmHg makes a 3 mmHg gap look like a doubling.
Fix. Start bar charts at zero. If the differences matter but are small, show points with confidence intervals instead of bars.
ggplot(d, aes(group, sbp)) + geom_col() + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA))
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Box plots hide the shape

Problem. Two groups can have identical boxes while one is bimodal and the other is not; small groups look as solid as large ones.
Fix. Add the raw points (jittered), or use a violin or raincloud, and print the n per group.
geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4)
In the course: Merged Visuals · data-to-viz





Avoid counter-intuitive encodings

Problem. Readers expect up = more, red = bad, bigger = larger. An inverted axis or a reversed colour scale makes them read the opposite of the truth.
Fix. Keep the usual direction; if you must invert (e.g. ranks), say so on the axis and in the title.
data-to-viz





Bars with error bars (“dynamite plots”) hide the data

Problem. A bar of the mean with an error bar shows two numbers and suggests values below the mean are the only ones that exist.
Fix. Show the individual points with the mean and its 95% CI, or a box/violin plot. State whether bars are SD, SE or CI.
stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = 'pointrange') + geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3)
In the course: Statistical Plots · data-to-viz





Be wary of two y-axes

Problem. The scales of the two axes are arbitrary, so any two series can be made to cross, diverge or move together.
Fix. Use two panels with a shared x-axis, or index both series to 100 at the start.
facet_wrap(~ series, ncol = 1, scales = 'free_y')
In the course: Matching Data to Plots · data-to-viz





Avoid 3D

Problem. Perspective makes nearer bars and slices look bigger and hides some values behind others.
Fix. Use the 2D version. Three numeric variables? Colour or size for the third, or small multiples.
In the course: Matching Data to Plots · data-to-viz





Do not cherry-pick the data

Problem. Choosing the start date, the sites or the subgroup that tells the best story misleads even when every point is correct.
Fix. Show the full period and all groups, and say why any are left out.





Draw proportions accurately

Problem. Icons or shapes scaled by height and width (both) exaggerate differences; a doubled value looks four times larger.
Fix. Make area (not radius or height and width together) proportional to the value, or simply use bars.





Respect time intervals

Problem. Unevenly spaced dates (2010, 2015, 2020, 2021, 2022) drawn at equal distances distort the trend.
Fix. Use a real date or numeric x-axis so the gaps are drawn to scale.
aes(x = as.Date(visit_date))   # not factor(visit_date)





Show the sample size

Problem. A percentage from 8 people looks as solid as one from 800.
Fix. Print the n on the axis labels, in the legend or in a caption; add confidence intervals.
scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) paste0(x, '\n(n = ', table(d$group)[x], ')'))





Beware of Simpson’s paradox

Problem. A trend in the pooled data can reverse inside every subgroup when the groups differ in size and level.
Fix. Colour or facet by the likely confounder before drawing a conclusion; adjust for it in the model.
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = group)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = 'lm')
In the course: Regression Analysis · data-to-viz

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Wrong chart type




Many thin lollipops or bars can shimmer

Problem. Dozens of closely spaced thin lines create a moiré pattern that is tiring to look at.
Fix. Use fewer, thicker bars, or a dot plot, or aggregate into groups.





The trouble with pie charts

Problem. People compare angles and areas poorly; slices of 23% and 27% look the same, and more than 5 slices are unreadable.
Fix. A sorted bar chart. Keep a pie only for 2–3 parts of a whole for a general audience.
ggplot(d, aes(reorder(cause, n), n)) + geom_col() + coord_flip()
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Radial bars distort length

Problem. In a circular bar chart the outer bars are longer than inner bars of the same value.
Fix. Use straight bars; keep radial layouts for a decorative overview with labels on the values.
data-to-viz





Maybe you do not need a map

Problem. A map draws attention to large, empty areas; if geography is not the question, it wastes space.
Fix. A sorted bar or dot chart of the regions answers “which is highest?” better than a map.
In the course: Maps and Choropleths





Two values per group? Try a dumbbell

Problem. Grouped bars for before/after (or men/women) make the reader compare bars across pairs.
Fix. A dumbbell (two points joined by a line) shows both values and the change in one glance.
geom_segment(aes(x = before, xend = after, y = site, yend = site)) + geom_point(aes(before, site)) + geom_point(aes(after, site))
In the course: Showcase





Use circular bar plots with care

Problem. Without a radial axis readers cannot read values, and the shape is driven by the order of the bars.
Fix. Label each bar with its value and sort it; prefer a straight bar chart for comparison.
data-to-viz

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Colour




Use colour on purpose

Problem. Colouring every bar differently adds a legend and implies groups that mean nothing.
Fix. One colour by default; add colour only to encode a variable or to highlight the message (grey + one accent).
geom_col(aes(fill = site == 'Hospital B')) + scale_fill_manual(values = c('grey70', '#C0392B'), guide = 'none')
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Choose the background on purpose

Problem. A dark or coloured panel background reduces contrast and changes how colours look.
Fix. White or very light grey backgrounds; theme_minimal() or theme_classic().





Keep enough contrast

Problem. Light-yellow lines or pale text on white disappear on a projector and in print.
Fix. Check contrast (text should be dark); avoid the lightest end of a palette for thin lines and text.





Avoid pure, saturated colours

Problem. Pure red, green and blue (#FF0000 …) vibrate next to each other and tire the eye.
Fix. Muted palettes (viridis, ColorBrewer, Okabe-Ito) with one stronger colour for emphasis.





Numbers need a sequential palette

Problem. A rainbow or qualitative palette on a numeric variable has no visual order.
Fix. One hue from light to dark (or viridis) so darker = more.
scale_fill_viridis_c()   # or scale_fill_distiller(palette = 'Blues', direction = 1)
In the course: ggplot2 Module 3





Too many colours kill the story

Problem. Beyond about 6 colours readers cannot match lines to the legend.
Fix. Highlight 1–3 groups and grey the rest, or use small multiples.
In the course: Best Practices





No gradient for unordered groups

Problem. A light-to-dark gradient on regions or treatments suggests an order that does not exist.
Fix. A qualitative palette (scale_colour_brewer(palette = ‘Set2’) or Okabe-Ito) for categories.





Avoid the rainbow palette

Problem. Rainbow scales have sudden bright bands (yellow, cyan) that create boundaries not in the data, and fail in greyscale.
Fix. viridis or a single-hue sequential scale.
data-to-viz





Diverging data, diverging palette

Problem. Change from baseline, residuals and correlations have a meaningful zero that a sequential palette hides.
Fix. Two hues meeting at a neutral colour placed exactly at the midpoint.
scale_fill_gradient2(low = '#2166AC', mid = 'white', high = '#B2182B', midpoint = 0)
In the course: ggplot2 Module 3





Think of colour-blind readers

Problem. About 1 in 12 men cannot tell red from green.
Fix. Colour-blind-safe palettes (viridis, Okabe-Ito), plus redundant cues (shape, direct labels).
scale_colour_viridis_d()
In the course: Best Practices

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Design




Align everything with something

Problem. Titles, panels and annotations that float at random positions look messy and hard to scan.
Fix. Left-align title, subtitle and caption with the plot; use the same margins across panels.
theme(plot.title.position = 'plot', plot.caption.position = 'plot')





Two fonts are enough

Problem. Many fonts and styles compete for attention.
Fix. One font family; vary size and weight for hierarchy.





Do you need that box?

Problem. Borders around the panel, legend and plot add ink without information.
Fix. Remove panel borders and legend boxes; let white space separate elements.
theme(panel.border = element_blank(), legend.background = element_blank())





Font size matters

Problem. Default 11 pt axis text is unreadable on a slide or a printed half-page.
Fix. Set base_size for the output (about 14–18 for slides); check the figure at its final size.
theme_minimal(base_size = 16)





Group what belongs together

Problem. Related bars or panels far apart force the eye to jump.
Fix. Order categories so comparisons are adjacent; group panels by the question they answer.





Make the title say something

Problem. A title like “SBP by group” makes the reader find the message themselves.
Fix. State the finding in the title (“SBP fell by 9 mmHg with the intervention”) and keep the description in the subtitle.
In the course: Best Practices





Declutter

Problem. Heavy grids, tick marks, borders and legends compete with the data.
Fix. Light or no grid lines, direct labels instead of legends, no redundant text.
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Maps




Do not move regions around

Problem. Moving or resizing islands and remote areas to fit the frame changes their apparent size and position.
Fix. If you must inset a region, frame it and say so; keep the same projection.





Mind the projection

Problem. Web Mercator inflates areas far from the equator, so a choropleth over-weights them.
Fix. Use an equal-area or local projected CRS for thematic maps (e.g. UTM for a district).
st_transform(blocks, 32644)
In the course: Spatial Data with sf





Normalise your maps

Problem. A map of counts is mostly a map of where people live.
Fix. Map rates (per 100,000) or ratios to expected; show counts only when workload is the question.
mutate(rate = cases / population * 1e5)
In the course: Maps and Choropleths · data-to-viz





Show missing data as missing

Problem. A missing area coloured like the lowest class looks like “no disease”.
Fix. Give missing areas a distinct neutral colour or hatching and a legend entry.
scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = 'grey85')





Do not let small regions vanish

Problem. Dense urban wards are tiny on a map, though they hold most people.
Fix. Add an inset or zoom, a cartogram, or a hexagon tile map.
In the course: Geographic Advanced

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Labels and legends




Prefer horizontal labels

Problem. Rotated axis labels are hard to read.
Fix. Flip the axes so long category names sit horizontally.
ggplot(d, aes(n, reorder(diagnosis, n))) + geom_col()
In the course: Best Practices · data-to-viz





Use legends sparingly

Problem. A legend makes the eye jump back and forth.
Fix. Label lines and groups directly at their ends; drop the legend.
geom_text(data = last_points, aes(label = group), hjust = 0) + theme(legend.position = 'none')





Do not put labels on top of the data

Problem. Text over points or lines hides what it describes.
Fix. Offset labels, use ggrepel, or place them in empty space.
ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = name))





Round your numbers

Problem. A value like “37.4285%” suggests a precision the data do not have and is harder to read.
Fix. Round to what matters (37%); use scales::percent() for axes.
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)





Annotation is crucial

Problem. Readers miss the event or threshold that explains the pattern.
Fix. Add a short note, a reference line or a shaded period where it matters.
geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date('2024-06-01'), linetype = 2) + annotate('text', ...)
data-to-viz





Do not label every tick

Problem. A label on every year or category crowds the axis.
Fix. Fewer, round breaks.
scale_x_date(date_breaks = '6 months', date_labels = '%b %Y')

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Dashboards and data stories




Keep colours consistent across charts

Problem. If “Intervention” is blue in one panel and orange in the next, readers mis-match them.
Fix. A named colour vector used by every plot.
arm_cols <- c(Control = 'grey50', Intervention = '#2C5F8D'); scale_colour_manual(values = arm_cols)
data-to-viz





Share the y-axis to compare panels

Problem. Panels with their own y range look similar even when one is ten times higher.
Fix. Keep scales fixed when the panels are compared (the facet default); free them only to show shape.





Leave margins between charts

Problem. Panels pressed together read as one figure.
Fix. Space and alignment between panels (patchwork handles both).





Link charts that share an axis

Problem. Separate charts with the same x (time) are hard to read together.
Fix. Stack them vertically with aligned x-axes, or link them interactively (crosstalk).
In the course: Interactive Plots

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Other




Sort your bar chart

Problem. Alphabetical order hides the ranking.
Fix. Order bars by value (unless the categories have their own order, like age groups).
aes(x = reorder(region, rate))   # or forcats::fct_reorder()
In the course: Basic Plot Gallery · data-to-viz





Histograms - mind the bin width

Problem. The same data can look smooth, bimodal or noisy depending on the bins.
Fix. Try several widths and choose a meaningful one (5 mmHg, 1 year); report it.
geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0)
data-to-viz





Size bubbles by area, not radius

Problem. If the radius doubles, the area quadruples.
Fix. ggplot2’s scale_size() already maps to area; avoid scale_radius().
scale_size_area(max_size = 12)
data-to-viz





The spaghetti plot

Problem. Twenty overlapping lines are unreadable.
Fix. Grey all lines and highlight one or a few, or small multiples with the others in grey behind.
In the course: Showcase · data-to-viz





Connect only connected dots

Problem. A line implies continuity between points; joining unrelated categories invents a trend.
Fix. Lines for ordered x (time, dose); points or bars for categories.
In the course: ggplot2 Module 1 · data-to-viz





Drawing order matters

Problem. The layer drawn last hides the others: a large group can bury a small one.
Fix. Draw the highlight last; use transparency.
geom_point(data = others, colour = 'grey') + geom_point(data = highlight, colour = 'red')
In the course: ggplot2 Module 4





Overlapping sets? Use an UpSet plot

Problem. Venn diagrams with more than three sets (e.g. comorbidities) are unreadable.
Fix. An UpSet plot shows the size of every intersection as a bar.





Stacked charts are hard to read

Problem. Only the bottom segment has a common baseline; the rest cannot be compared.
Fix. Grouped bars, small multiples, or 100% stacks with few segments.
In the course: Matching Data to Plots · data-to-viz





Mind the aspect ratio

Problem. Stretching a plot changes how steep a trend looks.
Fix. Choose the width/height on purpose (about 45° for the main slopes); set it in ggsave().
ggsave('fig.png', width = 7, height = 4)
data-to-viz





Make date axes easy to read

Problem. Default date labels can be dense or ambiguous (01/02).
Fix. Unambiguous formats (“Jan 2025”) and sensible breaks.
scale_x_date(date_labels = '%b %Y')





Reorder your heat map

Problem. Rows and columns in input order hide any structure.
Fix. Order by a summary or by clustering so similar rows sit together.
aes(y = fct_reorder(ward, cases, .fun = sum))
In the course: Showcase · data-to-viz





Beware of overplotting

Problem. With thousands of points the scatter becomes a solid blob.
Fix. Transparency, smaller points, hexbins or 2D density.
geom_point(alpha = 0.2)   # or geom_hex()
In the course: Intermediate Plot Gallery · data-to-viz





Too many distributions at once

Problem. Overlaid densities or histograms for many groups become a tangle.
Fix. A ridgeline plot, small multiples or box plots side by side.
ggridges::geom_density_ridges()
data-to-viz





Small multiples - rows or columns?

Problem. The layout decides what is easy to compare: aligned y values compare across a row, aligned x values down a column.
Fix. Put panels in one row to compare heights, in one column to compare positions on x.
facet_wrap(~ group, nrow = 1)
data-to-viz





Check the numbers on the chart

Problem. Percentages that do not add to 100, or totals that do not match the table, destroy trust.
Fix. Compute labels from the data in code; never type them by hand.
data-to-viz





Do not make readers do arithmetic

Problem. If the message is a difference, two lines make the reader subtract in their head.
Fix. Plot the difference itself (with its CI).
data-to-viz





Area is a weak encoding

Problem. People underestimate area differences; bubbles and treemaps give rough impressions only.
Fix. Use position or length when exact comparison matters.
data-to-viz





Grouped bars must look grouped

Problem. Evenly spaced bars hide which belong together.
Fix. Dodge within a group and leave a gap between groups.
geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7)
data-to-viz





Radar (spider) charts mislead

Problem. The area depends on the order of the axes, and values are hard to read.
Fix. A dot plot or parallel coordinates for several measures per item.
data-to-viz





Log scales for rates of change

Problem. On a linear axis exponential growth looks explosive and early changes look flat.
Fix. A log axis when relative change is the question; label it clearly.
scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma)





It is “choropleth”

Problem. The common misspelling “chloropleth” undermines a report.
Fix. choro (area) + pleth (quantity).

title: Data Viz Caveats: Flash Cards
text:
Self-check quiz

A chart shows the mean SBP of two arms as bars with error bars, the y-axis starting at 120 mmHg. How many caveats does it break?

None: the error bars make it an honest chart
One: the error bars alone are wrong
Two: the cut axis and the bar of means
One: just the axis start is wrong



You map dengue cases (counts) per block. What should you map instead, and why?

Cases per 100,000, so population does not drive it
The log of the counts, to compress the colour scale
Cases per km², so that large blocks look smaller
The rank of each count, so classes have equal size



Twenty ward lines overlap on one time-series chart. Which fix keeps every ward visible?

Give each of the wards its own bright, saturated colour
Small multiples, each ward over the rest in grey
A 3D chart with one ward per depth level
A dual y-axis for the larger and smaller wards



Change in SBP from baseline (negative and positive) is shown on a map. Which palette fits?

A rainbow palette from red to violet
A single-hue palette from light to dark blue
A qualitative palette with one hue per block
A diverging palette with white at zero

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
What is Grammar of Graphics?

A systematic framework for creating visualizations
Developed by Leland Wilkinson, implemented in ggplot2 by Hadley Wickham
Treats plots as layered compositions of graphical elements
Separates data from aesthetics from geometry
Enables infinite combinations from finite components
More flexible than traditional plotting systems


Core Philosophy: Build complex visualizations by combining simple, well-defined layers

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Why ggplot2?

Consistent syntax across all plot types
Flexible and extensible - easy to customize
Professional quality output
Reproducible - code-based approach
Large ecosystem of extensions
Industry standard in R community


vs Base R: More intuitive, consistent, and powerful for complex visualizations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
The Seven Layers of Grammar

Data - The dataset being visualized
Aesthetics - Mapping data to visual properties
Geometries - Visual marks (points, lines, bars)
Statistics - Data transformations and summaries
Coordinates - The plotting space and axes
Facets - Subplots for data subsets
Scales - Mapping data values to aesthetics


Plus: Themes for overall visual styling

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
1. Data Layer
The foundation of every ggplot2 visualization

Must be a data frame or tibble
Each row represents an observation
Each column represents a variable
Data should be in tidy format

Each variable in one column
Each observation in one row
Each value in one cell




Code
# Basic structure
ggplot(data = my_data)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
2. Aesthetics (aes)
Mapping data variables to visual properties

Position: x, y
Color: color (points/lines), fill (areas)
Size: size of points or line width
Shape: point shapes
Transparency: alpha (0 = transparent, 1 = opaque)
Line type: linetype (solid, dashed, dotted)
Group: group (for grouping data)



Code
ggplot(data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, color = var3))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
3. Geometries (geom)
Visual representations of data

geom_point() - Scatter plots
geom_line() - Line graphs
geom_bar() / geom_col() - Bar charts
geom_histogram() - Histograms
geom_boxplot() - Box plots
geom_violin() - Violin plots
geom_smooth() - Smoothed conditional means
And many more…


Key concept: Geoms are added as layers with +

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
4. Statistics (stat)
Data transformations and summaries

Many geoms have default statistics
stat_identity - Use data as-is
stat_count - Count observations
stat_bin - Bin data into groups
stat_smooth - Add smoothed line
stat_summary - Compute summary statistics


Usually implicit: Most geoms automatically apply appropriate statistics

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
5. Coordinates (coord)
Defining the plotting space

coord_cartesian() - Default Cartesian coordinates
coord_flip() - Flip x and y axes
coord_polar() - Polar coordinates
coord_fixed() - Fixed aspect ratio
coord_trans() - Transformed coordinates



Code
# Flip axes for horizontal bars
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
6. Facets
Creating subplots for data subsets

facet_wrap() - Wrap panels by one variable
facet_grid() - Grid of panels by two variables
Useful for comparing groups
Can have free or fixed scales



Code
# Facet by one variable
facet_wrap(~ treatment_group)

# Facet by two variables
facet_grid(gender ~ region)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
7. Scales
Mapping data values to aesthetic properties

Control how data maps to aesthetics
scale_x_continuous() - Continuous x-axis
scale_color_manual() - Manual color specification
scale_fill_brewer() - ColorBrewer palettes
scale_y_log10() - Logarithmic transformation
Control breaks, limits, labels, transformations



Code
scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
8. Guides (Legends & Axes)
Helping readers interpret the plot

Axes: Show scale of position aesthetics
Legends: Show scale of other aesthetics (color, size, shape)
Controlled by guides() function
Can be positioned, styled, or removed
Automatically generated from aesthetics



Code
guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Treatment Group"))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Building Plots Progressively
The power of layering

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +        # 1. Data + aesthetics
  geom_point() +                                       # 2. Add points
  geom_smooth() +                                      # 3. Add trend line
  facet_wrap(~ treatment_group) +                      # 4. Add facets
  theme_minimal()                                      # 5. Apply theme


Each layer builds on the previous, creating complex visualizations from simple components

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Data Preparation

# Create derived variables
bp_data <- bp_data %>%
  mutate(
    # BP change from baseline to 6 months
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    DiaBP_Change = DiaBP_6m - DiaBP_0m,
    
    # Age groups
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, 
                   breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    
    # Hypertension status (Systolic ≥140 or Diastolic ≥90)
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    
    # BMI categories
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI,
                       breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Handling Missing Data

# Check missing data
missing_summary <- bp_data %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))

# Display columns with missing data
missing_summary %>%
  select(where(~. > 0))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  ExerciseFreq ChronicDisease
         <int>          <int>
1            2              2



Key variables with missing data: ExerciseFreq (44), ChronicDisease (75)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 1
text:
Handling Missing Data: Strategies

# Strategy 1: Filter complete cases for specific analysis
bp_complete <- bp_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(ChronicDisease))

# Strategy 2: Use na.rm in calculations
bp_data %>%
  group_by(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m, na.rm = TRUE))

# Strategy 3: Explicitly show missing as category
bp_data %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = replace_na(ExerciseFreq, "Unknown"))

text:
Module 3 Overview
Previously: - Module 1: Foundations & Geoms - Module 2: Aesthetics & Faceting & Themes
This Module: - Color palettes & accessibility - paletteer package - Scale functions (manual, discrete, continuous, gradient) - Custom theme creation with theme() - element_text(), element_line(), element_rect(), element_blank() - Legend management

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Setup


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggthemes)
library(paletteer)  # For extensive color palettes
library(patchwork)  # For combining plots

# Load data
bp_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx") %>%
  mutate(
    SysBP_Change = SysBP_6m - SysBP_0m,
    AgeGroup = cut(Age, breaks = c(0, 30, 50, 65, 100),
                   labels = c("18-30", "31-50", "51-65", "65+")),
    Hypertension_Baseline = ifelse(SysBP_0m >= 140 | DiaBP_0m >= 90, 
                                   "Hypertensive", "Normal"),
    BMI_Category = cut(BMI, breaks = c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, 100),
                       labels = c("Underweight", "Normal", "Overweight", "Obese"))
  )

region_summary <- bp_data %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP_0m), N = n(), .groups = "drop")

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Color Theory Basics

Hue: The color itself (red, blue, green)
Saturation: Intensity/purity of color
Luminance: Brightness/lightness
Contrast: Difference between colors


Key principles: - Use color purposefully, not decoratively - Ensure sufficient contrast for readability - Consider colorblind accessibility (~8% of males, ~0.5% of females) - Limit number of colors (typically ≤7 for categorical data)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
scale_color_brewer() - ColorBrewer Palettes




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = Region)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal()



Types: Sequential, Diverging, Qualitative
Use: Professional, well-tested color combinations

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Colorblind-Friendly: Viridis




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol,
           color = SysBP_0m)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  theme_minimal()



Options: “viridis”, “magma”, “plasma”, “inferno”, “cividis”
Advantages: Colorblind-safe, perceptually uniform, prints well in B&W

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Viridis for Discrete Variables




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = Region)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "viridis") +
  theme_minimal()



**_d** for discrete, **_c** for continuous
Always prefer colorblind-friendly palettes!

paletteer: Continuous Palettes




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = BMI,
           color = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_paletteer_c(
    "viridis::mako") +
  theme_minimal()



Beautiful gradients for continuous variables
Explore with: paletteer_c_names

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Best Practices for Color

Use color purposefully - not just for decoration
Prefer colorblind-safe palettes - viridis, ColorBrewer, paletteer curated sets
Limit colors - typically ≤7 distinct colors for categorical
Use redundant encoding - combine color with shape, pattern, or position
Ensure contrast - especially for text and important distinctions
Consider grayscale - will it work if printed in black & white?
Cultural context - red/green may have different meanings
Test with target audience - especially for accessibility needs

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Scale System Overview

Scales control how data values map to visual properties
Every aesthetic has an associated scale
Format: scale_<aesthetic>_<type>()

aesthetic: color, fill, x, y, size, shape, alpha
type: continuous, discrete, manual, gradient, brewer, viridis

Scales control: breaks, limits, labels, transformations



Code
scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue"))
scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 20))

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
scale_color_manual(): Custom Colors




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Control" = "steelblue",
               "Intervention" = "darkred"),
    name = "Treatment")



Use for: Exact control over categorical colors
Can use named colors or hex codes

scale_color_gradient(): Two-Color Gradient

ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = BMI,

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
theme() Function Anatomy
The theme() function customizes non-data plot elements:

Element functions:

element_text() - Text elements (labels, titles, axis text)
element_line() - Line elements (axis lines, grid lines)
element_rect() - Rectangle elements (backgrounds, borders)
element_blank() - Remove elements completely




Code
theme(
  axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
  panel.grid = element_line(color = "gray80")
)

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
element_text(): Text Customization

ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Region, y = SysBP_0m,
           fill = Region)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(
      size = 16, face = "bold",
      color = "darkblue"),
    axis.text = element_text(
      size = 12, color = "gray30"),

      size = 20, face = "bold",
      hjust = 0.5)
  )

Using Serif Fonts

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Creating an Organizational Theme


Code
# Hospital/Clinical Report Theme
theme_clinical_report <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif") {
  theme_bw(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
  theme(
    # Professional serif fonts
    text = element_text(family = base_family),
    
    # Plot titles - centered and bold
    plot.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.3, face = "bold", 
                              hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, hjust = 0.5,
                                 color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, hjust = 1,
                                face = "italic", color = "gray50"),
    
    # Axis elements - clear and readable
    axis.title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, color = "gray20"),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    # Panel - clean with subtle grid
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray40", fill = NA, linewidth = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    
    # Legend - bottom position, horizontal
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = base_size, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Plot background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
  )
}

       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Legend Position




Code
ggplot(bp_data, 
       aes(x = Age, y = SysBP_0m,
           color = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom")



Options: “right” (default), “left”, “top”, “bottom”, “none”
Or coordinates: c(x, y) where 0 ≤ x, y ≤ 1

title: Grammar of Graphics: Module 3
text:
Global Theme Settings


Code
# Set global theme for all subsequent plots
theme_set(theme_clinical_report(base_size = 14))

# Update specific elements globally
theme_update(
  plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
  legend.position = "bottom"
)

# Now all plots use this theme!



Benefit: Ensures consistency across all plots in a document/report
