title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Choosing the Right Visualization for Your Data
text:
Choosing the Right Visualization for Your Data
A Practical Framework Based on Analytical Goals

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Your Roadmap for Visualization Selection

Identify Your Data Type

What kind of data do you have? (Numeric, Categorical, Temporal, etc.)

Define Your Analytical Goal

What do you want to communicate? (Compare, Distribute, Show Relationships, etc.)

Select the Appropriate Chart

What visualization best achieves your goal?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Color-Coded Framework









Goal
Symbol
Question
Purpose




Distribution
●
“What’s the spread?”
Show data spread, shape, outliers


Correlation
●
“How do things relate?”
Show relationships between variables


Ranking
●
“What’s the order?”
Compare values in order


Part of Whole
●
“What’s the composition?”
Show proportions/percentages


Evolution
●
“How does it change over time?”
Track trends and changes


Maps
●
“Where is it located?”
Geographic/spatial distribution


Flow
●
“How does it move?”
Movement, transitions, journeys

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Quick Reference - What Each Color Means
text:
Quick Reference - What Each Color Means

● Gold/Yellow = Distribution - Shows data spread, frequency, shape, outliers
● Blue = Correlation - Shows relationships, associations between variables
● Green = Ranking - Shows order, comparison of values, top/bottom
● Red/Salmon = Part of Whole - Shows composition, proportions, percentages
● Light Blue = Evolution - Shows trends, changes over time, trajectories
● Purple = Maps - Shows geographic/spatial distribution, location-based data
● Pink/Tan = Flow - Shows movement, transitions, journeys, hierarchies

Tip: When you see a colored dot next to a chart name, it tells you what analytical goal that chart serves best!

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
The 6 Data Type Categories








Data Type
Definition
Examples




Numeric
Continuous measurements
Age, weight, blood pressure, lab values


Categoric
Discrete categories/groups
Gender, disease status, treatment type


Ordinal
Ordered categories
Likert scale, tumor stages, severity levels


Time Series
Temporal/chronological data
Monthly incidence, patient vitals over time


Relational
Connections/networks
Patient pathways, disease networks


Map
Geographic/spatial data
Regional disease rates, location coordinates

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
How Variables Combine
SINGLE VARIABLE
├── Numeric → Histogram, Density, Boxplot
├── Categoric → Bar, Pie, Lollipop
├── Ordinal → Ordered Bar, Cumulative Frequency
├── Time Series → Line, Area
├── Map → Choropleth, Bubble Map
└── Relational → Network Graph

BIVARIATE (TWO VARIABLES)
├── Numeric × Numeric → Scatter, Hexbin, Bubble
├── Numeric × Categoric → Boxplot, Violin, Grouped Bar
├── Categoric × Categoric → Grouped/Stacked Bar, Mosaic, Heatmap
├── Time Series × Numeric → Multi-line, Stacked Area
├── Time Series × Categoric → Faceted Line, Interaction Plot
└── Any + Relational → Sankey, Chord

MULTIVARIATE (3+ VARIABLES)
├── Numeric × Numeric × Numeric → Bubble, Faceted Scatter
├── Numeric × Multiple Categoric → Faceted Box/Violin, Interaction
├── Multiple Categoric × Multiple Categoric → Sankey, Sunburst, Treemap
├── Time Series × Multiple Variables → Ridgeline, Faceted Line
└── Hierarchical → Treemap, Sunburst, Hierarchical Edge Bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole
Chart Options:

Bar Chart ● (counts/frequencies)
Lollipop Chart ● (alternative to bar, especially for long lists)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked comparison)
Pie Chart ● (≤5 categories only, part-to-whole)
Doughnut Chart ● (like pie, better labels)
Circular Bar Plot ● (aesthetic alternative)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease prevalence by state
Hospitalization by insurance type
Comorbidity frequency distribution

Decision Guide:

Few categories (<5) and need part-of-whole → Pie/Doughnut
Few-moderate categories → Bar chart (horizontal if long names)
Many categories (>8) → Lollipop or Cleveland dot
Need ranking emphasis → Ordered bar or lollipop

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Bar Chart ● (maintain categorical order)
Ordered Dot Plot ●
Cumulative Frequency Plot ● (especially for Likert scales)
Frequency Polygon ● (smooth trend)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1=Very Unsatisfied to 5=Very Satisfied)
Tumor stages frequency (Stage I → II → III → IV)
Pain severity distribution (None → Mild → Moderate → Severe)
Risk level counts (Low → Medium → High)

Decision Guide:

Likert scales → Stacked ordered bar or cumulative frequency
Natural progression (stages, severity) → Maintain order on axis
Show accumulation → Cumulative frequency plot
Compare between groups → Grouped ordered bar

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution
Chart Options:

Histogram ● (shows bin structure, distribution shape)
Density Plot ● (smooth, continuous estimate)
Boxplot ● (summary: median, quartiles, outliers)
Violin Plot ● (distribution + boxplot combined)
Dot/Strip Plot ● (individual points, best for small n)

Healthcare Examples:

Age distribution in cohort
Blood pressure measurements in population
Lab values (HbA1c, cholesterol, creatinine)
Hospital length of stay

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice
Why




n < 20
Dot/Strip plot
See every point


n = 20-100
Histogram + Boxplot
Balance detail & summary


n > 100
Density plot
Smooth, reduces noise


Want outliers
Boxplot
Shows extreme values clearly


Want shape details
Violin plot
Shows multimodality, skewness

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (standard for continuous time data)
Area Chart ● (emphasizes magnitude/volume)
Streamgraph ● (stacked area with flowing theme)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years
Hospital admission rates monthly
COVID-19 case counts by week
Patient vital signs during hospitalization

Decision Guide:

Single series, continuous time → Line chart
Show cumulative volume → Area chart
Multiple series, show total → Stacked area
Sparse time points → Line chart with markers

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Maps
Chart Options:

Choropleth Map ● (color-coded by region)
Bubble Map ● (circles sized by value)
Heat Map ● (geographic intensity)
Dot Map ● (point locations)

Healthcare Examples:

Regional disease rates (e.g., TB incidence by state in India)
Hospital bed density by district
Maternal mortality ratios by region
Vaccination coverage by area

Decision Guide:

Show rate/percentage by region → Choropleth
Show absolute counts by location → Bubble map
Show intensity/density → Heat map
Specific point locations matter → Dot map

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation | ● Distribution
Chart Options:

Scatter Plot ● (relationship between two continuous variables)
Hexbin Plot ● (2D histogram for dense data)
2D Density Plot ● (contour or heatmap of overlapping points)
Bubble Plot ● (3rd variable via size or color)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (body mass relationship)
HbA1c vs Blood Glucose (glycemic control markers)
Creatinine vs eGFR (kidney function)
Systolic vs Diastolic Blood Pressure

Decision Guide:



Scenario
Best Choice




Moderate sample, clear pattern
Scatter plot


Large n, lots of overplotting
Hexbin or 2D density


Want 3rd variable shown
Bubble (size) or color gradient


Focused region interest
Zoomed scatter with annotations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution | ● Correlation (Comparison)
Chart Options:

Boxplot ● (median, quartiles, outliers by group)
Violin Plot ● (distribution shape by group)
Jittered Dot/Strip/Beeswarm Plot ● (individual points by group)
Bar Chart with Error Bars ● (mean/median ± SD/IQR)
Cleveland Dot Plot ● (ranked group means)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c levels across treatment arms
BMI by disease status (healthy vs diabetic vs obese)
Blood pressure by gender
Hospital length of stay by admission type

Decision Guide:



Sample Size
Distribution Focus
Summary Focus




n < 30
Dot/Strip + Boxplot
Not recommended


n = 30-100
Violin or Boxplot
Bar with error bars


n > 100
Violin plot
Density overlay + mean line


Outliers matter
Boxplot + jitter
Always show


Group ranking focus
Ranked dots
Lollipop chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation (Probability)
Chart Options:

Logistic Regression Curve ● (smooth probability line)
Density Overlay ● (stacked densities by category)
Grouped Histogram/Density ● (overlapping distributions)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease presence/absence across age ranges
Treatment response (yes/no) by baseline score
Adverse event (yes/no) by medication dose
Mortality (yes/no) by APACHE score

Visualization:

X-axis: Numeric predictor (age, score, dose)
Y-axis: Probability or proportion
Two groups shown as overlapping curves or stacked

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: ● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole | ● Correlation
text:
● Distribution | ● Ranking | ● Part of Whole | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Grouped Bar Chart ● (side-by-side comparison)
Dodged Bar Chart ● (similar to grouped)
Stacked Bar Chart ● (shows totals + composition)
Stacked Bar (Proportional) ● (percentage/100% stacked)
Mosaic Plot ● (area ∝ frequency, shows association)
Heatmap ● (color intensity for cell frequencies)

Healthcare Examples:

Gender vs Disease status (M/F vs HIV+/HIV-)
Treatment arm vs Adverse event (Drug A/B vs AE Yes/No)
Hospital site vs Patient outcome (Site 1-3 vs Recovered/Died)
Risk level by comorbidity count

Decision Guide:



Goal
Best Chart




Compare totals & subgroups
Grouped bar


Show composition per category
Stacked bar


Show percentages only
Stacked bar (proportional)


Detect association strength
Mosaic or heatmap


Many categories, dense
Heatmap with color gradient

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Boxplot ● (boxplot by ordinal groups, maintaining order)
Ordered Violin Plot ● (violin by ordinal groups)
Ordered Jittered Points ● (points by group, groups ordered)

Healthcare Examples:

Medication efficacy vs dose level (Low/Medium/High)
Lab value vs disease severity (Stage I-IV)
Pain score vs treatment intensity (Mild/Moderate/Severe)
Functional status vs age group (Young/Middle/Elderly)

Key Point:

Always maintain explicit ordering on axis
Example: Severity I → II → III → IV (not random order)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution | ● Correlation (Trend)
Chart Options:

Line Chart ● (single series over time)
Multi-line Chart ● (multiple series overlay)
Area Chart ● (cumulative volume over time)
Stacked Area Chart ● (composition over time)
Connected Scatter ● (if sparse time points)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence trends over years (single disease)
Patient vital signs over hospital stay (temperature, BP, HR)
Medication effectiveness over weeks (Drug A vs B)
Mortality rates over decades by region

Decision Guide:

Single series → Line chart
Few series (2-3) to compare → Multi-line chart
Many series, want to show total → Stacked area
Series showing parts of whole → Stacked area
Sparse measurements → Line with markers or connected scatter

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (By Group) | ● Correlation (Group Comparison)
Chart Options:

Grouped Line Chart ● (separate lines for each group)
Faceted Line Chart ● (separate subplots per group)
Grouped Area Chart ● (stacked or overlapping)
Interaction Plot ● (lines intersecting showing interaction)
Ribbon Chart ● (flowing bands representing groups)

Healthcare Examples:

Mortality rate trends (gender comparison: M vs F)
Hospital admission trends by institution (5-year follow-up)
Drug effectiveness over time by treatment arm
Complication rates by age group over study period

Decision Guide:

Few groups (2-3) → Multi-line chart
Many groups (5+) → Faceted line plots
Want to show total + groups → Stacked area
Interaction patterns matter → Interaction plot (lines cross)
Space constraints → Faceting better than overlapping

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Ordered) | ● Part of Whole (Ordered)
Chart Options:

Ordered Grouped Bar Chart ● (bars by category, groups ordered)
Ordered Stacked Bar ● (stacked, ordinal categories in order)
Faceted Ordered Bar ● (subplots maintaining order)

Healthcare Examples:

Patient satisfaction (Likert: 1-5) by hospital ward
Pain severity (None/Mild/Moderate/Severe) by treatment type
Risk level (Low/Med/High) by comorbidity count
Functional status by treatment arm

Key Point:

Maintain ordinal ordering on one axis
Example: Satisfaction scale always: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
3+ Continuous Variables | ● Correlation
Chart Options:

Bubble Plot ● (x, y, size = 3rd; color/opacity = 4th)
Faceted Scatter ● (scatter by groups, multiple subplots)
3D Scatter (NOT recommended: distorts perception)

Healthcare Examples:

Age vs BMI (size=cholesterol, color=treatment arm)
HbA1c vs glucose (size=insulin, faceted by gender)
Systolic vs diastolic BP (colored by smoking status)

Decision Guide:

3 variables → Bubble plot (x, y, size)
4 variables → Bubble + color
5+ variables → Multiple faceted plots (don’t try to cram)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Correlation Matrix
Chart Options:

Correlation Matrix ● (numeric table of coefficients)
Correlogram ● (heatmap with color intensity = correlation strength)
Scatter Plot Matrix ● (pairwise scatter plots)

Healthcare Examples:

Lab inter-correlations: glucose, insulin, triglycerides, HDL, LDL
Vital signs correlations: BP, HR, RR, O2 saturation, temperature
Biomarker relationships in cohort study

Visualization:

Color intensity (warm = positive, cool = negative)
Cell size may represent correlation strength
Diagonal typically = 1.0 (variable with itself)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Faceted) | ● Correlation (Interaction)
Chart Options:

Faceted Boxplot/Violin ● (boxplot per group, subplots for 3rd variable)
Interaction Plot ● (lines connecting means by two factors)
Faceted Scatter + regression lines ● (by groups)

Healthcare Examples:

HbA1c by treatment type, faceted by gender (4 subplots: 2 treat × 2 gender)
Lab values by disease status, colored by age group
Drug efficacy by dose level, faceted by patient comorbidity

Visualization Strategy:

Primary grouping on axis
Secondary grouping via facets or colors
Show interactions: do lines cross? Do patterns differ?

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Chart Options:

Multi-line Chart with Faceting ● (separate subplots per group)
Ridgeline Plot ● (distribution by group, stacked vertically)
Slope Chart ● (start → end values, multiple series)
Animated Time Series ● (interactive exploration)

Healthcare Examples:

Disease incidence over years, separate lines by region (5 regions)
Patient vitals during admission, faceted by treatment arm
Hospital census by time, colored by department

Decision Guide:

Multiple time series + groups → Faceted multi-line
Distribution evolution over time → Ridgeline plot
Show change from start to end → Slope chart

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole (Hierarchical)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (flow from one category to another)
Alluvial Diagram ● (similar to Sankey, broader flows)
Treemap ● (nested rectangles for hierarchy)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles/rings for hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient flow (admission → diagnostic → treatment → discharge)
Alluvial: Disease progression stages (diagnosis → worsening/improvement → outcome)
Treemap: Hospital structure (Region → Hospital → Department → Ward)
Sunburst: Disease classification (Category → Subcategory → Specific condition)

Decision Guide:

Flow/transition/journey → Sankey or Alluvial
Nested hierarchy/parts → Treemap or Sunburst

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Correlation (Connections)
Chart Options:

Sankey Diagram ● (directional flows between nodes)
Chord Diagram ● (bi-directional relationships, circular)
Network Graph ● (nodes + edges, force-directed layout)
Arc Diagram ● (nodes in line, arcs show connections)

Healthcare Examples:

Sankey: Patient journeys through clinic system
Chord: Disease co-occurrence patterns (patient network)
Network: Hospital referral patterns (which hospitals refer to which)
Arc: Comorbidity networks (which diseases co-occur)

Visualization:

Nodes = entities (patients, diseases, hospitals)
Edges/arcs/flows = relationships (referral, co-occurrence)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Part of Whole | ● Flow
Chart Options:

Treemap ● (nested rectangles, size ∝ value)
Sunburst Chart ● (nested circles, size ∝ value)
Hierarchical Edge Bundling ● (connections in hierarchy)

Healthcare Examples:

Treemap: Hospital admissions by Region → State → Hospital → Department (size = admission count)
Sunburst: Disease classification by Category → Subcategory → Specific condition → ICD code
Hierarchical Edge Bundling: Referral patterns between hospitals at different levels

Decision Guide:

Static hierarchy focus → Treemap
Want circular aesthetic → Sunburst
Complex relationships in hierarchy → Hierarchical edge bundling

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Flow | ● Part of Whole
Waterfall Chart

Shows cumulative effect of sequential positive/negative values
Healthcare Example: Patient survival from enrollment → screening loss → randomization → completion

Start: 1000 enrolled
Drop: -50 screening failures
Drop: -30 withdrawn consent
End: 920 completed


Funnel Chart

Stages in a process, showing attrition at each step
Healthcare Example: Hospital admission pipeline

Emergency triage: 500
Admitted: 400 (20% filtered out)
Discharged: 350 (12.5% transferred)
Readmitted: 30 (8.6% recurrent)

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Evolution (Advanced) | ● Distribution (Temporal)
Streamgraph

Stacked area with flowing, organic theme
Example: Emergency admissions over time, stacked by department

Total volume trends visible + department composition


Calendar Heatmap

Daily/weekly patterns across entire year
Example: Hospital occupancy by day of week

Darker = higher occupancy
Pattern reveals peak days/seasons


Frequency Polygon

Line connecting histogram bins
Example: Age distribution comparison between cohorts

Multiple overlaid frequency polygons

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
● Distribution (Text) | ● Correlation (Networks)
Word Cloud

Text frequency visualization, size = occurrence
Limitation: More visual impact than analytic precision
Healthcare Use: Patient feedback themes, common symptoms

Arc Diagram

Network relationships with improved readability over hairball graphs
Example: Disease comorbidity network, cleaner than typical network graph

Hierarchical Edge Bundling

Complex relationship networks with hierarchy
Example: Referral patterns between hospitals (different organizational levels)

Scenario: “HbA1c levels across three treatment arms over 12 months”
Step 1: Identify Data Type

Combined: Time Series + Categoric + Numeric

Step 2: Define Analytical Goal

Step 3: Chart Options








Option
Chart Type
Visualization




A
Multi-line ± CI ●

B
Faceted violin plots ●
3 subplots (one per arm), violin at each timepoint

Individual patient trajectories, color-coded by arm

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
section: Scenario: “Top 10 competitors’ market share over 5 years by region”
text:
Scenario: “Top 10 competitors’ market share over 5 years by region”
Step 1: Identify Data Type

Time: Years (Time Series)
Competitors: 10 categories (Categoric)
Regions: Multiple regions (Categoric)
Market share: Percentage (Numeric)
Dimensions: 4 (too many for single plot!)

Step 2: Define Analytical Goal

● Evolution (trends over time)
● Ranking (who’s leading?)
● Correlation (how do regions differ?)
● Composition (what % of total?)

Step 3: Chart Options







Option
Approach




A
Stacked area per region (faceted: 3-5 subplots) ● ●


B
Grouped multi-line (each region = different color) ●


C
Animated bar chart (top 10 race by region) ● ●


D
Interactive dashboard (toggle region) ●



Decision:

Best static option: Faceted stacked area (shows time, composition, region comparison)
Best interactive: Animated bar or dashboard

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
❌ What NOT to Do
❌ Pie charts with 10+ categories

Why? Human perception fails with small angles
Solution: Use bar chart ●, lollipop ●, or split into multiple pies

❌ 3D charts

Why? Perspective distorts data perception (3D cone/pyramid/sphere)
Solution: Stick to 2D representations

❌ Dual-axis charts

Why? Can mislead by manipulating axis scales
Solution: Use faceting or separate plots instead

❌ Wrong color coding

Why? Color should reinforce analytical goal (not random aesthetic)
Solution: Sequential colors for magnitude, categorical colors for groups

❌ Overplotting (overlapping points)

Why? Can’t see density or exact position
Solution: Use transparency (alpha), jitter, hexbin ●, or density plots ●

❌ Stacked bars for detailed comparison

Why? Only first and last categories are easy to compare
Solution: Use grouped bar ● or faceting for detailed comparison

❌ Too many dimensions on one plot

Why? Cognitive overload, hard to extract insight
Solution: Split into multiple focused visualizations

title: Navigating the Decision Tree
text:
Core Principles for Effective Visualization
✅ Always start with your analytical goal - What question are you answering? (distribute, compare, rank, relate, etc.)
✅ Data types narrow your options significantly - Numeric vs Categoric vs Ordinal vs Temporal vs Spatial
✅ Multiple valid charts may exist—choose based on audience & context - Scientist ≠ Executive ≠ Patient communication
✅ Use color strategically to support your analytical goal - Sequential for magnitude, categorical for groups, diverging for contrasts
✅ Simplicity trumps complexity; avoid unnecessary dimensions - If 3D doesn’t add insight, keep it 2D - If faceting helps clarity, use it
✅ When in doubt, check data-to-viz.com or reference examples - Don’t reinvent the wheel; learn from established best practices
✅ Practice makes perfect—iterate on visualizations - First draft rarely optimal; refine based on feedback

title: Debugging Plots
text:
Debugging plots are essential tools for diagnosing issues in data visualization and analysis. They help identify problems such as incorrect data representation, scaling issues, or unexpected patterns in the data. In this guide, we will explore various techniques and tools for creating effective debugging plots.





Missing or incorrect data types
# Check data types
str(mtcars)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(mtcars))

# Visualize missing patterns
library(naniar)
vis_miss(mtcars)
Outliers affecting scales
# Check for outliers
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)

# Use robust statistics
library(robustbase)
summary(mtcars$mpg)





Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics
# Correct: Map color to variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# Incorrect: Setting color globally
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")  # This sets all points to red
Factor Level Issues
# Check factor levels
levels(mtcars$cyl)

# Reorder factors if needed
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl, levels = c("4", "6", "8"))
Geom Conflicts
# Error: Can't use geom_bar with y aesthetic
# ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + geom_bar()

# Correct: Use stat = "identity"
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")







# Check ggplot object structure
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
str(p)

# View plot data
p$data
p$mapping



# Build plot incrementally
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))
print(p1)  # Should show empty plot

p2 <- p1 + geom_point()
print(p2)  # Check if points appear

p3 <- p2 + theme_minimal()
print(p3)  # Check theme application



# Enable ggplot2 debugging
options(ggplot2.debug = TRUE)

# Check for warnings
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()






# Problem: Length mismatch
# ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = short_vector))

# Solution: Ensure vectors are same length or use single values
ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = factor(category)))



# Problem: Wrong scale type
# ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_continuous()

# Solution: Use appropriate scale
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_discrete()



# Problem: Typo in parameter name
# geom_point(size = 3)  # Correct
# geom_point(siz = 3)   # Incorrect

# Solution: Check documentation
?geom_point






# Residual plots for model diagnostics
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
plot(model)

# QQ plots for normality
qqnorm(mtcars$mpg)
qqline(mtcars$mpg)



# Correlation plots
library(corrplot)
corrplot(cor(mtcars))

# Pairs plots
pairs(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])



# Plot data distributions
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)






# When plot fails
tryCatch({
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
  traceback()
})



library(profvis)

# Profile plotting code
profvis({
  p <- ggplot(large_dataset, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  print(p)
})



# Check memory usage
gc()

# For large datasets, use sampling
sample_data <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), 1000, replace = TRUE), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()





Start simple: Build plots incrementally
Check data first: Validate input data before plotting
Use reproducible examples: Create minimal examples that reproduce issues
Read error messages carefully: They often point to the exact problem
Check package versions: Ensure compatible versions of ggplot2 and extensions
Use debugging tools: Leverage R’s debugging functions and ggplot2’s debug options
Document fixes: Keep notes on solutions for future reference

RStudio Community forums

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

text:
What We’ll Learn - Advanced


Complex Categorical Structures:

Treemaps (hierarchical proportions)
Sunburst charts (circular hierarchies)
Dendrograms (clustering)
Marimekko charts (two-way composition)
Waffle charts (unit visualization)


Analytical Goals:

🔴 Part of Whole - Hierarchical composition
🟢 Ranking - Within hierarchies
⚫ Correlation - Category associations
🟡 Distribution - Nested patterns

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Setup Code


Code
# Load required packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(treemapify)  # For treemaps
library(sunburstR)   # For sunburst charts

# Load dataset
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Create hierarchical data
hierarchical_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(Gender), !is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  count(Region, Gender, SmokingStatus, name = "count")

# Create theme
theme_custom <- function() {
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
}

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Treemap - Code

Purpose: Show hierarchical part-to-whole relationships
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Prepare data for treemap
treemap_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(Region, TreatmentGroup, name = "count") %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(TreatmentGroup, "\n(n=", count, ")"))

# Create treemap
ggplot(treemap_data, aes(area = count, fill = Region, 
                         label = label, subgroup = Region)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(color = "white", size = 3) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(
    place = "center",
    grow = TRUE,
    alpha = 0.5,
    color = "black",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 18
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    color = "white",
    place = "center",
    size = 10,
    grow = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Patient Distribution by Region and Treatment",
       subtitle = "Rectangle size proportional to patient count",
       fill = "Region") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Interpreting Treemaps


Key Features:

Size = Quantity - Larger rectangles = more patients
Color = Category - Each region has its own color
Hierarchy - Region (outer) → Treatment (inner)
Space-efficient - Uses all available area

Best Practices:

Limit to 2-3 hierarchy levels
Use clear labels
Consistent color scheme
Consider interactivity for complex trees


Our Treemap Shows:

East region largest overall

Most patients

Within each region treatment distribution visible

Relative sizes easy to compare

Quick identification of smallest/largest segments
Hierarchical structure immediately clear

Region → Treatment breakdown


Advantage: Efficient use of space compared to nested pie charts

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Sunburst Chart - Code

Purpose: Radial hierarchical visualization
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole (circular)


Code
# Prepare data in required format for sunburst
# Format: path-count pairs
sunburst_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(Gender), !is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  count(Region, Gender, SmokingStatus) %>%
  mutate(path = paste(Region, Gender, SmokingStatus, sep = "-")) %>%
  select(path, n)

# Create sunburst chart
sunburst(
  data = sunburst_data,
  count = TRUE,
  legend = list(w = 150, h = 25, s = 5, t = 25),
  breadcrumb = list(w = 0, h = 25, s = 5, t = 10),
  colors = list(
    range = c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#984EA3",
             "#FF7F00", "#FFFF33", "#A65628", "#F781BF")
  ),
  withD3 = TRUE,
  width = "100%",
  height = 500
)


Note: Sunburst creates interactive HTML widget. For static, use ggplot2 alternative.
Static Alternative (next slide):

  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(SmokingStatus)) %>%
  count(Region, SmokingStatus) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n) * 100,
    id = paste(Region, SmokingStatus, sep = "-")
  )

ggplot(radial_data, aes(x = Region, y = n, fill = SmokingStatus)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white", size = 0.5) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Never" = "#00A087", 
                              "Former" = "#3C5488",
                              "Current" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Smoking Status Distribution by Region (Radial)",
       subtitle = "Each segment shows proportion within region",
       fill = "Smoking Status") +

    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Marimekko Chart - Code

Purpose: Two-way composition (varying column widths)
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole (two dimensions)


Code
# Prepare data for Marimekko
marimekko_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region), !is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(Region, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  mutate(
    region_total = sum(n),
    pct_in_region = n / region_total * 100
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    region_pct = region_total / sum(region_total) * 100,
    cumsum_region = cumsum(region_pct) - region_pct / 2
  )

# Create Marimekko chart
ggplot(marimekko_data, aes(x = Region, y = pct_in_region, 
                           fill = TreatmentGroup, width = region_pct)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "white", size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Treatment Distribution by Region (Marimekko)",
       subtitle = "Column width = regional patient share | Height = treatment proportion",
       x = "Region",
       y = "Percentage within Region",
       fill = "Treatment") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text: Marimekko Chart - Output

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Interpreting Marimekko Charts

Unique Features:

Two dimensions of composition

Width would represent one variable’s total
Height shows breakdown within that category

Space = Area

Total area of each segment = actual count contribution

Compare both dimensions simultaneously

More information dense than standard stacked bars


Our Chart:

Treatment distribution fairly consistent across regions
All regions show similar proportions of each treatment
Visual balance suggests good randomization

When to use: Two categorical variables where both totals and proportions matter

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Waffle Chart - Code

Purpose: Unit-based visualization (each square = fixed count)
Goal: 🔴 Part of Whole (intuitive units)


Code
# Prepare data (each unit = 10 patients)
waffle_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(squares = round(n / 10))  # 1 square = 10 patients

# Create waffle chart
waffle_expanded <- waffle_data %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(id = list(1:squares)) %>%
  unnest(id) %>%
  mutate(square_id = row_number(),
         x = (square_id - 1) %% 10,   # 10 rows
         y = (square_id - 1) %/% 10)

# Plot with ggplot2
ggplot(waffle_expanded, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Treatment A" = "#E41A1C",
                               "Treatment B" = "#377EB8",
                               "Control"     = "#4DAF4A")) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Patient Distribution by Treatment Group",
       x = "1 square = 10 patients",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
  )

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text: Waffle Chart - Output

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Interpreting Waffle Charts

Why Waffle Charts Work:

Intuitive unit representation

Each square = fixed count (e.g., 10 patients)
Easy to count and compare

Avoid pie chart problems

No angles to judge
Better for exact comparisons

Visual impact

Engaging and memorable
Good for presentations and infographics


Our Chart:

Treatment groups balanced
Control group has similar size
Each square represents 10 patients
Visual counting easier than interpreting angles

When to use: Small to medium datasets, need visual impact

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Dendrogram - Code

Purpose: Show hierarchical clustering of categories
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + hierarchical structure


Code
# Calculate dissimilarity matrix for regions based on health metrics
region_profiles <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Region)) %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bp = mean(SysBP_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_chol = mean(Cholesterol_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI_0m, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_smokers = mean(SmokingStatus == "Current", na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  ) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Region")

# Scale variables
region_scaled <- scale(region_profiles)

# Hierarchical clustering
hc <- hclust(dist(region_scaled), method = "ward.D2")

# Plot dendrogram
library(ggdendro)
ggdendrogram(hc, rotate = FALSE, theme_dendro = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Hierarchical Clustering of Regions by Health Profiles",
       subtitle = "Based on BP, cholesterol, BMI, and smoking rates",
       x = "Region",
       y = "Distance (Ward's method)") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0))

text: Dendrogram - Output

title: Categorical - ADVANCED
text:
Interpreting Dendrograms


Reading Dendrograms:

Height = Dissimilarity
Branches joining lower = more similar
Clusters formed by cutting at height
Leaf = Individual category

Method Matters:

Ward’s - Minimizes within-cluster variance
Complete - Maximum distance
Average - Mean distance between clusters


Our Dendrogram:

East and North most similar

Join at lowest height
Similar health profiles

South different from North/East

Joins at higher level

West most distinct

Joins last, highest dissimilarity


Use Case: Identifying similar market segments, patient groups

Common Mistakes


Too many categories in treemap/sunburst

Solution: Filter to top N categories or aggregate small ones

Poor color choices making comparisons hard

Solution: Use consistent, meaningful color schemes

Solution: Add annotations explaining width/height meanings

Interactive charts not working in static reports

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Setup
Data: 200 simulated patients of a blood-pressure trial (data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx, see data/README.md).


Code
library(readxl); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)
library(ggeffects); library(interactions); library(broom)
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")
model <- lm(SysBP_6m ~ TreatmentGroup * Gender + Age + BMI + SysBP_0m, data = health_data)


The model adjusts the 6-month SBP for baseline SBP, age and BMI, and lets the treatment effect differ by gender.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Interaction Plot


Code
cat_plot(model, pred = TreatmentGroup, modx = Gender, interval = TRUE, int.width = 0.95,
         geom = "point") +
  labs(title = "Treatment effect by gender", y = "Predicted systolic BP at 6 months") +
  theme_minimal()



The intervention lowers SBP by about 9 mmHg in every gender group; the interaction test agrees (anova(model), row TreatmentGroup:Gender: p = 0.67). Test an interaction, do not judge it by eye.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Marginal Effects Plot


Code
effects <- ggpredict(model, terms = c("Age [all]", "TreatmentGroup"))
plot(effects) +
  labs(title = "Age and predicted SBP at 6 months, by treatment group",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted SBP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal()



Model-based predictions with confidence bands, other variables held at their mean or reference level.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Forest Plot (Effect Sizes)


Code
coef_data <- tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
ggplot(coef_data, aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), width = 0.2, orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Regression coefficients with 95% CI", x = "Difference in SBP at 6 months (mmHg)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()



Standard in medical research. Coefficients on different scales (per year of age vs per group) are not comparable in size.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Raincloud by Multiple Groups


Code
library(ggdist)
health_data |>
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Gender, y = SysBP_6m, fill = Gender)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.6, width = 0.5, justification = -0.25, .width = 0, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ TreatmentGroup) +
  labs(y = "Systolic BP at 6 months (mmHg)", x = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")



Distribution, summary and raw data at once, for nested groups.

title: Category vs Continuous - ADVANCED
text:
Bayesian Credible Intervals


Code
library(rstanarm)
bayes_model <- stan_glm(SysBP_6m ~ TreatmentGroup + Age + SysBP_0m, data = health_data,
                        chains = 2, iter = 1000, seed = 2026, refresh = 0)
plot(bayes_model, pars = c("TreatmentGroupIntervention", "Age", "SysBP_0m"), prob = 0.5, prob_outer = 0.95) +
  labs(title = "Posterior estimates (50% and 95% credible intervals)")



A 95% credible interval holds the coefficient with 95% probability, given the model and its (weak, default) priors.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Setup
Data: 20 providers and 74 referral links between them, January to June (data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx, simulated).


Code
library(readxl); library(tidyverse); library(igraph); library(ggraph)
providers <- read_excel("../../data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx", sheet = "Providers")
referrals <- read_excel("../../data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx", sheet = "Referrals")

edges <- referrals |> transmute(from = FromProvider, to = ToProvider, weight = NumReferrals, Month, ReferralType)
nodes <- providers |> transmute(name = ProviderID, label = sprintf("P%02d", ProviderID), Specialty, Region)
net <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE, vertices = nodes)

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Community Detection


Code
set.seed(42)
communities <- cluster_louvain(as_undirected(net, edge.attr.comb = list(weight = "sum", "ignore")))
V(net)$community <- factor(membership(communities))
ggraph(net, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight), alpha = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = label), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Community") +
  labs(title = "Provider communities (Louvain)") +
  theme_void()



Louvain groups providers who refer more to each other than to the rest; the groups can change with the random seed, so treat them as a hypothesis, not a fact.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Centrality Measures


Code
V(net)$degree <- degree(net, mode = "all")
V(net)$betweenness <- betweenness(net, normalized = TRUE, weights = NA)   # weights would be read as distances
ggraph(net, layout = "kk") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = betweenness, colour = degree)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = label), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Provider centrality", subtitle = "Size = betweenness | Colour = degree") +
  theme_void()



Degree = how many links; betweenness = how often a provider sits on the shortest path between two others (a broker: if they are absent, referrals take longer routes).

text:
Network Statistics Table


Code
stats <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Providers (nodes)", "Referral links (edges)", "Density", "Mean path length",
             "Clustering coefficient", "Modularity of the communities"),
  Value = c(vcount(net), ecount(net), round(edge_density(net), 3), round(mean_distance(net, weights = NA), 2),
            round(transitivity(net), 3), round(modularity(communities), 3)))
knitr::kable(stats)

Density = links present / links possible. A modularity near 0 means the communities are weak.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Bipartite Network


Code
bip <- referrals |> group_by(from = sprintf("P%02d", FromProvider), to = ReferralType) |>
  summarise(weight = sum(NumReferrals), .groups = "drop")
bp_net <- graph_from_data_frame(bip, directed = FALSE)
V(bp_net)$type <- V(bp_net)$name %in% bip$to                 # TRUE = referral type
ggraph(bp_net, layout = "bipartite") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = type), size = 4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 2.5, vjust = -1.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 2), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#2C5F8D", `TRUE` = "#E67E22"),
                      labels = c("Provider", "Referral type"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Who sends which kind of referral") +
  theme_void()



Two kinds of node, and links only between kinds: providers and the referral types they send.

title: Network - ADVANCED
text:
Dynamic Network (Time-based)


Code
library(patchwork)
set.seed(1)
coords <- create_layout(net, layout = "fr")[, c("x", "y")]        # same positions in both panels
half <- function(months, title) {
  sub <- subgraph_from_edges(net, E(net)[Month %in% months], delete.vertices = FALSE)
  ggraph(sub, layout = "manual", x = coords$x, y = coords$y) +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.4) + geom_node_point(colour = "#2C5F8D", size = 2.5) +
    labs(title = title) + theme_void()
}
half(c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar"), "January–March") + half(c("Apr", "May", "Jun"), "April–June")



Fixing the node positions makes the two periods comparable: only the links change.

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
What is Continuous Data?


Definition:
Data that represents numeric measurements or quantities

Can take any value within a range
Quantitative rather than qualitative
Often derived from measurements


Examples in Our Dataset:

Age (18-79 years)
BMI (11.4-37.3)
Cholesterol levels
Blood Sugar levels
Blood Pressure (Systolic & Diastolic)
Latitude & Longitude

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Continuous Data

What questions can we answer?

🟡 Distribution - What’s the spread? Shape? Center?
⚫ Correlation - How do two variables relate to each other?

# Preview numeric variables

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Histogram - Code
🟡 Goal: Distribution (show frequency across bins)


Code
# Create histogram showing age distribution
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +  # 30 bins
  labs(title = "Distribution of Patient Ages",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Frequency (Number of Patients)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +  # Serif font for professional look
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))




bins = 30 divides the data into 30 equal-width intervals
Adjust bins to find optimal visualization (too few = loss of detail, too many = noise)

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text: Histogram - Plot

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Histograms
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Ages range from 18 to 79 years (median 50) - Patients are spread over the whole range, with somewhat more between 45 and 55 - No single sharp peak and no long tail - No gaps and no impossible values
INTERPRETATION: - The study covers the whole adult age range - No age group dominates the sample - Age is not normally distributed, but that does not matter for using it as a predictor
IMPLICATIONS: - Results can be described across adult ages - Age can be used as a continuous variable; groups (e.g. 18–39, 40–59, 60+) are only for description - Every age band has enough patients for a description
ACTIONS: - Consider age as a covariate in treatment analyses - Change bins and check the picture does not depend on it

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Histogram with Mean/Median Lines - Code
🟡 Goal: Distribution with central tendency markers


Code
# Calculate summary statistics
age_mean <- mean(data_clean$Age, na.rm = TRUE)  # Calculate mean
age_median <- median(data_clean$Age, na.rm = TRUE)  # Calculate median

# Create histogram with reference lines
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = age_mean), color = "red", 
             linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +  # Add mean line
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = age_median), color = "darkgreen", 
             linetype = "solid", size = 1) +  # Add median line
  annotate("text", x = age_mean + 5, y = 15, 
           label = paste("Mean =", round(age_mean, 1)), 
           color = "red", family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Label mean
  annotate("text", x = age_median - 5, y = 15, 
           label = paste("Median =", round(age_median, 1)), 
           color = "darkgreen", family = "serif", size = 4) +  # Label median
  labs(title = "Age Distribution with Mean and Median",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))

       x = "Body Mass Index (BMI)", y = "Density") +

Scatter Plot - Code
⚫ Goal: Correlation between two continuous variables


Code
# Create scatter plot showing BMI vs. Cholesterol relationship
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = BMI, y = Cholesterol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "darkblue", size = 3) +  # Add semi-transparent points
  labs(title = "Relationship between BMI and Cholesterol",
       x = "Body Mass Index (BMI)", y = "Cholesterol (mg/dL)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
How to Read Scatter Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Points are scattered over the whole plot - No linear pattern (correlation r = 0.00, p = 0.97) - BMI ranges from 11.4 to 37.3; cholesterol from 151 to 299 mg/dL - A few BMI values below 15 sit far to the left
INTERPRETATION: - No association between BMI and cholesterol in this sample - BMI values below 15 are implausible for adults: check them before any analysis
IMPLICATIONS: - BMI alone does not predict cholesterol here - Other factors (diet, genetics, medication) are likely to matter - A scatter plot is the first data-quality check, not only a picture of association

                     name = "Treatment Group") +  # Custom colors

       x = "Age (years)", 
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +

Continuous Plots - Summary

When to Use

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Common Distribution Shapes


Normal (Bell Curve) - Symmetric around mean - Mean ≈ Median - Example: Heights
Right Skewed - Long tail to the right - Mean > Median
- Example: Income
Left Skewed - Long tail to the left - Mean < Median - Example: Age at retirement

Bimodal - Two peaks - Two distinct groups - Example: Customer segments
Uniform - Flat distribution - All values equally likely - Example: Random numbers
Outliers - Extreme values - Check for data errors - May need special handling

title: Continuous Plots - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Choose bins wisely - test different values for histograms
Density vs. Histogram - density better for comparing groups
Scatter plots reveal relationships - but don’t assume causation
Alpha transparency - helps see overlapping points
Always handle missing data - document your approach

Common Mistakes:

Too many/few histogram bins
Not handling outliers
Assuming correlation = causation
Ignoring data transformations when needed
Poor color choices for scatter plot groups

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
What is Time Series Data?


Definition:
Data points indexed by time or ordered sequence

Observations at regular intervals
Temporal ordering matters
Shows change over time
Can reveal trends and patterns


Examples in Our Dataset:

Blood Pressure at 0, 3, 6 months
Patient measurements over time
Baseline dates
Treatment progression
Longitudinal health outcomes

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Analytical Goals for Time Series

What questions can we answer?

🔵 Evolution - How does it change over time?
🟡 Distribution - What’s the pattern across time periods?
🟢 Ranking - Which time period is highest/lowest?

Charts we’ll learn:

Simple Line Chart
Multiple Line Chart (comparing groups)
Line Chart with Points

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Setup: Load and Prepare Data


Code
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)      # For data reshaping

# Load the dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")

# Reshape data from wide to long format for time series plotting
# Convert columns SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m to rows
bp_long <- data %>%
  select(PatientID, TreatmentGroup, SysBP_0m, SysBP_3m, SysBP_6m) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("SysBP"),
               names_to = "TimePoint",
               values_to = "SysBP") %>%  # Convert to long format
  mutate(Month = case_when(TimePoint == "SysBP_0m" ~ 0,
                           TimePoint == "SysBP_3m" ~ 3,
                           TimePoint == "SysBP_6m" ~ 6))  # Extract month number

# Preview the transformed data
head(bp_long)

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Simple Line Chart - Code
🔵 Goal: Show evolution over time (aggregate)


Code
# Calculate mean systolic BP at each time point
mean_bp <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE))  # Average across all patients

# Create line chart showing trend over time
ggplot(mean_bp, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +  # Draw line
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 4) +  # Add points at each time point
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +  # Show all time points on x-axis
  labs(title = "Mean Systolic Blood Pressure Over 6 Months",
       x = "Month", 
       y = "Mean Systolic BP (mmHg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10))

title: Time Series - BASIC
text: Simple Line Chart - Plot

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
How to Read Line Charts
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Baseline (Month 0): mean systolic BP 135.1 mmHg - Month 3: 132.2 mmHg (2.9 mmHg lower) - Month 6: 130.4 mmHg (another 1.8 mmHg lower) - Steady downward trend, no rebound
INTERPRETATION: - Mean blood pressure fell by about 5 mmHg over six months - This line mixes both groups: it cannot say whether the intervention caused the fall
IMPLICATIONS: - Plot the groups separately (next slide): the Control mean stays at about 136 mmHg, the Intervention mean falls from 134 to 125 mmHg - An overall mean can hide that only one group changed - A change over time is not a treatment effect without a comparison group
ACTIONS: - Always show a line per group in a trial - Add error bars or confidence intervals before drawing conclusions

title: Time Series - BASIC
text:
Multiple Line Chart - Code
🔵 Goal: Compare evolution across groups


Code
# Calculate mean BP by treatment group and time
mean_bp_group <- bp_long %>%
  group_by(Month, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  summarise(Mean_SysBP = mean(SysBP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Create line chart with separate lines for each group
ggplot(mean_bp_group, aes(x = Month, y = Mean_SysBP, 
                          color = TreatmentGroup, group = TreatmentGroup)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.5) +  # Draw lines
  geom_point(size = 4) +  # Add points

title: Time Series - BASIC

Key Time Series Concepts


Trend: - Overall direction (up, down, flat) - Long-term pattern - Calculate: moving average, regression
Seasonality: - Regular periodic fluctuations - Daily, weekly, monthly patterns - Example: Higher BP in winter
Volatility: - Amount of variation - High = unstable, Low = stable - Measure: standard deviation

Data Preparation: - Wide format: One column per time point - Long format: One row per observation - Use pivot_longer() to convert
Best Practices: - Always show all time points - Use consistent time intervals - Label axes clearly with units - Consider adding reference lines - Show confidence intervals when relevant

Connect the dots - use geom_line() to show continuity

Show uncertainty - confidence intervals add credibility
Wide to long format - essential for time series plotting

Common Mistakes:

Not connecting points (scatter instead of line)
Too many lines (>5 becomes cluttered)
Inconsistent time intervals without noting
Missing baseline comparisons
Not handling missing time points

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Reading Lollipop and Dot Plots
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - North region: widest column (33% of patients); East narrowest (20%) - Treatment share differs by region: Intervention 68% in East, 47% in North, 38% in South, 51% in West - The horizontal edges do not line up across columns - Chi-square test of Region × Treatment: p ≈ 0.05 (borderline)
INTERPRETATION: - Width of columns: regional sample sizes (North > South ≈ West > East) - Height within columns: treatment allocation within each region - Misaligned edges: allocation was not the same in every region - If this were a trial, region would need to be checked as a possible imbalance
IMPLICATIONS: - Report allocation by region, not only overall - Consider adjusting for region in the analysis - A mosaic shows this at a glance; a single overall percentage would hide it
Reading Mosaic Tips: - Misaligned tiles = association exists - Aligned tiles = independence (no association) - Area, not just height, represents proportion - Compare conditional distributions (within columns)

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Complex Mosaic - Code
🔴 Goal: Multi-way categorical analysis


Code
# Three-way mosaic drawn as rectangles (a mosaic is just rectangles):
# width = patients in each Gender : Treatment column, height = smoking shares
tiles <- data_clean %>%
  filter(Gender %in% c("Male", "Female")) %>%
  count(Gender, TreatmentGroup, SmokingStatus) %>%
  mutate(column = paste(Gender, TreatmentGroup, sep = " : ")) %>%
  group_by(column) %>%
  mutate(ymax = cumsum(n) / sum(n), ymin = ymax - n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()
cols <- tiles %>% count(column, wt = n, name = "col_n") %>%
  mutate(xmax = cumsum(col_n), xmin = xmax - col_n)
tiles <- left_join(tiles, cols, by = "column")

ggplot(tiles) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                fill = SmokingStatus), colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = (cols$xmin + cols$xmax) / 2, labels = cols$column) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Current smoker" = "#E74C3C",
                                "Former smoker" = "#F39C12",
                                "Non-smoker" = "#27AE60"),
                    name = "Smoking Status") +
  labs(title = "Smoking Status by Gender and Treatment Group",
       x = "Gender : Treatment Group (width = number of patients)", y = "Proportion") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 15, face = "bold"))

title: Categorical Plots - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Key Takeaways

When to use each: - Lollipop > Bar: When you have many categories or want cleaner look - Cleveland Dot: Perfect for before/after or male/female comparisons
- Mosaic: Test if two categorical variables are independent - Radial: Use sparingly (harder to read), good for presentations
Pro Tips: - fct_reorder() from forcats package is essential for proper ordering - Mosaic aligned tiles = independent, misaligned = associated - Remove gridlines for cleaner lollipop charts - Always label mosaic plot axes clearly (area = proportion!)
Common Mistakes: - Using radial charts for data without circular nature - Too many categories in mosaic plots (>12 becomes unreadable) - Not ordering lollipop charts by value - Misinterpreting mosaic plots (height alone doesn’t show proportion)

Raincloud Plot - Code

Purpose: Comprehensive view - combines violin + points + box
Goal: 🟡 Distribution (most complete visualization)


Code
# Create raincloud plot: Blood Pressure by Treatment Group
library(ggdist)  # For stat_halfeye

health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(SysBP_6m)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = TreatmentGroup, y = SysBP_6m, fill = TreatmentGroup)) +
  # Half violin (cloud)
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0, 
               justification = -0.2, point_colour = NA) +
  # Box plot
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5,
               position = position_nudge(x = -0.1)) +
  # Individual points (rain)
  geom_point(aes(color = TreatmentGroup), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.3,
             position = position_jitter(seed = 1, width = 0.05,
                                       height = 0)) +
  # Add mean point
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, 
               size = 4, color = "black") +
  coord_flip() +  # Flip to horizontal
  labs(title = "Systolic Blood Pressure at 6 Months by Treatment Group",
       subtitle = "Raincloud plot: density (cloud) + boxplot + points (rain)",
       x = "Treatment Group",
       y = "Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_custom() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Enhanced Grouped Bar Chart - Code

Purpose: Compare means across two categorical variables
Goal: 🟢 Ranking + ⚫ Correlation


Code
# Calculate summary statistics
summary_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Gender), !is.na(ExerciseFreq), !is.na(BMI)) %>%
  group_by(Gender, ExerciseFreq) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_bmi = sd(BMI, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(ExerciseFreq = factor(ExerciseFreq,
                              levels = c("Never", "1-2 days/week",
                                       "3-4 days/week", "5-7 days/week")))

# Create grouped bar chart with error bars and sample sizes
ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = ExerciseFreq, y = mean_bmi, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.9), alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_bmi - se_bmi, ymax = mean_bmi + se_bmi),
                position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), 
            position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = -1.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Mean BMI by Exercise Frequency and Gender",
       subtitle = "Error bars show ± 1 SE | Numbers show sample size",
       x = "Exercise Frequency",
       y = "Mean BMI (kg/m²)",
       fill = "Gender") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Male" = "#4DBBD5", "Female" = "#E64B35")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  theme_custom()

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Missing Data Handling

Always check for missing data:


Code
# Check missing data by group
health_data %>%
  group_by(Gender, ExerciseFreq) %>%
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    missing_bmi = sum(is.na(BMI)),
    pct_missing = round(100 * missing_bmi / total, 1)
  )


Options for handling:

Filter complete cases - filter(!is.na(variable))
Show as separate category - useful if missing is informative
Note in subtitle - “Excludes N missing observations”
Investigate patterns - Is missingness related to outcome?

text:
What We’ll Learn - Intermediate


Visualizing Relationships:

Network diagrams (nodes & edges)
Sankey diagrams (flow)
Chord diagrams (circular relationships)
Alluvial plots (categorical flows)
Correlation networks


Analytical Goals:

🔴 Flow - Movement between states
⚫ Correlation - Strength of relationships
🟢 Ranking - Most connected nodes
🟡 Distribution - Network properties

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Setup Code


Code
# Load required packages
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(igraph)      # For network analysis
library(ggraph)      # For network visualization
library(networkD3)   # For Sankey diagrams
library(circlize)    # For chord diagrams

# Load datasets
health_data <- read_excel("../../data/PublicHealth_BP_Dataset.xlsx")
network_data <- read_excel("../../data/Healthcare_Network_Dataset.xlsx", sheet = 2)

# Create custom theme
theme_custom <- function() {
  theme_void() +  # Clean background for networks
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
}

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Network Diagram Basics - Code

Purpose: Show relationships between entities (nodes)
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + 🟢 Ranking


Code
# Prepare network data (patient referrals between providers)
edges <- network_data %>%
  select(from = FromProvider, to = ToProvider, 
           weight = NumReferrals) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from), !is.na(to), weight > 0)

# Create network graph object
network_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)

# Calculate node importance (degree centrality)
V(network_graph)$degree <- degree(network_graph)
V(network_graph)$betweenness <- betweenness(network_graph)

# Plot network
ggraph(network_graph, layout = "fr") +  # Fruchterman-Reingold layout
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight, alpha = weight),
                arrow = arrow(length = unit(3, "mm")),
                end_cap = circle(3, "mm"),
                color = "gray60") +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, color = degree)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3)) +
  scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8)) +
  scale_size(range = c(3, 10)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  labs(title = "Healthcare Provider Referral Network",
       subtitle = "Node size = number of connections | Arrow width = referral volume",
       size = "Connections",
       color = "Connections") +
  theme_custom()

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Interpreting Network Diagrams


Network Metrics:

Node size - Degree centrality (connections)
Node color - Importance measure
Edge width - Connection strength
Edge direction - Flow direction

Key Nodes:

Hubs - Many connections (large nodes)
Bridges - Connect clusters
Periphery - Few connections


Our Network:

Central hubs identified

Key providers with most referrals

Clusters visible

Groups of closely connected providers
Possible subspecialty groups

Isolated providers exist

May need better integration

Referral patterns show hierarchy

Primary care → specialists
Direction matters

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Sankey Diagram - Code

Purpose: Show flow quantities between stages
Goal: 🔴 Flow + 🔴 Part of Whole


Code
# Prepare flow data: Patient journey through treatment
# Stage 1: Initial Assessment → Stage 2: Treatment Selection → Stage 3: Outcome

# Create flow data
flow_data <- health_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(TreatmentGroup), !is.na(Adherence_Status)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup, Adherence_Status, name = "count") %>%
  # Rename for Sankey format
  rename(source = TreatmentGroup, target = Adherence_Status, value = count)

# Prepare nodes and links for networkD3
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = unique(c(as.character(flow_data$source), 
                 as.character(flow_data$target)))
)

# Create links with node indices
flow_data$IDsource <- match(flow_data$source, nodes$name) - 1  # 0-indexed
flow_data$IDtarget <- match(flow_data$target, nodes$name) - 1

# Create Sankey diagram
sankeyNetwork(
  Links = flow_data,
  Nodes = nodes,
  Source = "IDsource",
  Target = "IDtarget",
  Value = "value",
  NodeID = "name",
  units = "patients",
  fontSize = 14,
  nodeWidth = 30,
  sinksRight = FALSE,  # Align target nodes to left
  colourScale = JS('d3.scaleOrdinal().domain(["Treatment A", "Treatment B", "Control", "High", "Low"]).range(["#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#FF7F00", "#984EA3"])')
)


Note: This creates an interactive HTML widget

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Sankey Diagram - Interpretation

Reading Sankey Diagrams:

Width of flow = Quantity

Wider flows = more patients

Color helps track paths

Each treatment group has its own color

Convergence/Divergence shows patterns

Where do patients end up?
Which paths are most common?


Our Findings:

Treatment A & B show higher adherence

Larger flows to “High” adherence

Control group has lower adherence

More patients in “Low” adherence

Visual proportions immediately show treatment effectiveness

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Alluvial Plot - Code

Purpose: Show changes in categorical composition over time
Goal: 🔴 Flow + 🟡 Distribution


Code
library(ggalluvial)

# Prepare data: Smoking status changes over study
alluvial_data <- health_data %>%
  select(PatientID, SmokingStatus, Gender, TreatmentGroup) %>%
  filter(!is.na(SmokingStatus), !is.na(Gender), !is.na(TreatmentGroup)) %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup, SmokingStatus, Gender)

# Create alluvial plot
ggplot(alluvial_data,
       aes(y = n, axis1 = TreatmentGroup, axis2 = SmokingStatus, 
           axis3 = Gender)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = SmokingStatus), width = 1/12, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_stratum(width = 1/12, fill = "gray90", color = "black") +
  geom_label(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum)), size = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Treatment", "Smoking", "Gender"),
                   expand = c(0.05, 0.05)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Never" = "#00A087", 
                              "Former" = "#3C5488",
                              "Current" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Patient Flow: Treatment → Smoking Status → Gender",
       subtitle = "Stream width shows number of patients in each pathway",
       y = "Number of Patients",
       fill = "Smoking Status") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Chord Diagram - Code

Purpose: Show relationships between categories in circular layout
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + 🔴 Flow


Code
# Prepare chord data: Comorbidity co-occurrence
# Simplified: Which regions refer to which treatment groups most

chord_data <- network_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(PatientRegion), !is.na(TreatmentAssigned)) %>%
  count(PatientRegion, TreatmentAssigned, name = "count") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = TreatmentAssigned, 
              values_from = count, 
              values_fill = 0)

# Convert to matrix
chord_matrix <- as.matrix(chord_data[, -1])
rownames(chord_matrix) <- chord_data$PatientRegion

# Create chord diagram
circos.clear()
circos.par(start.degree = 90, gap.degree = 4)

chordDiagram(
  chord_matrix,
  grid.col = c("North" = "#E41A1C", "South" = "#377EB8", 
               "East" = "#4DAF4A", "West" = "#984EA3",
               "Treatment A" = "#FF7F00", "Treatment B" = "#FFFF33", 
               "Control" = "#A65628"),
  transparency = 0.5,
  directional = 1,
  direction.type = c("arrows", "diffHeight"),
  diffHeight = -0.04,
  annotationTrack = "grid",
  annotationTrackHeight = c(0.05, 0.1),
  link.arr.type = "big.arrow",
  link.sort = TRUE,
  link.largest.ontop = TRUE
)

# Add labels
circos.trackPlotRegion(
  track.index = 1,
  bg.border = NA,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    sector.index = get.cell.meta.data("sector.index")
    circos.text(CELL_META$xcenter, CELL_META$ylim[1], sector.index,
               facing = "clockwise", niceFacing = TRUE, adj = c(0, 0.5))
  }
)

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Chord Diagram - Interpretation

Reading Chord Diagrams:

Arcs represent categories

Arc width = total connections

Ribbons show connections

Ribbon width = flow strength
Color indicates source

Circular layout saves space

Shows all connections simultaneously


Our Pattern:

East region sends most patients to Treatment A
North region more balanced across treatments
West region has more Control assignments
Treatment allocation varies by region (interesting!)

When to use: Many-to-many relationships, limited space

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Correlation Network - Code

Purpose: Visualize correlation patterns as network
Goal: ⚫ Correlation + clustering


Code
# Calculate correlations among numeric health metrics
cor_data <- health_data %>%
  select(Age, BMI_0m, SysBP_0m, DiaBP_0m, 
         Cholesterol_0m, BloodSugar_0m) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

# Convert to network (only strong correlations)
cor_network <- cor_data %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(from = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -from, names_to = "to", values_to = "correlation") %>%
  filter(from != to, abs(correlation) > 0.3) %>%  # Threshold
  mutate(abs_cor = abs(correlation))

# Create graph
cor_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(cor_network, directed = FALSE)
E(cor_graph)$weight <- cor_network$abs_cor
E(cor_graph)$cor_sign <- ifelse(cor_network$correlation > 0, "Positive", "Negative")

# Plot
ggraph(cor_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = abs_cor, color = cor_sign), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_node_point(size = 10, color = "#4DBBD5") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 3.5, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(1, 4)) +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = c("Positive" = "#00A087", "Negative" = "#DC0000")) +
  labs(title = "Health Metrics Correlation Network",
       subtitle = "Edge width = correlation strength | Color = positive/negative",
       edge_color = "Correlation",
       edge_width = "Strength") +
  theme_custom()

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Common Mistakes


Too many nodes/edges

Solution: Filter to top connections, increase threshold

Poor layout choice

Solution: Try different layouts (fr, kk, circle, tree)

Unreadable labels

Solution: Use repel = TRUE, adjust size, or interactive plots

Ignoring direction in networks

Solution: Use arrows for directed graphs

Color overload in complex diagrams

Solution: Limit to 2-3 colors, use grayscale for edges

Not showing flow magnitude clearly

Solution: Vary width, transparency, or both

title: Relational/Flow - INTERMEDIATE
text:
Interactive Networks

Benefits of Interactive Plots:


Code
library(visNetwork)

# Prepare data for interactive network
nodes_df <- data.frame(
  id = V(network_graph)$name,
  label = V(network_graph)$name,
  value = V(network_graph)$degree,  # Size by degree
  title = paste0(V(network_graph)$name, "<br>",
                "Connections: ", V(network_graph)$degree)  # Tooltip
)

edges_df <- as_data_frame(network_graph) %>%
  rename(from = from, to = to) %>%
  mutate(value = weight,  # Width by weight
         title = paste0("Referrals: ", weight))  # Tooltip

# Create interactive network
visNetwork(nodes_df, edges_df) %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE, nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE)


Features: Hover tooltips, zoom, drag nodes, highlight neighbors

title: Cleaning Messy Data
text:
Real data arrive with inconsistent labels, text in number columns, duplicates and impossible values. Cleaning is not glamorous, but every later result depends on it. This page gives a checklist you can reuse, on a deliberately messy file: data/ncd_messy.csv (313 rows from a field survey).

library(tidyverse); library(janitor)
raw <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_messy.csv", "data/ncd_messy.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_messy.csv", "data/ncd_messy.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE)




Never edit the raw file. Write a script that reads it and produces a clean copy; the script is your audit trail.
Inspect before you change anything: glimpse(), summary(), count() of every categorical column, range() of every number.
Change one problem at a time and re-check after each change.
Write down what you changed and how many rows it affected.


glimpse(raw)

Rows: 313
Columns: 9
$ `Pt ID`      <dbl> 249, 288, 67, 226, 201, 132, 10, 244, 176, 1, 47, 291, 11…
$ `Age (yrs)`  <chr> "55", "48", "45", "41", "49", "45", "61", "37", "45", "42…
$ SEX          <chr> "Female", "Male", "male", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Fema…
$ Residence    <chr> "Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Urban", "Rural", "Rural", "Ru…
$ BMI          <dbl> 24.0, 24.3, 22.1, 21.5, 25.2, 27.5, 28.3, 21.9, 23.0, 26.…
$ `Salt g/day` <chr> "11.7 g", "7.7", "8.5", "9.7", "8.4", "4.1", "10.8", "6.6…

What the glimpse already shows: awkward names (Pt ID, Age (yrs)), Age (yrs) and Salt g/day are text (some values are not plain numbers), and 313 rows although 300 people were surveyed.




d <- raw |> clean_names()

R - Language

A powerful language for statistical computing and graphics

Widely used by statisticians, data scientists, and researchers

RStudio: User Interface

Extensive libraries for data analysis and visualization

Active community support

Cross-platform compatibility (Windows, MacOS, Linux)

Integration with Python and C++

Free and open-source

Comprehensive statistical analysis tools

Advanced graphics capabilities with ggplot2

Rich ecosystem of packages (dplyr, tidyr)

Interactive and reproducible research with RMarkdown or Quarto

R vs Python


R

Designed for statistical analysis and visualization

Rich ecosystem: dplyr, ggplot2, caret

Preferred in academia and research



Python

General-purpose language

Strong in data science and ML: pandas, scikit-learn, TensorFlow

Versatile for web, automation, and more

title: Introduction to R
text:
Project: why not setwd()?

A Project (.Rproj) makes its own folder the working directory every time you open it
Paths are then relative to the project: read_csv("data/ncd_survey.csv") works on any computer
setwd("C:/Users/Asha/Desktop") only works on one machine, and breaks when you share the script
Keep raw data in data/, write all steps in a script (not only the console), and never overwrite the raw file
