title: Introduction to R
text:
New File — Core R Authoring

R Script — plain R code file for scripts and functions
R Notebook — interactive notebook with code, output, and narrative
R Markdown — reproducible reports combining R and text
Quarto Document — modern multi-language document format for reports
Quarto Presentation — slide decks built from Quarto content

title: Introduction to R
text:
New File — Documentation & Static Content

R HTML — HTML pages generated from R code and content
R Documentation — help files for packages and functions
Text File — plain text for notes, configs, or simple drafts

title: Introduction to R
text:
New File — Other Languages & Tools

Python Script — Python code file for reticulate and Python work
C++ File — C++ source for Rcpp or performance-critical code
SQL Script — SQL queries and database interactions
Stan File — Stan model code for Bayesian modeling
D3 Script — D3 JavaScript visualizations
R Sweave — LaTeX+R documents for PDF reporting
Shiny Web App — interactive apps built with Shiny
Plumber API — R APIs exposed as web services

title: Introduction to R
text:
Variables and Data Types

Numeric — numbers such as 3.14, 42
Integer — whole numbers with L suffix, e.g. 5L
Character — text values like "data"
Logical — TRUE or FALSE
Factor — categorical values with levels
Complex — numbers with imaginary parts like 1 + 2i



Show the code
x <- 5          # numeric
name <- "Alice" # character
flag <- TRUE    # logical
colors <- factor(c("red", "blue", "green"))



Variables store values in memory and can be reused later
R is dynamically typed: type depends on the stored value

title: Introduction to R
text:
Vectors and Sequences

Create ordered collections with c() and sequences with seq()
Useful for numeric data, indexes, and repeated values



Show the code
ages <- c(23, 35, 28)
seq(1, 100, 3)
seq(1, 2, length.out = 10)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Factors and Categorical Variables

Store categories or groups with fixed levels
Important for statistical modeling and reporting
Use factor() to make discrete labels or ordered categories



Show the code
gender <- factor(c("Male", "Female", "Male", "Female"),
                 levels = c("Male", "Female"))
physical_activity <- factor(sample(c(1, 2), 10, replace = TRUE),
                            levels = c(1, 2),
                            labels = c("Yes", "No"))

title: Introduction to R
section: Factor levels and the reference level
text:
Factor levels and the reference level


Show the code
res <- factor(c("Urban", "Rural", "Urban"))
levels(res)        # sorted alphabetically by default: "Rural" "Urban"


[1] "Rural" "Urban"



Unless you set levels = yourself, R sorts levels alphabetically; the first level is the reference in models
Choose it deliberately: factor(x, levels = c("Urban", "Rural"))
Text in quotes is a character, not a number: mean(c("45", "52")) fails. Convert with as.numeric()

title: Introduction to R
text:
Missing values spread


Show the code
wt <- c(60, 72, NA, 58)
mean(wt)                  # NA: one unknown value makes the mean unknown


[1] NA


Show the code
mean(wt, na.rm = TRUE)    # drop the missing value for this calculation (and report it)


[1] 63.33333

title: Introduction to R
text:
Lists and Matrices


Lists

Store mixed types in one object
Can contain vectors, data frames, functions, or other lists
Good for nested results and complex outputs



Show the code
my_list <- list(name = "Alice", score = 95, data = c(1, 2, 3))



Matrices

Two-dimensional arrays with a single data type
Ideal for numeric calculations, matrices, and linear algebra
Built from vectors using matrix(), cbind(), or rbind()



Show the code
m <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data Structures

Data frames are the most common table structure in R
They combine columns of equal length and can contain different types
Lists and matrices are also important foundational structures



Show the code
my_data <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva"),
  Age = sample(20:50, 5, replace = TRUE)
)

title: Merging Datasets
text:
This module explains how to combine datasets by rows, columns, and with joins.



data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), Age = c(23, 35, 28))
data2 <- data.frame(ID = 4:6, Name = c("David", "Eva", "Frank"), Age = c(45, 30, 40))
merged_rows <- rbind(data1, data2)
merged_rows

  ID    Name Age
1  1   Alice  23
2  2     Bob  35
3  3 Charlie  28
4  4   David  45
5  5     Eva  30
6  6   Frank  40






data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"))
data2 <- data.frame(Age = c(23, 35, 28), Height = c(165, 180, 175))
merged_columns <- cbind(data1, data2)
merged_columns

  ID    Name Age Height
1  1   Alice  23    165
2  2     Bob  35    180
3  3 Charlie  28    175






library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

data1 <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva")
)
data2 <- data.frame(
  ID = c(2, 3, 5, 6),
  Score = c(85, 90, 88, 92)
)

inner_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88

left_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88

right_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88
4  6    <NA>    92

full_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88
6  6    <NA>    92


These join types are useful for combining medical records, survey forms, and measurement datasets.



bind_rows() (dplyr) does the same job as rbind(): tables with the same columns, different people.

library(dplyr)
round1 <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(120, 135, 142))
round2 <- data.frame(id = 4:6, sbp = c(128, 150, 118))
bind_rows(round1, round2)

  id sbp
1  1 120
2  2 135
3  3 142
4  4 128
5  5 150
6  6 118





cbind() pastes by position and never checks who is who. If the two tables are sorted differently, the columns are silently mixed up. Join by a key such as id instead.




patients <- data.frame(id = 1:5, name = c("Asha", "Bina", "Chetan", "Dev", "Esha"))
labs     <- data.frame(id = c(3, 3, 5), hba1c = c(7.1, 6.8, 8.0))   # id 3 was tested twice
nrow(patients)

[1] 5

nrow(left_join(patients, labs, by = "id"))   # 6: patient 3 appears twice

[1] 6

count(labs, id)                                # check the key before joining

  id n
1  3 2
2  5 1


A left join keeps every patient, but a patient who matches two lab rows appears twice. Count rows before and after every join, and check that the key is unique in the table you join to.



The same blood pressures can be stored wide (one row per person, one column per measurement) or long (one row per person and measurement). ggplot2 and most models want long data.

library(tidyr)
wide <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(128, 142, 135), dbp = c(82, 90, 85))
long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(sbp, dbp), names_to = "measure", values_to = "mmHg")
long

# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id measure  mmHg

title: Merging Datasets
text: cbind() pastes by position and never checks who is who. If the two tables are sorted differently, the columns are silently mixed up. Join by a key such as id instead.

title: Merging Datasets
text:
patients <- data.frame(id = 1:5, name = c("Asha", "Bina", "Chetan", "Dev", "Esha"))
labs     <- data.frame(id = c(3, 3, 5), hba1c = c(7.1, 6.8, 8.0))   # id 3 was tested twice
nrow(patients)

[1] 5

nrow(left_join(patients, labs, by = "id"))   # 6: patient 3 appears twice

[1] 6

count(labs, id)                                # check the key before joining

  id n
1  3 2
2  5 1


A left join keeps every patient, but a patient who matches two lab rows appears twice. Count rows before and after every join, and check that the key is unique in the table you join to.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
One plot type rarely tells the whole story. Merged visuals layer two views of the same data so the reader sees, for example, the shape of a distribution and every individual value. Three ways to merge:
The rule for every merged plot: each layer must answer a question the other cannot. If a layer only decorates, drop it.
library(tidyverse); library(patchwork); library(ggridges); library(ggside)
ncd <- read_csv("../data/ncd_survey.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high")),
         htn = factor(htn, 0:1, c("No hypertension", "Hypertension")))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Categorical: bar chart + labels

edu <- ncd |> count(education) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n))
ggplot(edu, aes(x = fct_reorder(education, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3498db") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " (", scales::percent(pct, 1), ")")), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = "Education", y = "Adults", title = "Education of the 600 adults") +
  expand_limits(y = max(edu$n) * 1.1)








The labels give the exact numbers, the bars the comparison. Missing education (NA) stays visible as its own bar.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Continuous: histogram + density

ggplot(ncd, aes(x = sbp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 5, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 140, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Density", title = "Systolic BP: bins and a smooth curve")








after_stat(density) puts the histogram on the density scale, so both layers share the y-axis. The dashed line marks the hypertension threshold.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Continuous by group: ridgelines

ggplot(ncd, aes(x = sbp, y = phys_act, fill = phys_act)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7, quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Physical activity", title = "Distributions side by side, medians marked")








Ridgelines compare many distributions in little space; quantile_lines adds the median of each.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Category vs category: grouped bars + facets
text:
Category vs category: grouped bars + facets

ncd |> count(residence, tobacco, htn) |>
  group_by(residence, tobacco) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |> ungroup() |>
  filter(htn == "Hypertension") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tobacco, y = pct, fill = tobacco)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct, 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ residence) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(No = "grey60", Yes = "#e74c3c"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Tobacco use", y = "Adults with hypertension", title = "Hypertension by tobacco use, within residence")








The facets hold residence fixed, so each panel compares tobacco users with non-users in the same setting.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Continuous vs continuous: scatter + marginal histograms
text:
Continuous vs continuous: scatter + marginal histograms

ggplot(ncd, aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#e74c3c") +
  geom_xsidehistogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey70") +
  geom_ysidehistogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "grey70") +
  theme(ggside.panel.scale = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "The relationship and each variable's distribution")








The margins show that BMI is roughly symmetric and SBP slightly right-skewed: information the cloud of points hides.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Bubble chart + trend line

villages <- ncd |> group_by(village) |>
  summarise(bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), sbp = mean(sbp), n = n())
ggplot(villages, aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.5, colour = "#2c3e50") +
  geom_smooth(aes(weight = n), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Village mean BMI", y = "Village mean systolic BP", size = "Adults", title = "Villages: means, sizes and a weighted trend")








Each bubble is a village, not a person: a trend between village means is an ecological association and need not hold for individuals.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Category vs continuous: box + points, violin + box
text:
Category vs continuous: box + points, violin + box

p1 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.25) +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", title = "Box + every adult")
p2 <- ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(x = "Physical activity", y = NULL, title = "Violin + box")
p1 + p2








Points show how many people stand behind each box; a violin shows the shape. outlier.shape = NA avoids drawing outliers twice.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Time series: line + area

dengue <- read_csv("../data/dengue_wards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  group_by(year, month) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain = mean(rain_mm), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", year, month)))
k <- max(dengue$cases) / max(dengue$rain)          # put rain on the cases scale
ggplot(dengue, aes(date)) +
  geom_area(aes(y = rain * k), fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cases), colour = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous("Dengue cases (all wards)", sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / k, name = "Mean rainfall (mm)")) +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "Cases follow the rains by about a month")








A second axis is acceptable only when both series are clearly labelled and the scaling is stated; otherwise use two panels.

title: Merged Visuals
section: Map: choropleth + bubbles, with an inset zoom
text:
Map: choropleth + bubbles, with an inset zoom

library(sf)
blocks <- st_read("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
centres <- st_centroid(blocks)
main <- ggplot(blocks) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = centres, aes(size = dengue_cases), shape = 21, fill = NA, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "OrRd", direction = 1, name = "Per 100,000") +
  labs(size = "Cases", title = "Rate (colour) and count (circle) together") +
  theme_void()
box <- st_bbox(blocks); zoom <- c(xmin = box[["xmax"]] - (box[["xmax"]] - box[["xmin"]]) / 3, ymax = box[["ymin"]] + (box[["ymax"]] - box[["ymin"]]) / 3)
inset <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "OrRd", direction = 1, guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(zoom[["xmin"]], box[["xmax"]]), ylim = c(box[["ymin"]], zoom[["ymax"]])) +
  theme_void() + theme(panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA))
main <- main + annotate("rect", xmin = zoom[["xmin"]], xmax = box[["xmax"]], ymin = box[["ymin"]], ymax = zoom[["ymax"]],
                        fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8)            # where the zoom comes from
main + (inset + labs(title = "Zoom: south-east")) + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1))








Colour shows the rate (fair comparison between blocks of different size); circles show the count (where the work is). The second panel enlarges the south-east corner (the rectangle), where the high rates cluster.

title: Merged Visuals
text:
Checklist








Merge
When it helps
Watch out




Labels on bars
exact values matter
clutter with many bars


Histogram + density
shape and counts
density on the same scale (after_stat(density))


Points over boxes
small groups, show the n
overplotting: jitter, transparency


Marginal histograms
distributions of x and y
keep the margins small


Second y-axis
two series, same time
label both axes; often two panels are clearer


Inset or zoom panel
a detail within the whole
mark where the zoom comes from
